text:
Good Quality Heater- Not as good as I was hoping. When my two 21 year old ceramic heaters started showing signs of failing I started hunting for new ones. After a long and arduous search I decided to give this one a try. I am very glad I did. We have a living room that is about 400 sq ft. that opens to both a sun room and the kitchen, about 900 sq ft total. This heater was able to keep the entire area in the upper 60s when it was below freezing outside, no sunshine. It took 1 hour to heat this area from 58 to 68. I do believe if this was utilized in a closed area of 400 to 500 sq ft., it would be more than adequate.

The construction is pure and simple. It uses a small blower similar to what is used in your furnace to distribute the heat. It is much quieter than fan driven heaters, has a higher cfm (cubic feet per minute) output and the delivery of the heat is very warm, and "softer" than fan driven models. It tends to make a sizable area around it feel cozy as best as I can describe it. When plugged in and turned on high it doesn't seem to have any more loading on the circuit than a standard hair dryer. It is much more efficient in producing and distributing 1500W worth of heating than anything I've ever seen.

The unit does remain cool to the touch except one small area above the heater core on top where you might describe it as barely warm. The filter on the back is basically a hair screen, not a dust filter. The power cord is 6 foot long, adequately sized, with a standard 3 prong outlet connection. The casters are adequate for hard flooring, not carpet. But the unit itself does not feel like it is over 20 lbs. to me. The remote is cute.

I'll be curious to see the electric bill. We are now successfully using this one 1500W heater to warm the same area it required two 1500W ceramics to heat previously. My only last concern would be with longevity. With a 3 year warranty I expect with normal care and maintenance (cleanings) this heater should be around a long time. I will update if I run into any problems.

UPDATE 2-17-2014: This unit is now failing. It still produces heat on the Lo setting, but produces much less on the Hi side then when new. Now the high and low side are producing an equal amount of heat. The unit has been subjected to no rough handling whatsoever. The filter has been cleaned exactly as recommended. I can only conclude that something inside the unit has failed. Considering this unit has a 3 year warranty and has displayed a failure within 4 months is quite irritating. I will be inquiring how much this would cost me to ship it back to the manufacturer for repairs, but no matter what the cost I find failure within this short of a time span pathetic, thus I have revised my rating on this product. With this kind of performance I could NOT RECOMMEND purchasing this product based on longevity.

text:
Would Get Something Else. Bought as a gift. I did not expect it to be so heavy or thick, but it will hold up to vigorous use despite being not as balanced or nimble as my own Japanese knives. Will also take an edge, being VG-10. Good value for the amateur chef....if you can adapt to its weight. I don't think a pro would adapt quickly to a knife like this which is so different from the usual. Its weight makes it harder to use a pinch grip, but the blade isn't tall enough to comfortably use by holding just the handle, as your knuckles will hit the cutting board.

You can probably find better options. This knife would be much better if its spine thickness was reduced to maybe 2.5mm and it was a bit taller. It feels clumsy in hand.

Edit: There is virtually no distal taper on this knife and it tends to wedge on harder ingredients like carrots and squash. The knife steel was also changed to AUS-10 whereas the exact same knife was advertised at VG-10 before. This hints at unscrupulous and dishonest marketing, sorry.

Having used the knife for a prolonged periods at my friend's house, I can now safely say you should skip this purchase. I will need to thin the blade considerably to get it to cut better but it won't be worth it.

text:
Not comfortable, serious ergonomic design flaws, delivered with 2 defects. This is a very tough chair. It easily holds my weight and I do not doubt it could hold more. Unfortunately, this chair is far from comfortable, clearly designed by someone who is neither heavy nor tall.

Problem #1: The seat cushion is too firm and not thick enough, making this not an especially good chair to sit in all day long. I find after an hour or two I am sore and need to stand up and take a break (which I should be doing anyway). I wish the padding was thicker.

Problem #2: the seat fabric is not "grippy" they way it should be on a chair with strong back support. This means when the back support presses against your back (as it should), the result is predictable: you slide forward on the seat. This is *really* uncool. The only way to fix this is to adjust the tension in the back support (how strongly the seat back pushes against your back) to the point where it is no longer supportive. This would be almost manageable if the seat depth were sufficient, which is sadly is not (see next paragraph).

Problem #3: Seat depth. This is by far the biggest issue. The seat depth is listed as adjustable and if you go to the Steelcase site they have videos showing you how to adjust everything. The thing is, the normal seat depth adjustment does not apply to the big and tall version of this chair, which they do not tell you in the product listing. The seat depth adjustment control mechanism is simply ...not there. But wait - it gets better...

As the depth adjustment mechanism is apparently not installed on the big & tall version of this chair, it came with a card attached explaining that to adjust the depth on the seat, the chair has to be flipped over so you can remove the screws holding the seat to the base and reposition it to another of the available pre-drilled hole locations--a very manual process involving lifting up and inverting a 74 lb chair onto a work surface without damaging the arms. Once this feat is accomplished (careful you do not hurt your back; I recommend using use a narrow armless chair to flip it over onto so the arms can hang down over the sides), it becomes apparent there is a serious depth problem. The line of pre-drilled holed only allow you to move the seat cushion backwards, not forwards. This means the seat is adjustable in only one direction: you can make it shallower, not deeper. The seat is attached to the base at the furthest forward setting at the factory--there is nowhere to move it to, except further back, which is not helpful.

Net result: If you are 5"11 or more, and have average-length legs (as do I), the seat depth will be insufficient. Add this to the fact that the fabric is not grippy enough to hold you in place, and yes, you guessed it--you slide forward off the seat, repeatedly, all day long. Even if you adjust the seat cushion angle to tilt rearward to help offset the forward slide, as I have, the lack of depth is still a big problem (and this is not ergonomically sound anyway). I slide forward all day unless I wear pants which generate a lot of friction (forget about wearing dress slacks).

Additionally, and this is a little odd, I think my chair is defective in another way: the line of holes on the bottom of the seat where you screw the base onto the seat is not straight--they are not at a 90-degree angle to the front/rear direction of the seat, and seem to be a couple degrees off to the right. The net result here is the seat cushion is not facing directly forwards, but turned slightly to the right. text:
Not in a month of Sundays. What the packaging fails to say is that it takes this product about a month to make a semi-precious gemstone out of a rough rock. "But", they say, once you get inside to the instruction manual, "it takes Nature thousands of years to achieve this, and you can do it in just 30 days".

IMHO, this is a part of Nature's job description, and she's got countless streams and brooks to do the work. They also get the job done a lot more quietly, and they clean up after themselves.

In this imitation of life, you have to leave the tumbler running for almost a month, stopping only to clean out the gunk, wash the machine and chuck in a new size of grit. The motor only pulls 10 Watts, but the constant noise can be extremely irritating, and the clean-up is very messy.

I don't know about you, but a month is much too long to produce a smooth stone that looks nothing like the fancy stones on the box, especially after enduring the noise, cleaning up the mess and answering ad nauseam the "Is it done yet?' question.

As Jim Croce would have sang, if there were different lyrics for "Time in a Bottle"

If I would shake stones in this tumbler
The first thing that I'd have to do
Is to tumble away
`til the thirty days passes away
Just to see them get smooth

If I could make kids wait forever
To see if their gemstones come through
I'd spend every day with my earplugs and then
Again, I'd go clean out the goo

But there never seems to be enough time
To smooth the rocks you want to shine
Once you find them
I've used the grit enough to know
It oozes out through every hole
As it finds them

If I had a dime for each product
That works as you think it should do
My box would be empty
Except for the memory
Of dimes from 1972

In summary, forget this messy, noisy toy and go for a nature walk instead. It really is better not to mess with Mother Nature.

Amanda Richards, December 30, 2007

text:
Bilt by stoopid enguneers. The basic things I need in a toaster are:
1. Four slice at a time capacity
2. Wide enough slots for bagels or thick slices of bread
3. Cancel button to stop toasting when necessary
4. Cool-touch sides
5. Crumb tray for cleaning
6. Aesthetically pleasing design

This model has all of the above, so I should be ecstatically happy, except:
1. Due to a design oversight, the toasted product doesn't pop up far enough to allow you to remove it without risking burns or serious injury. Forget toasting smaller items like English muffins or waffles that are slightly bent out of shape.
2. The "frozen" feature is designed to evenly brown items like waffles that you use straight out of the freezer. This doesn't work - period. Waffles toast with burned middles and untoasted ends, or vice versa.
3. The bagel feature needs some experimentation with the settings before you get it right. The lower settings don't really do very much, and the higher settings can make charcoal.
4. Due to another design oversight, thin slices of bread or small items can get trapped by the inner grill thingy, causing the food to get jammed in the toaster.

Summary:
If regular machine-sliced bread is all you need to toast, then this toaster will work for you. The "cancel" button is a definite plus, and it fills all the basic needs as above.
For all else - fuggedabouddit.

Amanda Richards, October 7, 2011

I'll put brackets around reviews for the attachments that don't apply to this amazon package but for someone who was wondering about the extra pieces (which you can see here on the QVC website [...]

This vacuum sucks a lot of stuff out of our carpet. With a dog and two cats we have a lot of pet hair around, and every time I'm done vacuuming the canister is full of dirt and hair.

The cord isn't a long or short length. I use a vacuum extension cord anyway, but if I don't then I need to change the outlet once or twice while vacuuming my main floor.

[I use the bare floor attachment for my kitchen. It works okay, but when you run it parallel to the wall, it won't get any dirt or crumbs against the baseboard. Instead, you have run it at a perpendicular angle, so that's a little annoying since I have to often run over the same floor twice in two different directions just to make sure I get all the dirt/crumbs around the edges, and it forces you to slowly make your way down the wall a foot at a time, only as wide as the nozzle. It's irksome to say the least. I think I'll just start sweeping before I vacuum, which is pretty annoying.]

[I haven't used the dry dust mop attachment (microfiber pad) because I haven't had any real use for it when I have the bare floor attachment. The kitchen is high-traffic area and for the amount of crumbs from food and dog food that land on the floor, I'd rather use the bare floor piece rather than the dust mop. If I had a wood floor without as much traffic I might use it, but the rest of my house is carpeted!]

The regular "motorized floor brush nozzle" works well. I have to cut out the hair from the spinning brushes every few uses--it's amazing how much of my own long hair ends up on the carpet (gross, I know). I don't think it gets the edges of my carpet very well either, but I didn't seriously expect it to.

I wish the turbo brush could have somehow been motorized, but it wasn't with my last vacuum either so I didn't really expect it to be. I use it on my carpeted stairs, and it works ok but could definitely work better and more efficiently if it was motorized.

The vacuum is very tippy, [especially with the bare floor attachment. It almost can't stand up on its own with that attachment], so I always lean it up against a wall anytime I need to stop vacuuming (that goes for both floor attachments I use, [but the bare floor one hardly stands up at all without tipping over).]

My biggest issue with this vacuum is the "stretch hose." On the vacuum itself, it is 22" long. When fully extended, it's as long as 65". They want you to detach the floor attachment and use just the handle with stretch hose (with other attachments), OR you can detach the extension wand and use it with a floor attachment (like the dust mop piece in the pictures on QVC, turning the vacuum into a canister vacuum rather than upright).

However, the resistance of the hose is so strong that you can't extend the hose without holding on to the vacuum itself or else the vacuum gets dragged along with you (or tips over at the very least). If I wanted to use the vacuum as a canister vacuum rather than an upright, it'd be nearly impossible to do so since you can't tow the canister along with you. I have the biggest problem while using it on the stairs. I wish I could leave it at the top or the bottom of the stairs and use the handle with the turbo brush, but I can't go more than one step without the vacuum falling over because the resistance is so strong on the hose once you stretch it in the slightest. Instead, I detach the canister from the floor piece and extension wand, and just try to hold it in one hand while using the nozzle handle in my other hand. It's a big pain that I wasn't prepared for with this vacuum.

Overall, I don't think I'd recommend this vacuum just because of the inconveniences I have with it. I'm not very excited that I know I'll be stuck with this vacuum for a least a few years before I can try something else. All of the attachments make you excited about it, but I don't think they make up for the cons. The high ratings really made me think it'd be fantastic, but unfortunately I just don't think it's all that it's worked up to be.

11/7/2012 Edited to Add: I forgot to mention that this thing is a pain to empty. The bin holds very little until it is at is "max full." But if you have any sort of pet hair then it gets all clumped up in the top of the bin instead of the bottom. The bin is shaped so that all the hair/dust/dirt gets caught way up inside it and you have to reach your fingers up to pull it all out. I can't imagine this being possible for anyone with bigger fingers than I have, and my hands are fairly small. Another reason I'm very disappointed with this vacuum. Cannister vacuums are supposed to be easy to empty--just tip the bin upside-down and everything pours out. This vacuum is the opposite of that scenario.

It has a BRIGHT light.. This humidifier is ok for what it is. I used it in Montana and it seemed to be ok for a large room--small or medium would be more effective though. Now I'm in Arizona and I think it's even drier, and I don't think it works as well even in a smaller room, but I'm not 100% sure. It's a fine mid-range humidifier, I think.

Despite the "cool mist" advertisement it's not actually a misting humidifier. You're paying for a fan that sits over water.

It's easy to use, easy to clean, and I don't mind the noise. I prefer a fan sound at night so this does the job of my noisemaker when I use it.

I only have two complaints.

First, I'm annoyed at how expensive the filters have gotten. I used to be able to buy them at Target for like $8 (I've had this humidifier for years), but now I can't find them anywhere so I have to resort to Amazon where they're $12? Geesh. I've switched over to a different brand for filters (Fette Filter, filter A). To make the filters last longer, flip them over every time you add water (I usually did it every other day). I also put one of those Protec humidifier cleaning fish and it keeps the filter and tank clean for longer. Doing those two things, I would clean it about once a month while changing the filter when it got too crusty (maybe every two or three weeks?).

My second complaint is the blue light. It's BRIGHT. It's always on if the machine is on, no matter what. I have rolled up a hand towel and put it in front of the clear water gauge where the light is brightest, but because the machine is a light color it still makes the entire thing glow (and the wall or anything else around it!). I like a dark room at night, and sometimes I just don't have the determination to ignore the glowing blue light in my room so I don't always turn it on.

I've now switched to a BAYKA humidifier that really is a cool mist humidifier and it lets me turn the light completely off while running it. On top of that, I can put essential oils in a sponge ring where the air comes out, though that part isn't that effective like a real oil diffuser. I still like it more than this fan humidifier.

Leaks like a sieve. Update 1 month after purchase: I hadn't used it in a few days because the MOTOR is too loud so I was intending to move it across the room to see if that would help. When I woke up this morning, the humidifier was sitting in a bit puddle of water. When I carried it over to the sink and dumped it out and dried it off with a towel, I could see it was leaking more water out of a hole (or holes) in the bottom of the machine. What's the deal with that? And why did it just start leaking now? It's just dumb luck it didn't get anything else wet besides the metal table it was sitting on. Lucky for me it's within the return window, so I'm returning the humidifier.
----------------
I haven't had this humidifier for very long and so far it's OK. It puts out a lot of mist which is nice. I like how I can turn the blue light completely off, unlike most humidifiers. And I like how I don't have to buy or deal with filters.

The essential oils part--which is a big selling point--is a little useless. I've put up to 5 drops of oils on the sponge ring (the instructions recommend 3 drops) and I still can't detect any oils in the mist. Maybe if I stand right in front of it and blast myself in the face, but even then it's hardly potent enough to smell my oils. Can't say I'm impressed about that.

The only other complaint I have is that the power "button" doesn't work that well. It's less a button and more just a sensor like a touch screen. A poorly performing touch screen. It takes a lot of tries to get it to work so that's pretty annoying.

text:
Not powerful enough, slow, designed badly- not a good product. I bought one of these due to my 18 year old VitaMix unit needing a part that would cost more than this system. I found it for a price more than 1/2 off Amazon's price at a brick and mortar store so I took the plunge.

PROS: It is an elegant looking system with the chrome front on the motor unit. I like having 16 oz. individual smoothie cups that the blade unit attaches to for making single serving smoothies. Cleanup is easy if there are no 'complications' (see CONS).

CONS: This thing simply isn't strong enough to really make a decent smoothie in a short time (350 watts motor). If you are using the 16 oz. cups I would advise only putting about 12 oz. in it or it will bog down. The motor will shut off if it gets to be too much (all the blue lights will flash... after this happens 3-4 times you will have to wait 3-5 minutes before you can use the unit again- who has time for that?!). And most of that better be liquid- this thing cannot handle a lot of ice, fruit or veggies. If you decide to fill one of the cups be prepared to 'steady' the cup as the smoothie is being made while the motor shuts down repeatedly. If you don't 'steady' the cup it will wobble and cause the motor to shut down even quicker- terrible design flaw!

The 32 oz. cup needs the same advise- don't fill it up or you will be making smoothies for about 15 minutes! Pulsing the ingredients in a full container (whether it be the 32 oz. or 16 oz.) before you go full bore at making a smoothie in either container helps but not a lot.

The design of this unit is so poor that any leakage coming out of the 32 oz. container will go right into the motor unit. There is a drain hole in the motor unit to allow for such occurrences yet maybe Cuisinart should design the unit so nothing goes into the motor unit. It would appear that having liquids in that area is not a good thing. It is nearly impossible to get out any liquids that leak into the spinning area of the motor unit.

I have not used the dry items cutting cup... I don't think it will be much better.

BOTTOM LINE: I will use this unit until I get my part for my VitaMix unit. Once I get that part I will only use this for mixing powdered drinks- I cannot see this thing lasting very long making smoothies on a daily basis. Maybe I am spoiled by my VitaMix being able to handle anything thrown at it without shutting down or bogging down. After owning a VitaMix for 18 years (and replacing 3 parts over that time) I would say if you are serious about making great smoothies please spend the money on something similar to the VitaMix and avoid this Cuisinart.

Started wonderfully, now less happy after nearly 2 years.. Update(June 2012): hmm, not happy with it, the non stick became sticky. The coating obviously didn't last long. Decided it would be a waste of time to test the warranty as I don't want the same wok with the same problem. So I now have a ceramic coated wok.

Original review:
Almost a five star. The finish of the wok is truely high class, compared with a lot of the 'non'stick' varieties out there. We have been looking for a decent non-stick wok for almost a year: hunting from william sonoma, china town, crate and barrel and web sites. why this amount of passion? we love cooking with a wok, but our recent wok, a non-stick, and despite the seasoning - it just did not work. With a lot of claims on the non-stick material peeling off and the danger it poses to our health. We finally buckled as the cleaning and the sticking on the non-stick wok was just taking the enjoyment out of cooking. I think you have to bash this wok around before feeling happens. We think the non stick finish is a lot better than the All Clad brand, which we noticed had started to peel a few applications.

After a couple of heavy duty sessions with our wok, including a dinner party of 6, we love it. the only grip is that we wish it could be 2 inches deeper, as per traditional wok. hence you can toss and stir fry like in a traditional wok, but we are living with it as it as the food is not sticking/burning and the cleaning is a dream. Note that there is a 25 years warranty on this product so scan a copy of this invoice, note down the address that is attached to the wok and save it in your email box! If it serves me for 25 years, I think I certainly got my return on the cost! The 12 inch is not that wide, and I would highly recommend for a family of two to a party up to 8.

Makes me laugh & curse, but doesn't actually vacuum well at all. See photos. For ten days I have laughed out loud, cursed and finally just ignored this little robot vacuum cleaner for my own sanity. It seems like a great idea and if you live in a tiny house with nothing but tiny dust bunnies on slick floors then it might be a good idea. However, back here in my world... a big house with pets and a mix of tile, wood and carpet on the floors this machine is next to useless in most applications.

Where to start? It charges very fast and is relatively easy to operate once you read the instruction book and figure out the buttons & codes. The error codes are super easy to memorize and that's good because you'll see them often. The collection bin is easy to remove and clean out and this is also a good thing because it's tiny and you'll be emptying it multiple times per room. Well... multiple times assuming the machine actually picks anything up for you. The wheels are strong and it does actually move over surfaces pretty easily. Of course the brush that sweeps the debris up into the collection bin doesn't really make the transition as well from wood or tile to carpet. More on this in a bit.

The charging dock is a problem unto itself. It weighs far less than the vacuum unit. When the vacuum tries to set itself up to charge it can bump the dock and cause it to move. If your dock is on a wood floor and the vacuum gets in a robot induced spin of confusion this becomes a Monty Python type skit. I watched my Bissel robo vac chase it's charging dock down my hallway yesterday trying to park & charge, whacking the dock hard enough to cause it to slide a few inches away on the wood floor each time they touched. This silliness repeated over & over until the charging dock actually became unplugged from the wall! I laughed so hard I had tears in my eyes. I kept thinking "Dude! She's just not that into you."

The actual vacuuming is a problem here as well. On a basic tile floor with nothing but dry mud from our barn boots, the Bissel does fine - see the first two photos. If I could leave this unit in just the mud room and kitchen it would be fine. Using it in the foyer and dining room yields similar results - again simple wood floors and very little dog hair & some random dry shoe dirt, just the usual. The problems become very obvious on carpet. Transitioning from wood to carpet means the brush on the bottom of the machine rubs onto the carpet and deposits all the gathered dirt & hair & debris in a tidy little pile ONTO THE CARPET. You know... so I can use my real vacuum at my leisure later. See the last two photos.

The business of dropping piles of debris all over my carpet and any area rug it crosses had gone on every single time I have used this machine. I have cleaned it, I've checked to be sure the roller brush underneath is working properly, I've vacuumed with the big Dyson immediately before setting the little Bissel loose and it still happens. Despite having a big banner over the top that proclaims it's designed for pet hair, it is not suitable in any way shape or form for a house with any quantity of dog hair. I am giving this machine two stars - one for the simple amusement factor (my dogs think it's an indoor turtle and watching them stalk it cracks me up) and a second star because it is pretty good on bare tile floors with very limited amounts of dry dirt. Minus three stars for limited capacity, inability to reliably self dock & charge, and failure to actually vacuum more than just dry dusty dirt or actually do everything it claims.

Cheap materials, badly made, looks cheap and tacky, difficult to put together. This headboard arrived in a massive box with loads of padding and was very heavy. So we had high that it was indeed a luxurious piece of furniture made from "high quality" materials. Opening it and laying all the pieces out to put together was were our hopes were dashed and the cursing began. this is a two man job without question. And you need a mallet.

The main part of the headboard is in two large sections that attach in the center via a single dowel and then are braced on the top and bottom using six screws and two brace boards. Joining the two pieces together with the dowel requires two people and so much force, pushing and hammering with a soft mallet that we were sweating. Fine. It's in and done and there is a damage to one side now from the mallet where the cheap veneer dented and pealed back. See the photo. The bottom brace aligned and fit perfectly with almost no visible seam. The top brace...has a huge gap on both sides if you want the pre-drilled holes to line up. See the photo.

Pulling the padding and slip cover down over the assembled unit was amateur hour - the sides aren't smooth and the padding snagged and tore as it went down. It's not visible once you get the suede like slipcover in place, but none of it lies smoothly due to the bunching and snagging of the padding. This could be prevented entirely by making the padding case another quarter inch wider on both sides. Attaching this thing to the bed frame was another aggravation since the pre-drilled holes didn't match up to the standard queen size bed rails on the bed frame we already own. We had to rig it up and at this price point, that's beyond ridiculous.

Bottom line... Three star deduction for poor quality materials. Poor quality control on measurements at the point of construction. Further more the difficulty of assembling this headboard is overly complicated and poorly thought out. Honestly, this headboard could and should be shipped to customers completely assembled and ready to use - the size of the box it comes in would not need to change and the weight certainly would not change by pre-assembling the entire thing at the factory. At this price point I expected that! And most importantly, the final product looks cheap and tacky. It's fine for a little used guest bed, but by no means is this good enough for your master suite. See the photo. It's lumpy, uneven and the sand color is bland and looks like you grabbed a piece of random fabric at the hobby store. If this were priced in the under hundred dollar range it would be a 3 1/2 star rating, as it is...a two star is the best I feel it deserves.

text:
So much assembly and time required for a very unsatisfactory final product.... I had gotten something similar before and it was shipped to me fully assembled, and made of real wood. Here's the link to that one: https://www.amazon.com/IOTXY-Bathroom-Storage-Cabinet-Container/dp/B07ZV5MV3Y/ref=cm_cr_arp_d_product_top?ie=UTF8

So when I saw the product listing to this cabinet, I quickly assumed it was a similar product. Boy was I wrong! This thing is all MDF, and the effort felt like putting together an Ikea product. Not that Ikea furniture are difficult, it's just the end result of Ikea furniture's are worth it. You will NOT feel that satisfaction after putting together this little dinky cabinet. Screws and camlocks galore, you need to be a handy person to complete this job. I'm a handy person, and I found problems along the way that made me wonder how a non-handy person could do this job. I think they'd give up. Pre-drilled screw holes were misaligned, magnetic hardware uses screws so small that they eventually lose their grip on the MDF. You need to tighten the camlocks during assembly or else it's hard to balance the thing, but then if you do tighten them, at the end you'll be surprised to find out you cannot side the backboard in flush. You need to go back and loosen the camlocks to slide the backs in. The final product is okay if you spent 10 to 20 minutes on this. But you'll be at this for a long time, and the final results won't make you feel that it was time well spent. If you absolutely need something like this, I would get the one in the link above. That one isn't without issues, but at least it comes to you fully assembled and is made of real wood.

I took pictures of the instructions, take a look at them. Because I had assumed this is something similar to the fully assembled cabinet in the above link, you can imagine how unprepared I was to see this manual. LOL! Nevertheless, I wasted a few hours on this thing, and like I said, the end result wasn't worth the time. So look at that manual and decided for yourself if you want this little cabinet bad enough.

This warmer takes too long to get to a decent warm temperature.... Simply put, this warmer is not good. But in reading other reviews, and seeing how others are supposedly happy with it. I decided to give it one more chance this morning! I started my day with my usual hot cup of coffee, and I purposely didn't drink it all so that I could test the leftover cold coffee one more time on this warmer! I plugged the thing in, and let it sit on P2. Every hr. I would take a sip, and nothing changed, or you can say it was luke warm. In the 4th hour, you can say it was warm. Basically, this thing takes forever to warm up. This is my scale to better articulate what I'm saying:

10 - This is off the boiler hot, cannot sip.
8 - Still very hot, but you can manage little sips without burning yourself.
6 - No longer very hot, simply hot, and you can take big sips or gulps.
4 - No longer hot, but warm
2 - Barely warm, more like lukewarm.

In the first 2hrs of using this warmer, your coffee will be a #2 on my scale above. It does absolutely nothing to your coffee. In the 3rd or 4th hour, you may get to #4, and that's being generous. I feel there should be a #3 in my scale to explain this warmer. LOL! This warmer is just not practical because it takes eternity. If you want a warmer that can reach to #6 on my scale in about 30 minutes, check out the IWOXS version. It currently shows unavailable, but when available, you should get the IWOXS, and thank me later: https://www.amazon.com/review/R11A7OF8YQYR6C/ref=cm_cr_srp_d_rdp_perm?ie=UTF8&ASIN=B08CXD4LHL

As a matter of fact, to do this testing, I used the thin white mug that came with my IWOXS set. And it still took 4 hrs. Your mug at home is most likely thicker than the mug I used for this testing, so you can just forget about it. It will probably take you 8 hrs. I would be embarrassed to give this as a gift. Both this warmer and the IWOXS warmer are Vine items. I have no dog in this fight. Just my honest opinion. Don't buy this.

Not for beginners.... THE GOOD:
--------------
* Seems like a high quality machine. Very well built
* Default is set to seal 95mm cups, but you get three extra adapters for 85 and 90mm cups.
* Heats up fairly fast, 3 minutes is the specification.

THE BAD:
-----------
* They don't seem to be targeting regular homeowners because the instructions are woefully inadequate. If you are in the business, or have used these machines before, I'm sure you'll be okay. For me, it was all trial and error, and based on my trial and error, here are questions newbies will have, which a manual should have addressed:

1. Orientation of the roller film. They do have a diagram that I followed, only to realize the seal was upside down. A youtube video help me get it right, which I will talk about below.
2. How long do I press the cup without burning it? You know why I realize this is a question that should be addressed? Because some of my cups came out burnt, plastic melted. Look at my picture. LOL!
3. How far do we crank the handle? At times I felt like I might be crushing the cup and the drinks will spill. Because no matter how hard I push, the film just wouldn't cut. It would only create a perforation. I then manually separate it. This may have something to do with the height of my cup versus the level of the base. You can use a screw driver to move the base up or down. I will have to trial and error with the height of the base to figure out if this is what's causing the issue.

You see what I mean? There should be a manual with operational advice, recommendations and tips. There is nothing. You are on your own, it is 100% trial and error to learn this machine. If you want to know how to put the roller film in property, search YT using this phrase.. "Cup Sealer Machine Unboxing Demo - Verly." You will get an unboxing demo by a guy name Zian Vlag. He uses a different model, but I can see the roller guides for the film are the same. By watching him, I then realized my film was upside down. I am sure this is a 5-Star machine, but without an operational manual, or even company videos, this is a 2-Star product overall.

THE BAD:

I think it's one of those things where ignorance is bliss. If you want to be picky and compare levels and all that stuff, you'll end up not liking the majority of the humidifiers on the market. Sticky snow, not fluffy.... I really wanted to like this. I really want to let my children play with this. But unless I learn something new in the next few days, I can't let them play with this.

THE BAD:
------------
* Not fluffy. More like sticky.
* Despite a product listing on Amazon that is full of words, there is no advice on "how much" water per packet. They simply say add water. Even on the packet, all it says is add water. So if getting fluffy snow depends on the right mixture of water and powder... then good luck! It's trial and error.

DAY 2 UPDATE:
-------------------
* So, just as suspected, this won't feel like snow at all. Today, we purposely pour very little water to a packet and watch it fluff up. We continued to add water little by little, hoping there will be a stage where the snow will be both fluffy and sticky. Unfortunately, there is no such stage. Once there is enough water to make it sticky, the fluffiness is gone. So here are your options:

* Option 1: Less water equals fluffy snow, but you can't make a snowman or anything. It's just flaky or powdery, it does not take any form.
* Option 2: Keep adding water till it gets sticky. At this point, the fluffiness is gone. You'll be playing with clumpy goo, and your hands will always have gooey "snow" sticking to it. Real snow will flake off your hands clean. Not this gooey snow.

Lastly, it says this "snow" will dry out and return to powder form, and will be reusable. It's been several days, and my bucket of goo hasn't changed one bit. I think you would need to wait for eternity for it to return to powder form.

1-Star.

Good little coffee maker ... UPDATE Sep 14, 2016 -- not so good little coffee maker .... UPDATE: September 14, 2016
AAAaaannndd this one bites the dust. Lasted just under 18 months before it started putting out "small" cups. E.g., on the 8-oz setting, it started putting out 6 oz, then 4 oz, then today, 2 oz. Tried EVERYTHING -- descaled (twice), disassembled and cleaned every part that could be disassembled, changed the filter twice, installed a NEW filter holder. Nothing worked. It's done.

That's it. No more Keurig machines. I'm not going to pay Keurig's premium prices for something that lasts only 1.5 yrs.

Currently looking at other brands that can handle k-cups. (Love my k-cups; just have to find a good machine, or one that's cheap enough so that when it fails, it's not such an angst-producing event.)

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
My older Keurig bit the dust recently -- the pump went out after 5 years of daily use -- and the cost to repair made getting a new machine a reasonable choice.

Looking around and reading the reviews, I settled on this K45 system. It's not a "fancy" as my old one but has enough of the features that I've grown to love after 5 yrs of use.

I've had it a few months now, so I've had a chance to put it through its paces. It's easy to operate: fill the reservoir with water, hit the "on" button, load a cup into the receptacle, and wait for the "cup" lights to blink. I've learned over the years that for me, the middle setting (~8-oz cup) works best and gives me the best flavor. After a brief pause, out comes freshly brewed coffee. I usually use a large mug, so I brew 2-3 "cups" to fill my mug, and the "brief pause" can stretch longer since the water has to heat. Watch the lights, and you'll see what's going on. Just don't expect coffee to be dispensed immediately after hitting the "cup" button (that always seems to throw visiting guests who are using a Keurig for the first time ... ).

It's not perfect -- I wish it had a slightly larger heated water capacity so it didn't have to pause as long between cups -- but that's really a small quibble.

Overall, this is a solid machine, working great so far. I'll update this review if I notice any problems.

In week 5 of use, and not "heavy" use at that, the guide on one side split making it impossible to use. Needs some redesign to be competitive with similar products.... First things first -- this is intended to be used on sparkling wine bottles: champagne, prosecco, cava, etc. It won’t work on still wine bottles because the neck and lip of the bottle are shaped differently from sparkling wine bottles. No instructions were provided in the package but it wasn’t that difficult to figure out. The problem is that it doesn't work all that well. I have a couple of similar bottle sealers intended for use on champagne bottles so I’m familiar with the concept, but the problem is that this one just doesn’t seal all that well. The ”wing” -- that bit that wraps around the bottle below the lip -- isn’t all that sturdy. I’ve used this on only two bottles so far and I’m not sure it will last through another bottle. Plus, the seal isn’t really air tight.

For the same basic cost, you can get a similar stopper with double wings (each side of the bottle is ”gripped”), all constructed with metal.

Bottom line: thus needs some serious redesign to match or beat its competition. I’d start with the materials used in fabrication. Sorry -- I don’t like it. 2 stars.

text:
Mixed Feelings, Overall Satisfied for My Use. I have some mixed feelings about the NOXU White L Shaped Desk with Shelves. I assembled this myself, but for those that get overwhelmed easily with boxed furniture assembly, you may need a buddy to assist. I've assembled another desk that was also L-shaped of the same price range. In comparison, this one isn't as sturdy and the assembly was complicated. I've assembled many pieces of boxed furniture, and this isn't the worst piece to assemble, but much more complicated than it should be as there are no moving parts. Not all of the pieces were labeled, and some of the written instructions didn't match up to the diagrams. The instructions are in need of revision. When I was in doubt, I referenced the diagrams. Some of the bolt alignments that attach the frame to the desktop were misaligned. This isn't something I've observed in the desks I have assembled in the past. This took me about 30 - 40 minutes of assembly time using an electric screwdriver. I strongly suggest to avoid tightening all the bolts/screws completely until you have an entire section aligned for the best fit. Small tools are included, but I only used the wrench as I prefer my own screwdriver over the small one that was included. It's not something I would consider incredibly sturdy. There could be some engineering improvements to the frame at the point of the back corner assembly, which would make it much more sturdy. The corner section is the weakest point, and the section over the shelves is the strongest point. Two points of attachment for the foot rest would also lend to a more sturdy design. As it's designed, I do not consider the foot rest sturdy.

The desktop is thin as is the metal of the hollow tubes that make up the frame. On the upside, it's light-weight for the size. I'm using it in my hobby room where I do small crafting projects and sewing. This desk replaced two older mis-matched desks I was using before. It does make for an aesthetic improvement. For my purpose, it's a good fit for my space and works well enough. I was mostly attracted by the shape and white color that better coordinates with my shelving units. The shelves are handy to have, and do add some stability. The feet on the desk are adjustable, so with some fine-tuning, you should be able to make it level on most floors. The computer stand will only work well on a carpeted surface as it's a slide design (no wheels) and not attached to the desk. I had a couple pieces of the frame arrive warped, with no damage to the packaging. This is a quality control issue. It was still able to be assembled, but I have a tapered gap between one of the rectangle parts and the corner piece. It's not a deal-breaker, but looks a bit sloppy. I would not attempt to bend it back into the right shape without risking the integrity of a welded seam. There is also some paint that was scratched on the frame, not due to the packaging, another quality control issue. If I had not received this desk in exchange for a review, I would attempt to return it for another.

If it were not for the quality control issues, I would consider this a very fair value. However, based on my personal experience, I cannot strongly recommend this particular desk based on quality control and needed improvements to the frame engineering. On the same note, if this desk fits your ideal dimensions for your space, and you do not intend to use it for anything that would need to withstand a heavy weight, it is not anything I would strongly discourage. For the size, it is a budget-friendly desk, but keep in mind it's budget quality as well. I hope you find my personal experience helpful, and kindly will click the button below.

- if it aint obvious, the clips set on the inset rings so that the shelves do NOT align exactly at the inset rings.
- the space between wires on the 36x18 shelf is 5/8". so you likely won't need the plastic liner if your bits-n-pieces are bigger than that.
- if you aren't tall, you will pro'ly want to assemble the entire thing on its side. trying to reach up and align the poles with the holes in the shelf corners was a bit of work for me and i'm 6'1".
- they are pretty sturdy. i weigh 160 and stood on the bottom shelf to test it. no wobble at all.

to make things very clear - i'm buying another set of these and a pair of black shelves to split between the two sets.

rated a THREE since it does what i expected it to do and no more than that.

take care,
lee

What I received looks like it was made from a different species of pine or something..... The wreath I received looks like it was made from sprigs of a fake pine Christmas tree. The one shown in the listing shows smaller pieces and they're much rounder and bushier looking. The wreath is pretty and smells amazing but I honestly wouldn't pay more than about $25 for what I received. It does arrive kind of flat and you do have to fluff it out yourself- it makes all the difference! But even after some fluffing, it just doesn't look like the photo really. It looks like a 2nd hand company attempted to make one to look like it.

I didn't know much about wreath care so I did a search to find out they make wreath spray which is kind of overpriced so I went with the alternative method and sprayed it with hairspray after having soaked it overnight- completely submerged in water to hydrate it. text:
It’s Gonna Get Hot. I really wanted to love this set. However, the “space saving” design causes some problems.
First, I really love the size of these. We have a large family and these pans seem up to the task of our family in terms of size. I do have bigger stock pots, but this one is big enough for some things.
Second, I really like the nonstick on these. It seems very durable and it actually works. I generally shy away from nonstick coated pans, but these don’t bother me much.
Now on to my issues with these. First, the space saving design doesn’t same much vertical space. I have gotten used to storing pans nestled together and then lids separate. This just has you pretty much stacking everything without much nesting. That creates vertical storage issues. The pans are also wider than my taller under counter cabinets are. I can fit them in the cabinet, but have to slide them through the cabinet door sideways. When you’re stacking this huge heavy pan stack, that itself is problematic and I end up having to take every single item out and placing them back in order from bottom to top. I also had to clear out this particular cabinet because I usually store my pans in a higher cabinet, but the height wouldn’t work in those.
My next issues are functional. The handles of these pans always get blazing hot. Like cooking with an iron skillet, you cannot touch the handles without an oven mitt. Even on the stove top, the handles heat up with the pot. Even the skillet handle. I got quite a few burns before learning to treat these like an iron skillet.
My final issue is the lids. They are made with the lid handles to the side instead of on top. This means the entire lid, including the handles, is always hot. There is no simple lifting of the lid to stir. You have to use a pot holder every single time. Nice in theory- not user friendly. Great in theory and wanted to help the environment.. But, this just doesn’t seem very feasible in reality. Feels like a prototype! The item itself comes in a small capsule which the straw telescopes in on itself… The cleaning brush is kept inside the collapsed straw as well. I do like the fact that this item can easily be contained on a lanyard or a keychain etc.. however, when fully assembled there are a few things that make it difficult to function and be satisfactory.
Each time one uses the collapsible straw-
you remove from case, take out cleaning brush and put cleaning brush inside capsule that stay closed up and reattaches to keychain or item of your choice until done using... and this is doable.

However, I am not certain how logical it is to store cleaning brush inside of straw? Yet, you want to house cleaning brush with you if using on the go… It will make clean up after use- so much easier. But, it seems like it’s not the most sanitary way to do this.. and sure, I understand the reasoning to keep size to a minimum, it just doesn’t feel sanitary!

Next, try as I might I can’t Rid of metallic/metal taste well using the straw… I did try some of the tricks offered online to rid the metallic aftertaste when using a canteen or, the likes… But, it didn’t seem to help? Maybe it’s mind over matter- or, planet over mind over matter??! Either way – this was not something I could get used to very easy.

Lastly, if you have ever used a large at straw for a milkshake? Be prepared for that type of opening with the straw.. it’s jumbo!! I realize the need for this with the telescoping closable feature but, this was the breaking point for me. Probably we’ve been spoiled in a world with plastic straws at an adequate size- I get it’s going to take a lot more tweaking and awareness to move away from the world with straws available at your leisure… BUT, this was not the end product I was hoping for- I believe there will be more revisions of the reusable straw in the future.. and they will trouble shoot these issues. So, I feel while people figure out the remedy for plastic straw consumption.. this is a middle step.. toward progress- not, perfection!

So, IF size of straw can be jumbo without bothering you AND metallic twang does not hinder your taste buds… AND you are not “germ afraid”’like myself – this may be something you’re interested in. As mentioned, the size and convenience of clipping this onto a keychain/backpack/wallet/lanyard is nice and let’s it be user ready when you need it..

text:
Great gadget but the saddest nonstick pan on the planet. I have owned this Pizzazz for about 6 years I think. Goes back to before I started using Amazon, and I can't even remember where I bought it but it had to be brick & mortar.

I LOVED this thing. For frozen pizza, fantastic. But I have my own pizza recipe with my own homemade dough and that proved to be the downfall of pan #1. I think I made two frozen pizza and on the next pizza night, my own homemade. It was a long time ago, I think I smeared some olive oil on it with a paper towel (NO PAM, NEVER use PAM on any nonstick, I know that). The pizza crust ultimately was fuzed to the pan. It was very sad. I scraped it off with a plastic spatula and soaked it for hours. I didn't even have a dishwasher in that apartment so I certainly couldn't have abused it. It turned dark brown more places than not, almost like a shellac or varnish and I took pictures of it and wrote customer service at Presto. The lady was very nice and sent me a new pan.

Well, tossed a frozen pizza on that baby, it came off reasonably OK. Popped into the sink, and I never saw so much non stick coating float away in my life. It looked like a mosaic. I had not even taken a sponge to it.

So, for years my Pizzazz sadly sat in a cupboard. On occasion when it was too hot to fire up my real oven, I would cover the pans with foil and make my own or a frozen pizza. It was always fine. Really like the oven. Hate the pan.

text: Received as a gift no previous to compare. I have never owned a bread machine so with nothing to compare it to am being neutral as possible. Too dark a crust, I always use light setting since I can always pop into my convection oven if necessary but can't undo a 1 inch hard crust around it.  The paddle hole on some breads can make it nearly impossible to slice nicely as the bread crumbles when you get near that. SMOKE often.  I haven't noticed any bad spills between pan and oven I didn't clean before it got to work but I still have smoking and can only assume it is from the flour that does get tossed up a bit. The cover can come off a bit too easily but I think if you have cabinets in the way of opening it completely you would see it useful.  Paddle got too loose on its spindle and did get thrown away inside a bad loaf.  This, after being loose enough to come loose in dense whole wheat dough and go kerboing around pan with the dough. I picked up replacement paddles and I put a thin slice of silicone oven liner in paddle hole to tighten it up a bit. Can also be difficult to clean around the spindle/gasket for paddle.  But overall I think bread machines are helpful appliances - just make do for folks that can't knead anymore whether it be time or physical constraints.  I am satisfied, in cooler weather now I may take more of it out to bake in oven rather than machine.

OK if you don't mind the clean up. Fed up awhile ago with George Foreman grills. Awful to clean and the best one I had the paint melted off the back of it and smoked and ran if I cooked for more than a few minutes, and well, that was the best one I had.

I replaced it with a very heavy Hamilton Beach grill with temp control, removable plates that were also non stick and dishwasher safe. It has served me for a couple of years but like with many of these double grills, the food always seemed more steamed than grilled. It was also monstrously heavy and though pretty compact, you had to be real careful the heavy plates were secured when you moved it.

I saw a grill similar to this one in a catalog and thought I would look into what was out there. I was torn between this and the more expensive Zojirushi. Really could not decide. I guess it was the cover that won me over. And that the grill plate was immersible. The cover does come in handy if you don't want to splatter the place up and you don't mind a little steaming going on. I don't find it causes as much steaming as two sided grills - the cover is loose so it doesn't steam up as much as it could. The grill marks are definitely better, probably because of the higher heat and reduced steaming. I was not sure I would like the little griddle part but it is nice. I can make little potato wedges pretty quickly on it, usually faster than the meat, have to watch that. Put a couple of slices of bacon on it another time.

I am still in a learning curve with timing but hoping to nail a london broil soon. I am notorious for killing london broils on anything but an outdoor grill and so far have had two flops. Both going by recipe time or booklet time. Some day. Maybe I will get that perfect medium rare and not gray throughout.

Then there is the cleaning. Oh. Well, I have not tried to put the grill surface in the dishwasher yet. I don't care to wreck nonstick in the DW. I would put my HB's grill plates in once in a while but didn't want to run down the nonstick. So I have been soaping up in a sink and letting the suds sit for a bit and scrubbing with a George Foreman grill sponge. It does an adequate job. But often have to use a grout type brush to get in between in the slats. It still does not come out perfectly clean but I can usually take a soapy dishcloth and get the last spots while it drips on the counter. I dry it and pop it in the stand. The water tray is another tricky deal. You definitely don't want to put too much water in there, very difficult to get it to the sink or a coffee can or wherever you are going to dump it. It is best to transport it in the plastic base as close as possible to where you will be dumping. I sometimes dump it in the DW if there is room. Otherwise, it is really not difficult to wash in the sink. The lid is similar though I often stick that in the DW if I need room in my drainboard for other things.

It did a nice job on burgers and steaks. And of course the potato wedges were a nice surprise. Pork chops were not good but I think it was really a case of bad tough pork chops to begin with. Chicken I overcooked, which like London broil I tend to be challenged by. It is nice, a little more work to clean so as not something I want to use everyday but I can use it once or twice a week without be traumatized by the clean up.

UPDATE: I have put it in the dishwasher and was pleasantly surprised. I mean I put the grilling grate in there. I have a tiny, cruddy little apt dishwasher and it just fit but I put the socket end toward the door so it would not get too soaked and I have got to say it came out nice. It also rusted on the bottom. Such is putting anything metal in the dishwasher. I would certainly not put this any more often in the dw than I did my Hamilton Beach grill grates. But when you have the room, don't have the time or patience to deal with it in the sink, yeah, it is what I would call dishwasher safe.

UPDATE - the second trip through DW will be its last. It didn't get it clean and there was a nasty grease film on everything else in the DW. Won't do it again. The coating seems more worn than ever I have used it 5 times and twice tried to use DW. Backing it down to three stars because cleanup is practically impossible from what I see/have experienced at this point

bearings went just under warranty - mfr replaced. I have been using the Norpro manual meat grinder for years now and was very satisfied with it. However, like all grinders it takes considerable time to clean. Since I could not do much of a quantity with my little Norpro I felt the ground meat output to clean up time ratio could stand some improving. So I looked for an inexpensive grinder that could do a larger quantity thereby making clean up time worthwhile.

This fits the bill. I knew going in it was not terribly powerful but I am not putting up mass quantities of ground beef or grinding up a deer or anything like that. It worked fine on a mix of chuck, sirloin and round. I did between 2-3 pounds which is about two weeks' worth for me. That would have been a good amount of grinding by hand.

Clean up is somewhat more complicated than the Norpro and this (and scant directions especially concerning "kubbe" sausage? attachments) are why I took off a star. Aluminum is lightweight and won't rust but it is a pain to clean when dealing with raw meat in that you cannot use a bleach solution on it. So it takes a lot of soaking/scrubbing in very hot soapy water. The mostly plastic Norpro can be cleaned with bleach ensuring that you are doing a good job sanitizing it. Of course grinder plate and blade needs to be hardened steel but I wouldn't mind a plastic hopper or chute.

Speaking of blade, whoever says this or any grinder won't grind at all almost certainly has the blade in the wrong way. It seems illogical when you have it facing against the grate but that is the proper way for any grinder to work.

UPDATE - the bearings (what it sounds like) have apparently gone after about 20 uses in 11 months. I have used this for 11 months as I said before, every 2-3 (lately more like 4) weeks. It is such a pain to clean (ALL grinders are) that I try to do a quantity of a couple pounds a time since I will be cleaning for at least an hour or two. I am NOT grinding Bambi's mommy. I am grinding cubed sirloin, round and chuck. Anyhow, after a session two weeks or so ago that went alright, today I cubed about 4 pounds of sirloin, chuck and round in preparation to grind. I assembled grinder and put some meat in hopper. IMMEDIATELY hear a horrible knocking sound and after a minute or two there was a smoky smell. I thought I had assembled something wrong so took it all apart with raw chunks of meat and put it back together, turned on the switch and same loud KNOCKING. OK, took off the whole hopper assembly and grinder, nothing but the motor and sure enough switch it on and the knocking and smoke. OK, it is the motor, probably bearings. This thing was NOT used heavily at all by my standards.

I threw it in the garbage and am debating if I should fish it out and try and get warranty service. (supposedly there is a one year warranty on this thing). I just went through HELL and back getting a warranty replacement on a convection oven from a mfr with customer service in my state (cost only 11 dollars to ship the thing back to them) it took about 3 months to get a replacement. These people, I have no idea where to start. I will update if I go for warranty service.

Otherwise, have to say AVOID. Really moderate use and nothing heavy. Motor should not have given out, that knocking is bearing, not some plastic gear. I know a bit about motors and this just stank (and does stink)

At first, they gave me the same Mfr email in China and even suggested I call them (kidding? Moral of story is it pays to be persistent about warranty service/replacement if it doesn't cost too much to ship back or if they don't ask for the broken item. But it can take awhile. I would like to give them two and half stars since they did replace it but you can't give halves so will go with three. Persistent burning plastic smell. I am a long time devotee of turbo type ovens. Probably going on about ten years and this would be my third oven - four if you count a Fagor warranty replacement unit (see my review of that). I had purchased this while waiting for the Fagor replacement and I unfortunately did not get a chance to use this for months because I lost my job and my home and everything wound up in storage. I toted the Fagor to a relative that was putting me up and when the Fagor replacement in turn died I got this out of storage.

It cooks very nicely. I prefer these infrared (glowing coil) types to the halogen (Fagor) for their more even cooking and durability. I have no complaints on how it cooks. The timer does seem to "hang" awhile on the last minute. That last minute can be a couple of minutes. The fan is a teensy bit louder than the Fagor.

My major complaint and why I am putting this back in storage is the burning plastic smell. We should all be familiar with heating appliances that give off an odor for a bit on first use. Toasters, blow dryers, heaters. That is a protective coating on the elements. At first I thought this was all it was. I have now used this three times and the smell is not abating. It is rather noxious. In the dead of winter with no real ventilation I simply can't use this anymore. The smell is similar to a George Foreman deluxe type grill I had. It stank forever and then the paint and plastic melted on the back of it.

Unfortunately since I was not able to use this sooner I don't have much in the way of return options. Nobody else seems to have reported a stink so I guess it is just an anomaly. But I will continue to look into reviews elsewhere where perhaps somebody else has had this problem to see if they were able to remedy it. Otherwise it will be consigned to use as a patio type appliance if I ever have a patio again.

UPDATE - had to fall back on this one when the power cord on my Fagor failed. With it in use once or twice a week for several months the smell has lessened. It will come back if I cook something on higher settings for longer periods of time. But for a quickie cook I can get by without needing windows open. Upping it one star for its longevity. It is shame, probably just something plastic coated too near something that heats up in there.

text:
Nice, But With Issues. UPDATE: The next paragraph has my original review. At the end (under UPDATE INFO), I compare the Mop Away to the original Jaadoo spin mop, but as a pre-summation, I believe that each has its advantages and disadvantages and I prefer the Mop Away's bucket design and performance.

This Mop Away Wet/Dry Mop could have gotten four to five stars from me if the mop head screwed on or snapped on easily, but it doesn't. Below, I examine the pros and cons, while I consider possible users who might benefit from this product. Before I continue, however, please know that there are two other units out there, including one by O Cedar, which might be better than the item that I'm presently reviewing, since the mop head appears to attach easier. A third manufacturer is Hurricane. All are made in China. You might also want to check the Korean made Jessy and the Smart Twin mop/buckets. They are fascinating to say the least and I suspect that any of these buckets, especially the Korean ones can double as portable small garment manual washing machines and wringers. The Hurricane and Jessy models offer mop heads that appear to snap on and off easily, since they connect at the circular base instead of at the end of the pole. The Hurricane, Smart Twin, and Jessy mops also spin while you're cleaning. The Jessy boasts a sturdy stainless steel pole. The O Cedar's triangular base allows you to reach into corners. Any of these mops are good for dusting by making the handle shorter.

Positives:
It arrived with three mops and a duster; very nice. The mop's pole assembly is easy. It comes in three parts that screw into each other, producing a nice tall, sturdy pole that offers 90 degree bending in opposite directions, making it possible to clean walls and windows with the mop, if you have the strength and dexterity to attach the mop to the pole.

I love the foot operated mechanism that twirls the basket and the mop. As the piston and gears spin out of sight and below the basket, the basket and mop head rotate, producing a centrifugal force that squeezes the water out of the mop. The ball design at the bottom of the pole allows the mop to spin while the pole remains steady in your hands.

The bucket is well weighted, so you don't need to worry about it tipping over while you operate the pedal.

Negatives:
Because of the foot operated mechanism, this bucket is understandably heavier and wider than an ordinary bucket. Its oblong design accommodates the mechanical parts. The added weight and design could be a problem for individuals like me who suffer from arthritis, but people with healthy joints and muscles will probably not have a problem with the bucket's weight and shape.

Another issue for people with arthritis or who may have balance issues is the height of the foot pedal. I would have preferred it a little lower. I operated the pedal with my back against the wall and believe it will also be easy to operate from a sitting position. So, if you're in a wheelchair and have functional limbs, you will probably be able to operate that pedal.

As I mentioned above, my pet peeve is with how hard it is to attach the mop head to the pole. Having small, arthritic and weak hands it's a major problem for me. However, a healthy young man offered to snap it in for me and I noticed that he too had trouble with it. After about four attempts, he managed to get the head to remain in place. The problem is due to the poor design at that contact point - there is no release/hold mechanism, but simply two square shaped pegs on either side of the pole that are supposed to fit into the square openings on the mop head. That thoughtless design has convinced me that the head will probably snap off repeatedly while the mop is on spin mode. I've learned that it doesn't pay to return certain things, so I freed myself of future headaches by getting rid of this spin mop/bucket combo. I can't see myself dealing with the problem every time I need to replace a dirty mop.

Yes, you can machine wash the mop and reuse it. However, machine washing such an item could clog household pipes, causing additional problems. So, to save yourself from that headache, I suggest you wash the mop in the bucket with a little bleach. Also, I recommend that you keep filled buckets away from small children and pets in order to prevent drowning and other hazards.

Now, I hope to have a look at the O Cedar competitor. It will be my third attempt at trying to recapture past memories with a good mop and bucket. I hope that the third time's the charm. Walmart is selling the O Cedar combo for $29.99; free home delivery with $45 qualifying orders.

UPDATE INFO: During further research, I decided to purchase the original Jaadoo spin mop and bucket instead of the O Cedar. The drawbacks for the Jaadoo are: the bucket isn't as steady or sturdy as the Mop Away; the wringer spin basket is too small for the mop; the bucket's spin mechanism jams while the Mop Away spun smoothly; without hesitation (however, I gave each a dry run; I didn't wet either mop in case that became a problem for my arthritic hands - I can't wring out most items by hand, if it came to that, and a full bucket increases its weight, not worth the trouble for a test). The Jaadoo's pole is 64", about 1/3 taller than the Mop Away, which I didn't measure before I got rid of it. I suspect that the added Jaadoo's pole length, attributed to perhaps an extra extension, might be a mistake, since the dealer (which was NOT an Amazon affiliate) sent me a unit that was obviously a reject, judging from the smudges on the bucket's handle and the pole's base, which also smelled of ammonia. It doesn't pay to return the item(s) to the Jaadoo dealer, since they want a 25% restocking fee and I have to pay for shipping. While Jaadoo's bucket comes with two spinners (one for washing the mop inside the bucket and the other for wringing), the bucket's flimsy design and the mops being too large for the wringer as well as the pedal/spinner's tendency to jam reduce the dual spinners' appeal. Unlike the Mop Away, the Jaadoo's mop heads snap on and off the pole easily. If I hadn't gotten rid of the Mop Away set, I would have had a functioning Mop Away bucket and two good Jaadoo mop heads and pole that would have wrung out nicely in the large and steady Mop Away bucket. I provide an honest review, but I obviously didn't make a good decision by dumping the Mop Away bucket the same day it arrived.

Finally, I filled the Jaadoo bucket to see if it could be used as a small garment washer/wringer. It failed that test too because the water immersed spinner is placed too high, in addition to the jamming problem, and the wringer needs a cover to retain a garment within the strainer. The bucket's combined oblong/rectangular design also makes it difficult to toss out the water. If you have a house wares/hardware store in your area, you might want to test a few of these buckets, mops, and poles side by side, but I found Sears' prices to be overinflated. You shouldn't pay more than $30 or $40 for any of these spin mops/bucket combos.

UPDATE - The O'Cedar bucket (Sept. 19, 2013):
At $29.99 (postage included at Walmart) the O'Cedar spin bucket was the least expensive. The others (mentioned above) were $40 and $70 (postage included). The positive about the O'Cedar bucket is that it's lighter and smaller than the others.

The negative is in the foot pedal. It allows the strainer to spin well, but its length is too short. It's probably good for people with small, thin feet. My feet aren't that big (6M-6 1/2M, depending on what I'm wearing). I operated the pedal with my slippers, which wasn't a good idea because the clearing between the pedal and the housing is narrow, and yes my big toe got pinched in the limited space. Another negative: the bucket's upper lip extends beyond that foot pedal, so as you stand above the bucket the pedal isn't easily visible for operation.

If I feel industrious enough, I could duct tape a metal or wooden lever to the pedal, thus extending its length and making it easier to operate. But, the longer a lever is, the higher it will be along the angle's trajectory. The solution to its height, curving the lever, would involve too much work.

Given the problem with the pedal, I didn't bother with the mop attachment because I doubt I'll be using this O'Cedar device.

OK Serving Bowl for COLD Foods. If you are shopping for dishes for the first time in a while you’ll notice a plethora of dishes made of Melamine. The prices are reasonable and the design choices plentiful. As a potter who understands the dangers dishes can pose due to the glazes used, I decided to dig into what Melamine is and whether I wanted to use it with my family.

So let’s start with what exactly is Melamine?

Melamine is an organic compound also called urea or carbamide, that is mixed with formaldehyde to form a polymer resin. Melamine can also be mixed with other inorganic compounds to become a flame retardant, a fertilizer and a plasticizer for concrete.

Melamine is commonly used to make strong hard plastic dinnerware but is made using formaldehyde and the safety of melamine dishes is controversial.

Any heat can cause these chemicals and resins to migrate into your food, so it’s wise to stay away from plastic and melamine tableware options as they aren’t exactly the safest dishes to use for health.

Melamine plates are not oven safe and the FDA advises against using melamine in microwave ovens. Melamine is made from melamine-formaldehyde resin, and the melamine can contaminate food at 160°F and above.

Pfaltzgraff?

I decided to do a bit more digging... Like many, I have been eating off Pfaltzgraff dishes my entire life. I have the dishes my mom had that I then inherited - they are Pfaltzgraff dishes that have been in daily use for 45+ years.

Pfaltzgraff had been produced in Pennsylvania since 1811 with the first factory opening in 1865. Pfaltzgraff was truly an American standard that many of us knew, grew up with and the name carries weight.

In 2005 the Pfaltzgraff Co. was sold to Lifetime Brands, Inc. It was at this time the vast majority of production moved from the US to Mexico and China. After doing quite a bit of digging, from what I can decipher, of course this information is not easily found, it appears the Melamine lines are produced in China.

So My Thoughts on this Melamine Serving Bowl...

There is no question that it’s plastic. This will be a personal preference to some degree but I think plastic serving dishes look cheap. Yeah the outside looks like marble - kind of. It is lightweight and Melamine is harder to break than ceramic - though it will break, especially if it’s cold.

After extensively researching Melamine dish safety I’m not comfortable with the potential risk of chemical leaching when temperatures are over 160°F or if foods are acidic. These dishes are definitely not microwave or oven safe. Something I always have to keep in mind is that while I would know not to microwave anything within this bowl that doesn’t mean my son or a guest would know that.

This bowl is one that I store in a different cabinet and use when we are going to a pot luck and I want to take banana pudding or the like. It works ok for that, it washes well and looks nice. Beyond that type of use I would not recommend it.
