OK LED Smart Strip Light Set at a Reasonable Price. I have been using SmartHome products for more than 10 years, very close to when they started being produced and widely used. A few years later, I began testing, reviewing and writing about these products for several non biased comparison sites. Due to the experience within this particular area I have a broad base of knowledge within the Smart Lighting arena.

There are several considerations that need to be taken into account when choosing the appropriate Smart Light for a particular situation.

I have tested and written about literally dozens of LED strip lights over the last 10 years. I have tracked the advancements in the technology, understand the most likely areas of product failure and what separates the best LED strip lighting from the others.

In terms of light output, strip lights, of which this review focuses, is typically used for ambient or mood lighting rather than light to work or read by. Similar to the Hue Smart Strip Light, and frankly most major branded strip lights, this BIHRTC Light Strip can only produce one color at a time. In comparison, the LIFX Z Light Strip has 8 distinct controllable zones in every meter of light strip which allows for rainbow colors, animation effects and a full host of special effects.

The materials this BIHRTC Light Strip is constructed from are pretty standard in quality. The rubber covering the LED bulbs is thick yet very flexible. The 3M adhesive tape is standard on these smart light strips although people regularly have issues with them sticking.

The best advice I have as to getting any light strip to stay is to first thoroughly clean the surface the light is going to be attached upon. I first clean with a typical cleaning product such as a Lysol wipe, then thoroughly dry and then clean with an alcohol pad. Personally I don’t use the 3M double sided tape to hang the lights as it’s so prone to coming loose. I recommend the Gorilla Glue double sided tape which will be guaranteed to hold your lights where intended until you move them.

In comparison to other Smart LED Light strips this BIHRTC strip light is lower in lumen output to the Hue Smart Light Strip sets. While the colors are significantly less vibrant when compared to the Hue.

When comparing the duoco strip App (the actual name of the app used to control these lights) to the Phillips Hue App - the Phillips Hue app is much more robust and easier to use. When considering either of these two smart LED light strips to the LIFX Z, I have found the LIFX Z has the best colors, most versatility and best app - but it is also by far the most expensive.

In terms of the duoco strip App I had no issue connecting to the light via Bluetooth, due to it connecting via Bluetooth and not WiFi, range will be far more limited in terms of controlling, but this is rarely an issue. The app has plenty of pre programmed lighting modes, allows for syncing to music and custom colorization. Due to this being a product specific app I have yet to find a way to integrate it with my SmartThings hub.

A huge bonus to this BIHRTC LED Strip Light set that is rarely seen is the ability to control it with a connected control module. Consisting of only 3 buttons it allows the lights to be turned on, change colors and switch between modes. The set also comes with an IR remote that allows for greater control and, of course, the app which allows for even more.

This product, BIHRTC LED Strip Lights is decent quality - especially at this price point. The other sets I compared it with cost approximately 4-6 times as much - I chose those as they are the ones people are most familiar with.

In terms of value and functionality this is decent LED Strip Light Set that I recommend if you are not looking to integrate with other SmartHome products.

Nice machine; most versatile of the ones I've used, but still leaves watery coffee.. After visiting a friend with a Keurig we caved and got one for ourselves. The coffee was convenient, and we've used plenty of Keurig machines in the past, so we had a substantial idea as to what we were getting. I spent about a good week messing around with all the different settings to finally land on the ideal settings for me--but it still isn't "perfect." As a Dunkin aficionado, I prefer black coffee with a bit of flavor swirls, and sometimes a bit of sugar depending on my mood. I found that, with this Keurig, it's best to make a smaller cup so I get that concentrated taste, and add flavored syrup and a bit of water to get it close to how I like. I can never get that concentrated taste I like, and by the second cup I always toss the rest out after I finish half of it.

I also like to point out that Keurig doesn't make it easy to recycle these things. I knew of the environmental factor before purchasing, but as I had no reason to look up actual recycling services until after purchase I was shocked to find out they don't make it easy for consumers. I have to send it to third parties to get that done.

I do like the versatility and convenience. Visitors can easily make a cup of tea, hot chocolate, coffee, or cappucino in less than a minute. For that alone, Keurigs are well worth it. But as for everyday use I find it better to get some Dunkin from the local shop.

text:
Could use stronger lower back support.. Out of the past four office chairs I've used, this is definitely the best, but it still isn't perfect.
When I got the huge box at my front door, I was excited to get it assembled; my old chair had been losing the left arm, which had broken off some time ago but was kept in place by some duct tape. Assembling this chair was extremely easy, and it was set in my office in no more than ten minutes.

While this chair has more gizmos and levers than any previous chair I've owned (with the exception of a headrest, however), there is one huge flaw for me: the seat cushion doesn't recline as far backward as I'd like. The seat angles forward quite a bit, but it's almost flat when I recline it all the way backward. Also, the whole chair itself doesn't lower as much as I'd prefer, though it's got quite the height at its highest. I'm 5'8" if that matters.

The levers on the bottom right are very easy to reach. They put icons on them for ease of use, but I sometimes still find them confusing to interpret and have to maneuver them all to find the one for which I'm looking. For instance, to adjust the seat forward, there's a lever that has an image of a person sitting on the chair, with the chair highlighted in white. There are green lines to show what the lever does (green lines in front and in back of the chair, indicating it moves the back forward and backward), but there's green crossing into other areas of the chair which the lever does not control. It would've been best to just leave green and omit the rest, this way I would know that the lever controls that specific function.

The four levers, (three on the right and one on the left) control height, angle of the seat, seat glide, and the angle of the back.

Now, the back of the chair provides great support, though I wish it could lower just ever so slightly. Still, it's great, but I have noticed that over time it has loosened, so who knows how much longer it'll last at a tight angle.

All in all, this chair could be better. The fact that it doesn't angle more forward or provide a little lower adjustment make it slightly less comfortable for shorter people. At least it is for me. Otherwise, it's the better of the four office chairs I've owned and used.

Robust, useful, but lacks one major feature I'd like.. While I've had ADHD all my life and had pretty noticeable symptoms, I was diagnosed with it only last year. Following that came lots of professional, life-changing help and advice. One of those was using a TIME TIMER to manage my time; it's been a daily routine since then. I use it at work and at home. I saw this offering for a watch version and thought, "Now I can take it with me on the go!"

There are three mods of the watch: regular watch, TIMER mode, and stopwatch. Of course, the TIME TIMER mode is the one I planned to use most. Works Well as Simple Dehydrator; Slower, Less Versatile Than More Expensive Competing Product. [[VIDEOID:moTYGPGLRDB4O4]]This bargain-priced (about $24) OSTER FPSTDH0101 ELECTRIC FOOD DEHYDRATOR works well as a dehydrator, but the more expensive (about $60) [[ASIN:B0090WOCN0 Nesco FD-75A 700-Watt Food Dehydrator]] works faster, is easier to clean, has adjustable temperature settings, and accommodates more trays. See the accompanying video slide show for my side-by-side comparison of these two dehydrators. (I purchased the Nesco Pro model from Amazon, and received the Oster model through Amazon Vine.)

SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCES: The Oster and Nesco models have two very significant differences. First, the Oster electrical drying unit is bottom-mounted, while the Nesco electrical drying unit is top-mounted. The bottom-mounted drying unit is a real disadvantage, because fruit, vegetable, and meat juices invariably drip into the base from the drying trays above. Since the electrical base cannot be immersed in water, the base must always be cleaned carefully by hand. This isn't difficult, but it's much harder to remove juices from the base than from the trays. In contrast, the top-mounted Nesco drying unit stays clean throughout the drying process. At most, it requires a quick wipe with a moist cloth or paper towel. The bottom tray of the Nesco model is even easier to clean than the trays.

Second, the Oster drying unit is equipped with an on/off switch, while the Nesco drying unit is equipped with an adjustable temperature-setting dial. In this respect, the Nesco model is far superior to the Oster model, because the Oster model with the simple on/of switch has only one drying temperature. With the Nesco model, you can start your food drying at a higher temperature, and dial it down after a few hours to the "normal" 135-140 degrees, to speed up the drying times. You can also adjust the temperature from 95 degrees to 160 degrees, to accommodate foods needing lower (e.g., herbs) or higher (e.g., jerky) temperatures to dry optimally. A disadvantage of the Nesco model is that it lacks an on/off switch, and can only be stopped by unplugging the whole unit.

SIZE AND CAPACITY: The Oster and Nesco dehydrators are almost exactly the same size, and take up the same amount of countertop space. However, the Oster has only four (4) trays, and doesn't appear to be expandable. (The instruction booklet makes no mention of the availability of expansion trays.) My photos show the Nesco model with 4 trays, but the basic Nesco Pro model has five (5) trays, and is expandable to 12-14 trays.

With only 4 trays, the Oster dehydrator's capacity is limited to the equivalent of what you see in the photos: 1/2 cup blueberries, 1/2 apple, 1 pear, 2 extra-large bell peppers (1/2 pepper in green, red, orange, yellow). With the Nesco model, you can dry more food at one time, by using more trays (and maybe use a bit less electricity). With 9 trays, the Nesco model will dry 9 extra-large peaches.

TRAYS: The Oster and Nesco trays are also nearly identical in size. The Oster trays are made of a flexible plastic-netting material, the Nesco trays are made of a hard plastic more like Bakelite. The Oster trays are dishwasher-safe; the Nesco trays can be washed in the dishwasher if you remove them before the start of the drying cycle.

However, the trays for both the Oster and Nesco models are quite easy to clean without even using a dishwasher. Just soak the trays for a couple of minutes in hot, soapy water; then use a soft dish brush to remove any sticky bits. Because of the differing "hole patterns", the Oster trays pick up a few more bits than the Nesco trays, but the difference is negligible. All the trays fit in a large kitchen sink.

FOOD PREPARATION: Fruits and vegetables should be cored and seeded, and cut into 1/4-inch slices. Food with edible skins (apples, pears) can be peeled or not. Fruits that turn brown if left exposed to the air can be tossed with orange juice, pineapple juice, or a product like Fruit Fresh to prevent this during drying. (I used Fruit Fresh in my test.) The easiest way to slice the food for drying is to put it through a food processor, using the widest possible slicing blade. This goes very quickly, and gives you uniform slices that will dry uniformly. The food processor cleanup is easy.

DRYING TIME: In my test, I halved a cup of blueberries (blanched first in boiling water), an apple, two pears, and four different-colored bell peppers; then I arranged them in similar tray patterns and stacked the trays in the same order. After 4-1/2 hours at 138 degrees, the Nesco model had dried everything except the blueberries to flexible-leather consistency; after 6 hours, the Oster model (at an unknown temperature) had accomplished the same thing.

The instruction booklet for the Oster model suggested 12-18 hours for the fruits and 14-18 hours for bell peppers; the instruction booklet for the Nesco model suggested 4-10 hours for apples, 6-16 hours for pears, and 5-12 hours for bell peppers. Obviously, both the Oster and Nesco units dried the food in less time. In my experience, foods usually dry in less time, so I always check back after 3 hours.

With both the Oster and Nesco models, you will need to remove some food or rearrange it on the trays, or rearrange the food trays themselves, before the full drying time is up. Even the most uniformly-sliced food will dry at slightly different rates because of air circulation patterns inside the stacks of trays.

After 9 hours, both the Oster and Nesco models were still working on the blueberries. Perhaps I didn't blanch the berries properly to break the skins. Some of the berries had dried and achieved raisin-like status, but most had a lot of liquid left inside. I decided it wasn't worth the cost of electricity to continue drying the blueberries, and abandoned the test there. If anything, the Oster was ahead of the Nesco after 9 hours.

CONCLUSION: If you're serious about drying food--making trail mix, preserving summer's bounty, drying herbs, making jerky, or stocking an emergency pantry--you will want a full-featured dehydrator like the Nesco Pro model. The Nesco Pro comes with 5 trays, and with clean-a-screen and fruit roll sheets (2 of each). These sheets are used, respectively, for drying herbs (to prevent the dried bits from falling through the holes in the trays) and for drying fruit purees. Nesco also sells a "jerky gun" as an extra food dehydrator accessory for making uniform strips of jerky from ground meat. (The jerky gun can be used with any food dehydrator.)

If you're not so sure about your commitment to drying food, then you may want to start with this 4-tray Oster model; or with Nesco's bargain-priced (about $31) 4-tray [[ASIN:B003I4F7AS Nesco American Harvest FD-37 400 Watt Food Dehydrator]], which has a top-mounted drying fan, is expandable to 7 trays, and can use the Nesco clean-a-screen and fruit roll sheets. Because of the single temperature setting and the bottom-mounted drying unit, I rate this OSTER 4-TRAY ELECTRICAL FOOD DEHYDRATOR at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

Great Receptacle, Not-So-Great Egg Separator. Because I regularly make meringue pies and home-made ice cream, I separate a lot of eggs. What I love about this WILTON BETTER BAKING EGG SEPARATOR is the 10-egg-white receptacle that stands firmly on your kitchen countertop--and the snug fit of the egg separator atop the receptacle. What I don't love about it is the design of the egg separator itself.

The egg separator design is fairly standard. There is a central round section for the yolk, with cutouts on both sides that allow the white to slip through. But the central yolk section is not very deep, and is not large enough to allow the yolk to move around. This means that if the white doesn't immediately drop through completely--and you have to gently rotate the yolk to finish the egg-separation process--you are at risk of breaking the yolk and contaminating the whites already in the receptacle. This is especially true if you are working with older eggs that have been in your refrigerator for a while.

Because of the less-than-optimal design, I rate this Wilton Egg Separator at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale). A couple of egg separators that I like better are the plain, bargain-priced [[ASIN:B0079G2EQ6 Mini Egg Yolk Separator]], and the excellent [[ASIN:B00A2KD8NY OXO Good Grips 3-in-1 Egg Separator]] that hooks onto bowls of all sizes.

Inexpensive Alternative to Custom Table Pad Protects Against Spills. This BENSON MILLS DELUXE VINYL TABLE PAD can easily be cut with scissors to fit any table that is smaller than the 52" x 90" dimensions given on the package. Placed between a finished wooden tabletop and a tablecloth, it provides an extra layer of protection from spills--particularly those horrible rings caused by water and wine glasses.

This table pad is made of thin white vinyl that is backed by a thin layer of flannel. It's no beauty--you will always want to cover it with a tablecloth. It should reasonably protect a tabletop from hot dishes, because it doesn't catch fire immediately when a lighted match is placed directly on the vinyl surface. However, the lighted match, if left there, does melt the vinyl and burn a hole, so the table pad won't protect against cigarette burns.

The flannel backing is a good idea, because it prevents the vinyl from getting permanently stuck to the finished (varnished) tabletop. However, the flannel backing also causes the protective pad to slide around on the tabletop. A tablecloth will help hold the pad in place, but a thin table pad like this one lacks the weight it needs to stay firmly in position.

This 52" x 90" table pad (about $20 on Amazon) is an inexpensive alternative to a custom table pad, and offers good protection against ordinary spills. However, because I wouldn't want to rely on it to protect a tabletop that I really cared a lot about, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

Well-Made, Works Well, But Not Best Available Corn Stripper Tool. If it weren't so fiddly to use, I would really love this RSVP SHUCK DELUXE CORN STRIPPER. The product's clear plastic outer tube is both its best and its worst feature. The best, because the tube catches all of the stripped corn kernels, and is easy to empty. The worst, because the tube must be opened and closed for every single ear of corn; each ear of corn must be carefully positioned inside the tube; and the yellow cap at the bottom of the tube has screw threads that run in the "wrong" direction. (To unscrew something, the mantra is "righty tightey, lefty loosey"--but this tube opens when turned right, and closes when turned left. Probably it's designed this way so it won't unscrew when the corer is twisted.)

The stainless steel "corer" is sharp, and it cuts the kernels off the cob with very little downward pushing effort. However, it misses all the kernels at the narrow end of the ear. The gadget is a little confusing at first, but simple to use once you understand how it works. You cut the kernels off by twisting the scalloped yellow part that's attached to the stainless steel corer; then you use the knobbed yellow part to push the stripped cob out of the corer. It's easiest if you take the knobbed part out before you strip the corn kernels off the cob. All of the corn stripper parts are sturdy, and they are all dishwasher safe.

This RSVP Corn Stripper is slightly more efficient than my [[ASIN:B000V78JGO OXO Good Grips Corn Stripper]], which has to be emptied several times for each ear of corn, and is a bit awkward to take apart and reassemble each time. However, my favorite tool for this job is the [[ASIN:B006GDRD9G Zyliss Corn Stripper]], which strips an entire ear of corn completely with 4 or 5 quick downward strokes (when you hold an ear of corn over a bowl or plate, you don't need either a tube (RSVP) or a container (OXO) to catch the stripped kernels).

Because it's fiddly and not the best available tool for the job, I rate this well-made product at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

Excellent All-Purpose Kitchen Timer With Independent Memory Function. EDITED August 11, 2012:
After about 4 months of use, the part of the display that shows the second number for the minutes went partially blank. This happened even though the timer had not been dropped, and had not gotten wet. The timer still keeps track of the time, so it's still useable. However, because of the defective display, I'm reducing my star rating from 5 stars to 3 stars ("it's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
This battery-operated CDN Digital Timer is a terrific all-purpose kitchen timer. A slider on the side makes it simple to switch between the three main functions: (1) an accurate 24-hour digital clock, (2) a count-up timer (stopwatch), and (3) a count-down timer (food timer). The display shows time in hours, minutes, and seconds-- the maximum time is 23 hours, 59 minutes, 59 seconds. The timer is powered by a single flat, round LR44 battery (included).

The timer's best feature is the independent memory function that will recall your most frequently used time setting. I keep the memory set at 20 minutes--the time it takes to freeze homemade ice cream--but the memory can be easily erased and reset to something different whenever you like. You do NOT have to set the timer and allow it to run to completion to invoke the memory function (a requirement with many other kitchen timers). Instead, the memory is set independently, by using the regular Hr.-Min.-Sec. buttons and then hitting the Memory button. The timer has a built-in stand, plus a fairly strong magnet that you can use to attach the device to any convenient metal surface.

I rate this timer at 5 stars ("I love it" on the official Amazon scale). The only negative thing I have to say about it, is that it is quite small. At 2" high by 2-5/8" wide, it is slightly smaller than a credit card. Because my household has two cooks, I use this timer alongside another excellent timer, the [[ASIN:B004PYA3B8 Robic Three Memory Timer]], which is limited to 99 minutes but which remembers three frequently used time settings.

Dinnerware Is 'Twixt and 'Tween Casual and Formal Table Settings. This MIKASA ITALIAN COUNTRYSIDE 4-PIECE PLACE SETTING is high in quality, but it's rather thick and heavy for porcelain. Of course, this is a "countryside" pattern, so Mikasa may have intended for it to resemble the humble stoneware more than the elegant porcelain.

(Note: In one place, the Amazon product page description says "crafted from stoneware"; in another place it says "made from quality porcelain". However, the retail box and the actual dinnerware pieces all say "porcelain". My everyday dishes are Heath stoneware seconds, and these feel different, so I'm guessing porcelain.)

The all-white pattern is a raised design formed from vertical bars beneath a narrow scrollwork band that goes all around the edge of each piece. The edges of the design are NOT crisp and cleanly stamped into the porcelain; and my personal preference in this style of dinnerware pattern is for crisp lines. Again, Mikasa may have intended this effect to suggest a rougher, "countryside" appearance.

Nevertheless, this dinnerware is kind of 'twixt and 'tween casual (everyday) and formal (guest) dinnerware. The all-white, raised design is basically elegant; the heavy porcelain emulating stoneware is basically casual. It doesn't really feel right in either setting--the formal design is just "too much" for use in everyday dinnerware; the weight and lack of crisp patterning make it "inelegant" for formal dinnerware.

This line of Mikasa porcelain is microwave safe and dishwasher safe, which is nice. The bowl is large and deep, good for soup or cereal; the cup has a pleasing upright mug shape that doesn't require a saucer; the dinner plate and salad/dessert plate are generously sized. However, because this Mikasa "Italian Countryside" has a split personality, and doesn't seem quite right either for casual or formal table settings, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

Beautiful Cookware That Requires Special Care to Keep Its Looks. This ALL-CLAD MC2 PROFESSIONAL MASTER CHEF 7-PIECE COOKWARE SET is drop-dead gorgeous. It is meticulously designed, machined, and hand-finished. However, it's a poor choice for me, because (1) my kitchen has a ceramic-top electric range, (2) it's heavier than my all-stainless-steel cookware, and (3) it requires hand-washing and a lot of extra care to keep it looking beautiful.

In general, aluminum cookware is the most energy-efficient, which is why "stainless steel" cookware usually has an aluminum core. Aluminum cookware is also lightweight. However, cookware made entirely from aluminum poses some toxic risk in regular use, because minute amounts of aluminum can leach into food during cooking (particularly into acidic foods like tomatoes).

This All-Clad cookware has a stainless steel interior that won't react with food. Thus it's completely safe for all cooking. It cooks efficiently, because it has an all-aluminum core plus an all-aluminum brushed exterior. However, it isn't particularly lightweight. The 9-inch All-Clad frying pan from this set weighs 1 lb. 9.9 oz., while my 9-inch Cuisinart stainless steel frying pan with aluminum-core bottom weighs 1 lb. 6.6 oz.

My ceramic-top electric range is not friendly to aluminum cookware, because aluminum has a fairly low melting point. The manual for the electric range suggests using extra caution when cooking with aluminum cookware, because aluminum can leave scuff marks on the cooktop, and because a pan allowed to boil dry can melt, fuse with the cooktop, and severely damage the cooktop. Of course it's fine to use this All-Clad cookware on a ceramic-top stove, but the cook needs to exercise particular care (1) to never turn the heat on under an empty pan, and (2) to follow the All-Clad recommendation and always use low or medium heat, except when boiling water. (The recommendation to use low or medium heat is NOT just for ceramic-top ranges, because high heat can warp any cookware.)

However, the main reason that I'm disappointed with this All-Clad cookware is that it requires so much extra care to maintain its stunning appearance. The All-Clad instructions include the following cautions: (1) to avoid the formation of white dots or pits in the cookware, bring water to a boil or wait for foods to begin cooking before adding salt; (2) to prevent water spotting, rinse in hot water and dry immediately; and (3) to prevent discoloration, avoid overheating (produces brown or blue spots), remove food films before reheating, and avoid high-iron-content water. In addition, for ordinary cleaning, the stainless steel interior should be cleaned with a paste of fine powder cleanser, washed in hot soapy water, and dried immediately. (You musn't use oven cleaners, oven cleansers, or chlorine bleach.) The aluminum MC2 exterior should be cleaned with commercial aluminum cleaner, and rinsed in lukewarm water.

In short, this cookware is "not recommended for dishwasher use". Because this All-Clad cookware is beautiful, but requires pampering to stay that way, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

With a pedestal fan, you don’t need to use precious desk, countertop, or tabletop space to hold the fan--it has its own stand. You can place it anywhere in the room, as long as the cord (or the cord with an extension cord) can reach an electrical outlet. Also, a pedestal fan moves the air in the top half of the room, where it does the most good.

However, in recent years I’ve become a fan of the Vornado whole room air circulators (see, e.g., [[ASIN:B00TX79BK6 Vornado Vintage Jr. air circulator]]). You can put one of those in the corner of a room, aim it toward the opposite ceiling corner, and the air will be turned over throughout the room.

Heavy Weighted Blanket Doesn’t Work as Throw. This TRU LITE BEDDING TRU BLANKET (Weighted; Happiness Embroidery; 60"x 80"; 15 lbs, Gray) is pretty, but it does NOT work as a throw. It’s far too heavy to wrangle around for snuggling up inside it. Fifteen pounds may not sound like much, but it’s a lot to deal with in a blanket that’s large enough to cover a regular double bed.

In my opinion, the weighting is a gimmick. It is true that when you’re underneath this blanket, you feel very warm and protected. However, you can get the same effect from several layers of bedding (combining blankets, comforter, heavy bedspread, etc.).

I can’t imagine this being acceptable to a couple sharing a bed, unless one person is an incorrigible “bedclothes hog”. The weight is the problem--it restricts bed mobility. For that reason, this blanket is a terrible choice for an elderly or disabled person. It makes it very difficult to turn over and change positions at night.

The blanket is quite well made, with the word “Happiness” embroidered on the underside of the silky “slipcover” for the weighted, quilted interior blanket portion. The appearance of the slipcover is a bit misleading--the textured polka dots are part of the weave of the fabric, and do NOT have anything to do with the weighting. (For some reason, I thought that the dots indicated little round weights.)

If you’re young, healthy, and strong, and dislike extra layers of bedclothes, then you’ll probably love this blanket for its “swaddling” effect. If you’re elderly or disabled, you probably won’t be able to use this blanket at all.

There are features that I love--the lighted display that shows how much charge is left; the built-in crevice tool extension--but the usefulness of this "hand vacuum" is severely limited by the 2-inch-wide nozzle. The battery holds enough charge to vacuum a flight of carpeted stairs on the high-speed "power boost" setting (impressive!), but it takes a zillion passes to do stairs in 2-inch-wide strips.

The suction is okay on the low-speed setting, and very good on the high-speed setting. It takes 5 hours for a full charge, so you'll probably want to store it in the plugged-in charger (wall-mounting hardware is included) to keep it topped off, as the manual recommends. The charger light turns off when charging is complete, but removing the device from the charger for even a few moments will cause the charger to restart for a few minutes.

The crevice tool extension makes this ideal for cleaning my stairway, which has a stair lift installed. (The support posts for the stair-lift track not only collect dust, but are hard to clean around.) However, the release button for the extension is stiff, so that it's often difficult to push the extension back into the nozzle for storage. The crevice tool extension is great for cleaning crevices in overstuffed furniture. The nozzle without the extension does a good job of dusting a smooth rubber floor mat.

The hand vacuum is fairly easy to clean. The big cyclonic element in the handle releases easily, and the whole thing pulls out sideways. Dust, dirt, and larger particles collect around the plastic filter module, and are easily dumped into a trash container. However, thick dust accumulates quickly on the cloth filter inside the plastic filter--and it clings, so the "dust bunnies" must be pulled off by hand. (This isn't good if you have allergies or asthma.) Filter reassembly is simple, and the filters are washable.

This is a vacuum for dry materials only. After washing, the filters need to be completely dry before you operate the vacuum. The cyclonic element is not particularly capacious, so I can't see this device as indispensable for ordinary kitchen cleanups like cereal, flour, or dry pet food spills. It is lightweight, and well-balanced for hand vacuuming.

As good as this device is for cleaning crevices in upholstered furniture and for cleaning carpeted steps, it is expensive for such a specialized tool. Also, it requires storage space and an electrical outlet to keep it charged and always available for ready use. For these reasons, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

Space heaters of all kinds make me nervous, and this NEWAIR PORTABLE INDOOR SMALL ELECTRIC HEATER (NIH040WH00) (with Silent, Energy Efficient Operation, White) is no exception. It has desirable safety features--automatic shutoff function, tipover kill switch--but it has snap-on feet that leave me wondering about its stability.

If an oil-filled heater tips over or leaks, it can cause a fire. Oil-filled heaters stay warm for some time after they are turned off (which adds to their energy efficiency), but it also means they can set fire to combustible items (e.g., fabrics) that contact them even after they are turned off. Generally, combustible items should be kept at least 3 feet away from any oil-filled heater, even if the heater’s surface remains cool.

Given the safety issues surrounding oil-filled heaters, I’m NOT comfortable using this one (or any other model). I was interested in this model because of the slim panel design and small size, but it was a mistake for me to order it.

In my bedroom, this MOLEKULE MINI AIR PURIFIER (with PECO Purification Technology, White) doesn’t seem to be as effective as my [[ASIN:B01LCX9QWG GermGuardian Air Purifier]] at clearing particulate matter from the air. The GermGuardian does come with a UV light for killing germs, and the light does seem to make a difference in how clean the air feels. The Molekule Mini is more expensive than the GermGuardian, and much noisier. I find that the Level 3 fan setting (out of 5) is the highest “always on” fan setting that is reasonable, and even this setting makes it hard for a nearby Amazon Echo device to hear the wake word.

The Molekule Mini requires expensive replacement filters every 6 months. The GermGuardian also requires replacement filters, but they’re less expensive, and the GG is pretty forgiving if you don’t replace the filters right away.

The Molekule Mini is kind of heavy, and has a surprisingly large footprint on my bedside table. Unlike the GermGuardian, the Mini lacks a display that shows the particulate matter count, and it doesn’t have an Auto setting that makes the fan speed up automatically if extra pollutants are present in the air. (There is a new, more expensive model of the Molekule Mini that does have some kind of particulate matter display.)

Overall, I was extremely disappointed with the Molekule Mini. After using it for 6 months, I decided to take it out of service. It doesn’t improve the air quality in my bedroom (over what I get with the GermGuardian); it’s too noisy; and the filters are too expensive.

Budget-Priced, But Not Recommended for Reduced-Salt Bread. This OSTER BREAD MAKER WITH EXPRESSBAKE (1.5 or 2 Pound Capacity) is budget-priced (about $112 on Amazon). It makes a nice vertical loaf of bread, IF you weigh your bread flour and follow the included recipes exactly.

However, baking a loaf strictly according to the recipes is difficult, because the recipes do NOT include the flour weight. This is true even though the booklet advises you to weigh your bread flour! The recipes call for cups of flour, so you will need to do the weight math. Your bread flour packaging should tell you how many cups there are to a pound (for example, Gold Medal white and whole wheat bead flours have 3⅓ cups to a pound, which works out to 408 grams in the 3 cups required for Basic bread).

If you need to adjust your ingredients (for example, if you need to reduce the salt for a no-salt-added diet), your first loaves will collapse badly in the middle while baking. I had to make a dozen experimental loaves to find the specific combination of 1 tsp. salt, flour, and water that would produce the 30% whole wheat flour loaf shown in my photo.

When I followed the included recipe for basic raisin bread exactly (1½ tsp. salt), the loaf was beautiful–but it was inedible for someone who has been on a no-salt-added diet for some time. It tasted incredibly salty.

Bread machine recipes found by Googling say that salt can usually be reduced by one-half, with no adverse results. This was true with my old Regal bread machine, and is true with my more expensive [[ASIN:B0044WWC7E Panasonic SD-RD250 Bread Maker]] (about $260 on Amazon). With the Oster machine, reducing the salt requires a lot of experimentation.

I like the Panasonic machine a lot. It makes a horizontal loaf, and it is flexible regarding the amounts of salt and other ingredients that I want to play around with. However, a number of reviewers have stated that the Panasonic machine quits after a few months. I haven’t been using my Panasonic machine (purchased to replace this Oster machine) for long enough to know whether it will offer more than a few months of service.

There are differences in the way that the Oster and Panasonic machines make Basic bread. The included recipes for the two machines are quite similar, but the kneading and overall times are different. The Oster machine begins kneading as soon as you press “Start”, and takes a total of 3 hours for a Basic loaf. The Panasonic machine leaves the ingredients to “rest” for up to 2 hours before kneading begins, and takes a total of 4 hours for a Basic loaf. Both bake the loaves for about an hour.

Both machines have settings for French bread, dough, etc. (check the product page descriptions for the exact types of things that the machine is intended to make). Both machines also have “express bake” settings that will bake a loaf faster than the normal 3 or 4 hours.

Beautiful But Heavy 12” Skillet Needs Lots of Storage Space. This CALPHALON PREMIER SPACE SAVING NONSTICK 5QT SAUTE PAN WITH COVER is a beautiful nonstick cookware item. It’s a capacious 12” skillet (12½” across the top, with 2½” sides) made of heavyweight hard anodized aluminum. The two handles are stainless steel, which stays cool when you’re cooking on a stovetop (gas, electric, glass top). The hard nonstick surface is okay with metal utensils.

The space-saving claim is somewhat exaggerated, because it refers to the skillet’s ability to stack VERTICALLY with other cookware (with the same 12” diameter) from the “Calphalon Premier Space Saving” series. In fact, this very large and heavy 12” skillet consumes a lot of horizontal storage space, because it measures 23½” from the handle on the left to the tip of the long (primary) handle on the right. The skillet is almost two feet wide! If your plan is to buy several 12” diameter pieces from the series and stack them, don’t forget to calculate the total stack height to make sure it will fit in your storage area.

The tempered glass cover is flat (for vertical-space-saving stacking) rather than domed like most glass skillet lids (which may or may not store upside down in their skillets). The flat glass cover takes a little getting used to, if you’re accustomed to domed covers, and it is NOT vented. The glass cover has its own long stainless steel handle, which adds to the substantial total weight of the skillet plus cover.

The skillet is oven safe to 450 degrees Fahrenheit. (My kitchen has a rule against using long-handled cookware in the oven. The skillet is quite heavy when empty; I need to use two hands to handle it safely when it is filled with food or covered with the lid.

The skillet is dishwasher safe. However, the dark gray exterior may bleach out to a streaky lighter gray if you wash it regularly in a dishwasher—this is what happened with my Classic Calphalon anodized aluminum cookware. text:
possible water/germ/food entry at point of handle & plastic overlay. KitchenAid makes a good ice cream scoop. I have this in the color, Pistachio.

It is a metal scoop with a plastic overlay on the handle. I was perplexed by those mentioning

1. water possibly getting into handle
2. plastic pulls away from handle.

I went in for a closer look and sure enough, these things happen. I placed the scoop in a mason jar filled with water, waiting 20 minutes and checked. I would not have noticed this before since I never let my scoops sit in water, and I don't put them through the dishwasher (in the past, doing so seemed to make them get pit marks, especially if it was an aluminum variety). So I hand wash...It's ice cream.. I just rinse and dry and then back in the drawer it goes. I may use it 10 times a year, and that's if I don't use a spoon to dig out ice cream. Anyway, I took scoop out from water, dried it, and shook it. I thought I could hear something. So then proceeded to pull on the handle to try to separate metal from plastic, and sure enough a couple drops of water came out.

As for plastic overlay pulling away from the metal, that does happen but only if you are looking to do so. I took it a step further and twisted and pulled to see how far I could go with it. No damage. I doubt it will ever fall part. However, the fact that it can be manipulated means that it is a pressure seal. It is likely why it is "possible" for water to get in. It isn't going to happen by just rinsing it. I bet I never ever experience that outside of this contrived experiment due to the way I handle my scoop. BUT if you are inclined to run it through the dishwasher or let it sit in the sink with water, then your experience may vary. No one should need to even be concerned with that, so I can't rate fully based on that.

It does get really good rating across several "best of" articles. OXO seems to win out, but this is considered a good one. I think it is a good one. I like the feel of the handle. It feels just a tiny bit heavier than my older Farberware one. It definitely cuts through hard ice cream. The slightly wider, thicker grips gives me a better grip. I do wonder if the handle may be too smooth for some people.

As a rarely used item, I will have this a long time. As a rarely used item I am more liberal with what is acceptable, particularly since it is just a means to grab some ice cream. However, I'm a little grossed out at the possibility of water or other gunk possibly building up where the handle and plastic overlay meet. It takes two hands to demonstrate it, so I would need assistance to take a picture. I don't know if it is a design flaw, over sight, or somehow intentional (the extra gives allows more pressure to be place into handle to scoop extra hard ice cream)?

I do love KitchenAid, and I normally highly recommend their wares. But this item of this design style does not impress me like everything else.

Again- great feel, good grip, cuts into hard ice cream, typical scoop shape, attractive

BUT, that spot where steel meets plastic.. Nope.

3 stars.

It holds a cup of liquid, which is actually PLENTY to do a wide floor area, and can last many many cleanings for spot cleaning. I have had a few different spray mops, and most hold 1.5 cups, and I always get several cleanings out of a fill up. I guess it depends on WHAT you use, and how much you use. I always start with a damp cleaning pad.

Perfectly fine for any floor. It is just a micro fiber mop head. You use your own cleaner.

Mop head is pretty standard, and I find that I can use this mop pad on other spray mops, or use other mop pads on this. No surprises here.

Has same spray (fine) as others, has same easy to engage spray handle. The main difference is where the water reservoir (in head versus further up pole). Has same rotation. Has same slim profile and ease of storage. I find out of the 3-4 spray mops I have used that they are nearly all the same. One of the few things that can be purchased based on price. But for my preference the Amazon one has been my consistent go to.

The "stand out" feature is the ability to wring it out using a slider. I find that I dont use it. I find that I prefer to take the mop pad off and wring it out in the sink, then after I am done for the day I toss in the washer. I find that it is more annoying then helpful. By the way, I clean homes for a living, and using this feels like an extra step.

SO OVERALL- its fine. I think it is "OK". Not great, not bad. Middle of road rating of 3. I simply find the extra features to be not so extra. In fact, I find them a little annoying. But you may love it. Some stuff simply comes down to preference.

decent bags for light duty use, all 100 02 absorbers are packed together, inc labels. 3-4 stars for the bags. 2 for the absorbers if only based on how they are packaged (all together).

Bags are of nice size and thickness, with gussets for standing. Though not as thick and robust as some bags I have. These would be (for me) for short term storage. Think snacks and such that can benefit from "mylar" storage, but maybe not for super long term storage, unless storing these in a container for long storage (think of food grade buckets filled with mylar bags filled with food). You do you though.

I normally dont buy these kits for the oxygen absorbers. For that, I prefer to buy a very trusted brand, since it is all about the 02 absorbers in terms of effectiveness. Cant risk it, and I dont really have a way to test it in a manner that I would/could comfortably do (seal some food, come back a year later and see if it molded, or went bad in another way). But I do appreciate the inclusion of O2 absorbers, and here again I will use them for stuff that I am not concerned about for long term storage. More is better, so feel free to use extra in your bags. So, maybe a batch of cookies I made, or storing some chips, powders, etc.

Yet, I still factor the 02 absorbers into my rating. I consider them "good enough" if they are individually packaged, and pretty much useless if all stored together. Once open, they have all been exposed to air. I'm fine with a handful being in one vac sealed packet, but not all 100. And so, if you buy this for using the whole kit, then plan to use up the 02 absorbers quickly as well. I suppose some can be used, then just tightly packaged the unused ones back up.. but I'm not chancing it.

I wish companies would say if the absorbers are all packed together (unwrapped) or packed together but also individually wrapped. I come across both scenarios and this is the former. Figured I would mention it in case you are looking for that info too (the pic they include doesnt quite clarify).

Overall, the kit is "OK". Which is 3 stars, and means just that-- it is OK. Not great, not bad. Has pros and cons. Will be up to you to decide. I just have my preferences, and it wasnt something I could totally detect from their description or pics alone.

States in headline, description, and my order information that this is for nespresso compatible capsules (or pods, whatever you them) ONLY. Does what it's supposed to, just be careful.. I purchased this 1-gallon water distiller for producing water for my carnivorous plants (they are sensitive to contaminants.) It produces distilled water as it should, but I have a few gripes.
First, and most importantly, the unit's design is two pieces. A top containing the fan lifts off, and the bottom contains the water chamber and heating elements. The top piece has its own plug which must be plugged into the base. Then, the base has its own plug, which is removable and plugs into the outlet.
If you are not careful, there is a *serious* risk of electrocution and/or damaging the unit due to this design. The plug on the base of the unit is pretty much guaranteed to be exposed to water dripping down the sides when you remove the lid to add more water. I highly recommend covering the back side of the unit with a dry towel when you remove the top. Water that has evaporated in the machine will still be present in the top and will drip all over the place.
Additionally, when you go to fill up the tank, ensure you don't allow any water to drip over the side of the base. (The water tank is not removable from the base, you have to tote the whole thing to the sink or bring a pitcher of water to the machine.)
Despite the flaws in its design and a lingering suspicion that cleaning this thing will be difficult, I would still recommend it for those who need distilled water on demand. It saves you so much trouble buying and lugging it from the store. Just use caution!

text: Not Really What It is Advertised As, but a decent quality frying pan. There is a lot of hype about these red copper pans being non-stick and scratch resistant.  Don't believe it.  I have cured the pan a couple of times, according to instructions and while it helps a little, for a while, to prevent sticking, food still sticks and sometimes sticks badly, especially eggs.  In TV commercials they show the eggs sliding around the pan freely.  Maybe if you keep moving the eggs around that would work, but wouldn't it with any pan?  The scratch resistance is hype too, as my pan scratched after just a few uses, although they are minor scratches and don't seem to impact the cooking much.  (I didn't use metal implements either.)  On the plus side, the pan does heat evenly and appears to be able to take high temperatures without warping.  I have been using mine for months and no visible warping.  The pan cleans up without too much scrubbing, even with stuck on food.  The stay cool handle works, sort of.  It stays pretty cool on the part you would normally grab, but don't reach too close to where it hooks on the pan, as it gets hotter, the closer you get to the pan.  You might not burn yourself, but you wouldn't want to hold on for very long.  Also after you cure the pan in the oven, the handle will be too hot to grab, so you have to use a holder and let it cool down.  I wouldn't buy another one of these, as it is only slightly better than an average pan.

text: Good Suction; Nice not to deal with a cord; power head is heavy. I haven't used this for very long, but I like to review things based on first impressions, as often they seem the most accurate.  First of all, this is easy to assemble; together in 5 minutes with no tools needed; just snap the sections together.  One thing that I didn't like right away is that the two included attachments don't have on-board storage.  Apparently Shark sells an overpriced accessory to hold the attachments.  For the high price of this vacuum, they should include this.  The second thing I noticed right away is the vacuum cannot stand upright without collapsing and folding down the handle (but that is easy to do).  I gave it a quick cleaning run around in several rooms in the house and it seems to have strong pickup capability and actually almost drives itself, so it moves along smoothly and rapidly.  Simple switch to go from hard floors to carpet and back again.  The biggest issue that I would have with this vacuum is that the power head (which also doubles as a hand vacuum, which is easily detachable), is quite heavy.  You have to hold most of that weight of the power head while using the machine, as the angle that it has to be held at in order to clean puts most of the weight on your arm.  If you are young and strong, maybe not a big issue, but if you were doing a whole house, your arm might hurt after using it for more than a few minutes.  If you can't lift much weight, then this is not the vacuum for you, but the total weight is not bad; it is lighter than a typical vacuum.  The collapsing handle is a nice feature for getting under furniture, so I should be able to clean some places that haven't been in a long time.  Not having to deal with a cord is a huge plus and the two rechargeable batteries that you can swap are also great.  The batteries seem strong, but I haven't run the vacuum long enough to know if they last as long as claimed.  They do take a while to charge.  The battery packs are easy to swap in and out and have indicator lights showing charge progress and how much charge is left; they are well designed.  I should give this more than a 3-star rating, but having to hold the weight of the power head/hand vac while using the machine could be a real problem if using it for an extended period of time.  The dust cup is small too, so will no doubt fill up fast, but they couldn't really make it any larger without adding more weight and bulk.  Overall it is a well designed vacuum, but I know if I let my house cleaning crew use it, they will break it fast, as they will forget that you can't stand it upright without folding down the handle; they already broke one vacuum that way.

text: Well Designed, Light, Convenient, not the best on heavily soiled carpets. I have mixed feelings about this carpet cleaner.  I am spoiled by having used a Rug Doctor, which really does an excellent job.  My old Rug Doctor is on its last legs, so thought I would give this cleaner a try.  I had bought a Bissell carpet cleaner several years ago, but ended up returning it as it didn't work that well.  Thought I would try again as I assumed that improvements had been made over the years.  It does seem like it is a better machine than the one from several years ago and it really seemed to get a lot of dirt out of the carpet and pulled out a lot of lint too.  I would classify it as an adequate cleaner if your carpets are not heavily soiled.  It didn't work as well as my Rug Doctor to get out ground in dirt, but when you consider that it is 1/2 to a 1/3 of the price of a Rug Doctor, it does a lot for the price.  I like the idea that the tank you fill will hot water comes out and you can take it to the sink and leave the machine plugged in and not have to move it.  With my Rug Doctor, every time I need to fill the water, I have to unplug it and take the whole machine to the sink, dump the dirty water and fill it with clean water from a pitcher.  With the Bissell, you just run the water directly from the faucet into the tank.  The power cord is a reasonable length.  It's long enough so you don't have to move the machine too often, but short enough not to get in the way.  The machine is light and easy to manuveur. Rug Doctor uses one backwards pass to clean.  The Bissell uses one forward and one backward pass dispensing cleaning solution and then a foward and backward pass to vacuum up the water.  It's 4 passes instead of one, but the machine is not that heavy so it's not a big deal to make the 4 passes.  I liked the hand attachment that you use with the built-in hose; it worked very well.  The machine noise is about normal for a carpet cleaner, approximately like a vacuum cleaner.  Very easy to assemble the machine; just a few screws.  So what's wrong with this machine?  On heavily soiled carpets, it seemed to leave a lot of streaks and put out too much soapy mixture.  It's possible I used too much cleaning solution as the small included bottle said double strength, but I used the included measuring cup, so I assumed it was the right amount.  I also had a hard time figuring out how the built-in hose was supposed to wrap around; there is no picture or diagram.  My sister figured it out right away how to do it, so chalk that up to my being a dummy.  The biggest issue I had with this machine is that when you turn it off and start to move it, it drips a lot of water out and can spot up the carpet; then you have to run it again over the spots and they don't come out easily.  I also noticed that the restricted area that sucks up the water is narrow enough that lint accumulates and requires cleaning just about after each use.  This is a decent machine for the money and I would give it a solid 3 stars; maybe 3 1/2.  If you don't have a lot of very dirty carpet, this might be perfect for you.  It beats paying double or triple the price for a more heavy duty machine, unless you need the heavier duty cleaning power.  If you clean your carpet regularly, this should do the job just fine.  If you have a lot of dirt and have pets, this might not quite do the job, unless you use it often.

text: Great for raclette grilling and not much else; cord is a bit short. Know what you are getting if you order this, as it wasn't quite what I expected.  I thought I was more or less getting a conventional two-tier (two surface) grill (if there is such a thing), but this is really designed best for preparing raclette.  Raclette is a Swiss specialty and generally consists of potatoes or other vegetables and sometimes bread that is grilled and then covered with cheese.  The bottom portion of the grill has 8 tiny grilling "pans" that are best used for melting the cheese that goes on the food that is grilled on the top.  I guess you could also use the tiny pans to grill other small items or cut up pieces of vegetables.  The heat for the 8 pans comes from the top, so keep that in mind.  The single heating element is under the top grill pan, so it provides heat upwards for the top grill surface and down for the small grilling pans.  Since heat rises, you might get more heat at the top than the bottom, but I couldn't determine that for sure.  I thought this would be great to use to grill something inside when the weather is bad outside.  One main problem is that you can't grill anything that has any significant amount of fat, as the top grill pan has small outer edges and the grease has no place to go; it just sits on top of the grill pan.  That's a less healthy way of grilling, as the grease does not run off, plus if you get too much grease it will overflow the pan, going into the bottom or onto the heating element.  Potentially I guess you could have a grease fire if that happens or at least a smoke problem when the grease burns when it hits the hot coils.  So forget trying to grill burgers unless they are very lean.  Best for a small amount of meat or pieces of meat that has very little fat.  Otherwise you will have to keep wiping off the fat accumulation.  You also won't get the taste of flame grilling that you get with a regular BBQ grill.  The only other problem that I noticed is that the power cord is very short, so you need an outlet very close to where you will be grilling. You might be able to use a heavy duty extension cord, but generally that is not recommended for anything that heats up.  If you are familiar with raclette and have it more than once in a while, it might be worth getting this.  It is good for up to 8 people who could each have their choice of cheese.  If you don't expect to use this very much, probably not worth getting and storing for the time you are not using it.  Unless you eat raclette often, It seems more like a novelty item for use once in a while. In a way, it is not unlike fondue.  Many of us had fondue sets that now are unused, once the novelty wore off.  Even my George Foreman grill that does have a cup to hold grease runoff sits unused for a long time, because it involved a lot of cleanup after use; this one will be even worse in terms of cleanup because all the grease will sit on the top grill plate.  You have to wipe off the grease because if you wash it in the sink, the grease can potentially clog your drains.  This is really designed to grill low fat or no fat items, such as bread, vegetables and maybe small pieces of meat that is very lean.  Seems like a fun party item to introduce raclette to those who are unfamiliar with it.  Nothing really wrong with it; just an item that generally is designed for a very specific type of grilling and not suitable as a general purpose grill.

text:
Rival Smart Pot: IQ of about 100. Rival's "Smart Pot" is a pretty good crock pot that offers an oval shape for easy handling of longer pieces of meat and an hourly time control that automatically switches to warm at the end of the heating cycle. This crock pot is a little fancier than others and it offers a more modern look and appeal.
However, there are some flaws with this product- flaws that I didn't really notice or even think about until I started to use the pot. First of all, there is no way to set the crock pot directly on warm. The pot will switch to warm only after a timed cycle has ended. This is bad for those situations when all you need is to keep something warm. Second, there are only four timed settings to choose from: 4 hours, 6 hours, 8 hours, and 10 hours. Third, the crock pot can get very hot and doesn't have an opening at the top to let steam escape. Be careful when you lift the lid- if it's really hot, the steam can burn and cause you to react quickly by dropping the lid.
Another problem that occurs some of the time is burning. If you have a small amount of food and the liquid doesn't fill to the top, you could end up with burnt marks on the side of the ceramic container. As long as the pot is full, this isn't a problem. But it's something to watch out for if you plan to cook smaller meals.
I like the large capacity of this crock pot (six quarts) and I like the neutral color. It's also nice to be able to remove the interior pot for cleaning. It's bulky, but it's better than other crock pots (those that do not have a removable pot) that have to be cleaned by scrubbing directly.
Taken as a whole, this is an acceptable crock pot that has its good points and bad points. With a few more improvements, it could be much better. As it is, it's only average- suitable for those of us to don't do much cooking but inadequate for the more serious chefs among us.

text:
Nice Kitchen Aid, but has its Limitations. Kitchen gadgets are great for reducing the time it takes to prepare food and the Vidalia Chop Wizard Food Processor is one of many time- saving devices that make it easier to slice and dice food. Cutting onions into hundreds of small squares is easy with the Vidalia Chop Wizard Food Processor and it is also very useful for certain other foods such as pears, potatoes, and more. The sharp, stainless steel blades chop food into uniform pieces, saving much time and effort.

The Vidalia Chop Wizard Food Processor doubles as a quick measuring tool and this fact adds convenience. Once you have pressed the food through the blades, all you need to do is lift the device and turn it upright. You can then view the amount of food by looking at the cup and milliliter markings on the sides of the base. This eliminates the extra step of measuring the chopped food in a measuring cup.

Probably the greatest disadvantage with the Vidalia Chop Wizard Food Processor is the fact that it comes with only two blade inserts. For more experienced and more creative chefs, this isn't going to be nearly enough and it greatly limits the chopper's usefulness. Also, one needs to remember that certain foods require a much harder push than others, to pass them through the blades. Often, it will be necessary to cut up food into smaller pieces first, making the device less convenient than it would otherwise be.

Vidalia Chop Wizard Food Processor is dishwasher safe and it does come with a special cleaning device to make it easy to help with the process. Unfortunately, the claw- like cleaning aid is quite limited in its usefulness. It is better than nothing, but I find that I often need to reach for a butter knife to dislodge the bits of food.

So how does the Vidalia Chop Wizard Food Processor stack up overall? Well, it is a decent kitchen aid and a tool that I find fairly useful for simple chopping jobs. It is completely manual and it takes a good push to chop certain foods, but it is still better than no assistance at all. Looks Nice on the Countertop, but Heat is an Issue. Large in size and requiring sufficient space, this counter top oven from Cuisinart is designed to combine the heating ability of a convection oven with the speed of a microwave oven. It offers both abilities in one, and can add convenience to most any kitchen.

This oven does have a nice appearance and it looks good on a large countertop. Its stainless steel matches well in my kitchen, with its abundance of stainless steel appliances. You need to make sure to have plenty of space for ventilating in the rear and on one side of the unit, but other than that, it easily makes the grade from an appearance standpoint.

But besides being pretty, a micro/convection oven needs to work well at heating up food and this one seems okay in most instances. The microwave works as well as any other, but I do have some other issues with this oven, and chief among them is that the outside of the unit gets very hot. You can feel the heat radiating from the inside- out and a quick check of the exterior will confirm that the heat is exiting through the outside walls of the oven. This will surprise some users at first, but you get used to it. You just have to make sure to keep your hands- and those of kids in the house- away from the unit while in operation.

This oven has several different settings from which to select. Besides the microwave setting, it has a defrost setting, warm, convection, convection bake, and convection roast. It even comes with a recipe book so you can utilize these special settings and prepare food like a pro. But one fact to keep in mind is that this unit can take a long time to heat up to high temperatures. It has little problem reaching, say, 350 but if temps get into the mid to upper 400 range, it can take longer than is worth it. For these high- temp cooking jobs, a regular oven is best. I'm not an expert on heat transfer, but it seems like the loss of heat described above is part of the problem.

Ovens are a must for any kitchen and having a microwave/convection combo is nice for certain cooking purposes. This Cuisinart model works well for the most part, but the issues with the heat convince me to rate it only average overall.

Breadman Works, but You Need to be Patient. Breadman BK1060S Two Pound Professional Bread Maker is a good bread machine for making creative loaves of bread, hot and fresh, right in your own kitchen. This bread maker offers a nice, professional- looking appearance with its metal exterior and it has many extras like fourteen different settings for specific types of bread; a fruit and nut dispenser; a built in memory that stores your settings for up to seven minutes in case of a power failure; and the ability to program the bread maker to start up to fifteen hours ahead of time.

All of these extra features are nice, but what matters most is the performance and quality of the finished product. My experiences here have been mixed, but they have improved. My first attempt resulted in a compressed block of bread that was inedible and had to be discarded. I followed the instructions presented in the included recipe guide, and later discovered the problem: The recipe book contains several errors. The recipe I consulted did not have an accurate measurement for the liquids and after looking through the guide, I noticed others errors in other recipes. One recipe, for example, calls for a tablespoon of raisins, which is obviously incorrect. I am a little surprised that the manufacturer hasn't realized these glaring mistakes and made a greater effort to correct them.

Beyond my first experience with this bread maker, I have enjoyed positive results. My more recent attempts with this bread maker have resulted in good, fresh loaves of bread and my confidence in the machine has improved. However, there are still a few areas of concern. One is that the loaf of bread, once removed, often has a patch of flour on one of the corners. This is because the paddle doesn't always mix the ingredients as well as it should and you end up with a flour- coated corner. Another area of concern is the metal paddle. When you release the loaf of bread, the paddle often pops out with the bread and lodges itself in the bottom of the loaf.

Breadman BK1060S Two Pound Professional Bread Maker is generally good, but I have noticed other peculiar qualities that are misleading at first. There are multiple points in the process where the bread maker will go several minutes without making any sound. You will think there is a possible problem with the machine and will be tempted to open the lid, check the settings, and possibly even reset, but you need to resist the temptation. The machine is fine and needs to be left alone. And, I have also learned that if you open the door early on and you have ingredients in the fruit/nut dispenser, it will often drop the extra ingredients into the bread as soon as you close the door. Again, you have to trust that everything is okay and resist the temptation to open the lid. And you need to be careful where you touch- the metal exterior looks nice, but it also conducts heat very well and can get quite hot to the touch.

Hot, fresh bread is a great addition to any meal and the Breadman BK1060S Two Pound Professional Bread Maker is a good small appliance for the purpose of making tasty, creative loaves of bread just like a professional. If you use the included recipe book, make sure to examine the recipes closely for typos and above all, exercise patience. The lack of noise and other distractions are not cause for alarm. Just let your Breadman complete its process and enjoy the finished product.

Fast Hot Water with Bodum. I like the occasional glass of hot chocolate or hot tea. Creating these beverages requires a hot water source and the Bodum Bistro Cordless Electric Water Heater is ready to assist. Bissell Easy Sweep: A Little Much, in Many Ways. A broom and dustpan are the usual tools used for small cleanups in the kitchen or on other smooth, flat surfaces. This manual method works, but there are other options; options that get the job done without bending or stooping. One of then is the Bissell Easy Sweep Cordless Rechargeable Sweeper.

Taking this device out of the box, assembly is the first thing to complete. It is simple- you just snap the handle together, then plug it in. The sweeper can then be unplugged and used for ordinary sweeping. It can be used on flat floors or on carpet as long as the carpet is flat.

I have used this tool many times now and it is definitely a device with its share of good and bad. Looking first at the good points, this cordless sweeper works well on small jobs and picks up crumbs and other small debris without much effort. It is VERY lightweight, starts with the press of a large, flat button, and empties with the press of another button. There is no bag to empty or replace and with cordless, plug- in action, you don't need batteries.

The positive points make this device sound like a winner, but once you have used it a few times, you realize that Bissell did overlook a few important points. First, let's talk about this weight issue. It is always nice to have a sweeper that is lightweight, but the lightness in this instance is almost too much- it makes it seem low in durability and quality. The swivel action is also too much- it swivels in every direction, like it is barely held together. It seems like it is on the verge of breaking at every moment.

As for the cleaning ability, this Bissell products is only average overall. It has no problem picking up small crumbs of food, but it isn't very powerful and you often have to go back over the same area to pick everything up. Another annoyance is with the handle. Pick up the sweeper and shake it in any way, and there is a chance the handle will fall apart and have to be reattached.

So, how do I rate the Bissell Easy Sweep Cordless Rechargeable Sweeper? Well, as you can see, it has its share of good points and bad points and I can understand perfectly why some have rated it below average. I am going to go ahead and rate it at the middle, three- star level. It is not without flaws- that is certain. But it does come in handy when you need to clean up small jobs in the kitchen and as long as you keep its limited abilities in mind, it should work okay for your simpler cleaning tasks.

Taylor Digital Food Scale not Big on Intuition, but Acceptable. Those who are serious about dieting often consider a food scale an essential part of the weight management process and the Taylor scale is a handy little tool for this purpose. It checks a food's weight, matches it to the type of food, and then delivers a calculation for total calories, helping dieters and others control food intake and keep calories in check.

This scale takes a little effort to set up. The battery compartment uses watch- style batteries and it has to be opened with a very small screwdriver. It would be better, and easier, if the compartment could be opened without a screwdriver and I would like it better if it used ordinary batteries, but the setup process was acceptable at this point and I was now ready to use the scale. The manufacturer says that 1000 food items are already pre- loaded into the scale, so in most instances, it is just a matter of finding your food item in the database, placing it on the scale, and waiting for the display to show the total calories. If you have a food that is not in the database, you can add it manually, into the scale's memory, for future reference.

The Taylor scale is a useful device for checking food weight and caloric values, but I must say that it isn't the most intuitive when it comes to programming and food lookup. As I said before, you can input your own food items manually, but it takes time because all you have is a 10- key keypad, similar to a standard phone. You have to press the numbered key containing the desired letter either once, twice, or three times depending on its position on the button. This can take some time, depending on the word. Then, you have to be ready to input the number of calories in a 100 gram serving. It is a good idea to have a calculator handy for this purpose.

Serious dieters will enjoy this scale the best, but others can benefit from it as well. We could all use a little better diet management and this Taylor scale does come in handy for this purpose. It could use a little more intuition and perhaps a few more bells and whistles, as well as larger keys, but it is still a good starter unit that has the basics covered.

Cuisinart Thermal Coffee Maker Looks Nice, but has a Few Issues. The Cuisinart DCC- 1150 10 Cup Coffee Maker is a decent coffee maker overall with an equal share of pros and cons. I have owned several different coffee makers over the years and have used several Cuisinart coffee makers, but I never owned one until now. I was attracted to this particular model due to its appearance and its ability to save electricity. The unit automatically shuts off after it finishes brewing, then keeps the coffee warm in the thermal carafe as you gradually consume one cup at a time.

This coffee maker brews in a similar fashion to other modern coffee makers and it does have some nice features worth mentioning. I like the water filter and the permanent filter because it means cleaner, fresher tasting water, greater convenience, and less money spent on paper filters. I also like the automatic shutoff, at least in theory, because it helps conserve electricity. The carafe is unbreakable, which is nice, and the programmable functions work well. These are all good, useful features and the unit scores points in each of these areas.

Now, let's talk about the potential problems with this Cuisinart coffee maker because there are a few. The first problem I noticed when I started using this coffee maker is the difficulty in cleaning. The opening at the top of the carafe is very narrow and only the smallest hands and fingers will be able to fit inside. I have found it necessary to use a brush for cleaning purposes because there is just no way to get my hand inside. This also means, of course, that drying is a challenge. I usually turn it upside down and air- dry because other than using a hair dryer or some other air- blowing source, it is just too difficult to get inside to soak up the excess water.

The next potential problem area is the one mentioned by most consumers who own this coffee maker, and that is its inability to keep coffee hot over an extended period. The manufacturer did what it could to engineer the carafe in such a way as to maintain heat, but there are still limits to its ability. The lid seals itself shut at the end of the brewing cycle and the carafe is double- walled to keep the heat inside, but it is still limited in its capabilities so you need to hurry up and finish drinking as quickly as possible or else be faced with a pot of cold coffee.

One other potential drawback with this coffee maker is one you wouldn't think about at first. Because the carafe is metal and is non- see through like a glass carafe, there is always a chance you will forget about making a pot of coffee and just let the carafe sit there for days or even weeks without cleaning. You cannot see the actual coffee and because of this, it is very easy to forget that coffee and coffee grounds are still inside the unit. I have experienced this more than once. I pulled out the carafe and basket to prepare for a fresh pot of coffee, only to notice that the carafe still contained some leftover coffee and the basket was still filled with coffee grinds, along with some mold/mildew. I never had to worry about a problem such as this with a glass carafe because I could easily see the leftover coffee.

Cuisinart is known for its many fine products, but the Cuisinart DCC- 150 10 Cup Coffee Maker is not the picture of coffee- making excellence I was hoping for. I can fully understand why the reviews of this coffee maker are so mixed, because it does have some potential problems that could make its use impractical for some. I find it sufficient for my limited, fast- drinking needs but I can see how some consumers will have a problem with the lack of heat, cleaning, and other issues.

Warm Coffee from Beginning to End. Thermal carafe coffee makers are nice for those who like a nice, warm cup of coffee and want to save electric power. These coffee makers do not heat continuously- the metal carafe receives the hot liquid and attempts to keep it insulated and warm, from the first cup to the final drink.

I have owned two different thermal carafe- style coffee makers and have found them useful, but not perfect. This Frigidaire model is the second one I have owned and it is about as good as my Cuisinart, which means it is good, but does have some issues. The greatest issue is that it doesn’t brew very quickly and this is particularly true when you dial the strength up to high, which you will want to do because the other settings produce coffee that is too weak. In this full strength setting, you have to wait and wait for the unit to complete the brewing cycle. I haven’t timed it, but I am sure it is over 10 minutes for a full pot. This is much too long and impractical when you’re in a hurry. You are forced to brew a smaller pot when time is tight.

Cleaning/drying is another issue. This is the same problem I had with my other thermal carafe. The way it is shaped, you have a very difficult time reaching inside, under the rim, to dry after washing. If you have VERY tiny hands, it might work but even then, it will be a challenge.

Some people will not like the fact that this coffee maker isn’t capable of brewing a really HOT cup of coffee. It is true- the coffee is not as hot as the coffee produced from an ordinary coffee maker. But I don’t mind this.
