They Work, but Try to Protect from the Sun. My patio has several type of furniture, one of which is a carry over from my previous home of 2 years ago. The furniture that was brought with me from old home is my glass table, patio chairs, and umbrella set. The furniture itself has stood the test of time, but the cushions, well, I have had to replace them for various reasons. And one set that I purchased for a quick replacement is Pillow Perfect Rounded Outdoor Chair Cushions.

I wanted cushions with a blue color scheme and that is what convinced me to buy these. The size was right and the price was right, so I went ahead and made the purchase. Attaching the cushions to my patio chairs was simple enough and required simply tying the strings on the back of the cushion, to secure them to the chair.

The comfort level of these cushions is certainly good. They are thick and I can sit on them for a while and still feel comfy. This is certainly important, but there are two concerns I have with these cushions that could influence if I buy them again: The tendency to fade and the tendency of the strings to break off. The fading is due, of course, to exposure to the sun and because of where my table and chairs are situated, they are exposed to a good deal of sunshine. This has caused the colors to noticeably fade, even after a single summer season. If possible, it is a good idea to keep your cushions in a shaded space or remove them during the colder season and store in a safe, dry, unsunny place.

Then, there is the tendency of the strings on the back- the ones you use to tie the cushions to the chairs- the break off. When this happens, there is no easy way to fix. I have found that, as long as only one string breaks, I'm usually fine because the other will hold the cushion in place. If two break, well, your cushion may very well start to flop in the wind. It really depends on how often you use the cushions. If you sit in them and move around a lot, like we do, then eventually, the strings are going to break.

Chair cushions are necessary when you on a patio set like mine and these cushions are fine for occasional use. Like I said, you can extend the life of the cushions and prevent fading by keeping out of the sun, but the issue with fading and the tendency of the strings to break off convince me to lower my rating to average overall.

It's Okay, but the Pump Design Needs Improvement. Permanent liquid soap dispensers are nice to have around. They are refillable and they cut down on costs because you can purchase a larger bottle of soap and save money per ounce. For this reason, I was happy to give the InterDesign Midi Soap Pump Caddy a try. It seemed like a nice addition to the kitchen, next to the sink, so I loaded it with liquid soap and put it to use.

From the outside, this dispenser has a nice appearance. The brushed nickel is attractive and I like that the soap dispenser is clear and completely see- through because that means I will know when the soap is about to run out. The two caddy holders are nice, too, because they can be used to store sponges and other items, for easy access.

As for the soap dispenser itself, it does look nice, but I have issues with the design that convince me to lower my overall rating. The greatest problem I have is with the dispensing mechanism. You press down to release soap and it returns to its normal position, which is expected, but the problem is that there is not enough space to press down. The pump needs to be re-designed to elevate it higher above the base. This would allow for more clearance and result in the right amount of liquid soap getting dispensed. The way it works now, you have to place your hands very close to the base and, with so little space, a single pump dispenses only a small amount of soap, and to the edge of your hand. It would be better if the nozzle was not only higher up, but also if it stretched further from the base in order to deposit the soap closer to the middle of the hand.

If you can get past the frustration with dispensing, you will find that the InterDesign Midi Soap Pump Caddy is a decent product. It makes an attractive enough addition to the kitchen and it has enough weight that it doesn’t require holding the base in order to use, like many of the plastic bottles do. It holds enough soap that it should go far between refills and it does have added compartments for storing other items, even if they are not all that large. Still, it’s difficult to ignore the dispensing design and I can understand why so many people rate this below average. I’m going to be more understanding and give this product 3 stars, but the manufacturer should definitely spend time on making what should be simple improvements.

It Works but Description is Misleading. Storage containers are a necessity for any household. We have lots of excess stuff and we need places to put it and keep it out of harm’s way. This need led me to get the DII Home Essentials Large Plate Storage Bin, a storage container recommended for dishes, photos, etc.

It’s only fourteen inches square and just four inches deep so it is very limited in what it can handle. I find it sufficient for my plastic plates plus other small plastic items. It won’t do for much else, but what can you expect for something this size?

Storage containers are important and they especially matter to someone in the early stages of relocation. This storage bin is acceptable, but I’m still a little annoyed that the manufacturer led me to believe it would be good for storing china and other breakables. It might work for items like that if you’re placing the storage container in one place and not moving it. Keeps Your Beer Cold and Your Friends Amused. Keeping your beer chilled and ready to drink is important. Finding a way to accomplish this during a football themed party is made easy and fun with the Football Inflatable Cooler from Big Mouth, Inc.

Big Mouth manufactures many novelty items related to football and this cooler is one of a handful designed to keep items cold during a tailgate or other party. The cooler is easy to store because it comes in a small box and has to be inflated to use. I found that it does take a good effort to get it blown up and ready to use and the reason is because the blow hole has a tight seal that, even when you squeeze, doesn’t let in much breath. On the positive side, that means it also doesn’t lose air when you let go. The cooler’s interior air space volume isn’t very big but again, it is an exercise in lung power to get it inflated completely and ready for use.

The interior section of this cooler, where the beer is chilled, isn’t very large compared to the rest of the cooler, but it is big enough to hold roughly 12 bottles or cans of beer without any problem. It’s deep enough that you can stand the bottles upright and still cover them with enough ice to keep them chilled. You could possibly squeeze in more bottle or cans, but best to leave some space for the ice and purchase a second cooler if you anticipate having a large number of cans or bottles in need of chilling.

My greatest issue with this novelty item is its flimsiness. There is no solid backing and that means you need to be very careful if you use it indoors. Once the ice starts to melt and your cans/bottles are floating in slush, it will be difficult to transport it to the nearest sink or outdoors to dump. You could very easily spill the water and ice everywhere, making a big mess. This is why I recommend using it outdoors for the most part. With it safely outside, this worry is eliminated.

One other issue I have with a cooler like this is that it could get punctured and therefore may have a short usable life. The manufacturer does include a patch kit so you can repair a problem like this without too much difficulty. Still, if you’re the type who likes to play rough with your cooler, then a product like this may not last very long.

Beer is an important part of any football game experience and with the Football Inflatable Cooler, you can enjoy your beer and amuse your friends with your cool beer storage device made with football in mind. The fact that this is inflatable and plastic means it does have its share of pros and cons, but as long as you’re careful, you should find this a fun addition to your next tailgate experience.

Adequate for the Amateur Juicer. Juicing is a great way to improve health. You can purchase pre- made juice, but if you really want to taste juice in its most natural form, you need to produce your own. For that, you need a small appliance to extract juice and one possible option is the AmazonBasics Wide-Mouth, 2-Speed Centrifugal Juicer with Juice Jug and Pulp Container, Black.

Utilitarian in design and functionality, this juicer has two speed settings and consists of the usual parts: Extractor/centrifuge, pulp container, chute, and plastic pusher to press the fruits and veggies through the opening along with a plastic measuring cup to catch the juice. You just turn the device on, place the plastic cup under the spout, and start pushing fruits and veggies through the opening. In a matter of minutes, you will have a serving of high- nutrient green juice, ready for consumption.

I’ve owned my share of juicers and I like them for the healthfulness that they encourage. This AmazonBasics juicer, compared to others I’ve owned, is very middle of the road overall. Among its positive points, it takes up little countertop space and I like the included plastic cup and the way it hooks itself under the spout. The measurements on the cup are handy, too, because this way you know exactly how much juice you are drinking.

Looking for cons, I am able to find a few. My greatest problem is that the centrifuge itself isn’t as efficient as it should be. It loses its grip on too much of the food contents, hurling them into the pulp container to discard. I often use kale when I juice and more often than not, I will find large pieces of kale in the pulp container. This shouldn’t happen. The juicer should be able to grip the pieces of food and extract more juice than this. I have been tempted to take the contents of the pulp container and run them through the juicer a second time for this reason.

Another concern I have with this juicer is that it seems to be working really, really hard to extract the juice. The extractor slows down as you push the food through, which is normal, but it makes an agonizing sound. And this makes me question the juicer’s durability. It seems like it will burn itself out with frequent use.

Fresh juice is a great addition to anyone’s diet. A good juicing machine is a necessary appliance when you want to make your own and the AmazonBasics Wide-Mouth, 2-Speed Centrifugal Juicer with Juice Jug and Pulp Container is one solution, albeit a weak one, to your quest for better health. It’s fine for those who only juice every now and then, but it will prove woefully inadequate for the more serious juicers in our ranks.

Two Tiers are Nice, but.... Like most people, I own a dishwasher and rely on it for most of my dishwashing needs. But there is still and will always be a need to wash dishes by hand and therefore a dish rack is a must. I prefer a durable, metal dish rack to the cheaper, plastic varieties and the latest to make its way to my kitchen is the XIGOO Dish Drying Rack.

Two- tier in design, this dish drying rack can handle a moderate number of dishes. The top rack is designed to hold plates while the bottom rack is intended for things that don’t need to be held in place. There is a side attachment for utensils, a second attachment that can hold up to three glasses or cups, and a third attachment that is good for holding a cutting board.

After using this dishrack a few times, I have come away with almost an equal share of pros and cons. I like the draining on the bottom- the water is channeled toward a drain in the center and there is an extension on the bottom that can be directed to the sink. The way it is designed, you can direct this drain in any direction. That means you can place the rack length- wise or sideways and turn the drain extender toward your sink. Having a second tier is nice as well and I like the separate attachment for knives- makes it easy to slip them into their own slot for drying.

Looking at the cons, I have found a few. For one, the dish rack is on the small side. It’s a good thing there is a second tier because the bottom tier is far too small to handle many dishes. Another thing I don’t like is that the utensil holder isn’t positioned to drain into the drip tray. There are holes to release the water, but they end up on the kitchen counter. And the two extension handles on the top rack, while they seem good for hanging a cup, will not allow the cup to dry properly because it won’t be upside down. Thus, these extenders have limited usefulness. Another issue I have is the rack's tendency to slide on the counter. The dish rack itself had non- skid feet, but the drip tray in which it sits doesn't. That means if you use the drip tray- and you almost certainly will want to- you will have to deal with it the possibility of sliding.

If you don’t have too many dishes to dry, the XIGOO Dish Drying Rack could suit your needs. I am undecided on this rack so far, for the reasons listed, and I decided to keep my previous rack within reach in case I decide I like it better and want it back. So, with an almost equal share of good and bad points, I am rating this rack average overall.

Good for Storing and Serving Oils and Syrups. Olive oil, vegetable oil, and other oils and syrups are common to all households. You can always pour what you need straight from the bottle you purchased at the store, but a good alternative is this PARACITY Glass Oil Dispenser.

This small pitcher holds about 20 ounces and can be used for most any type of oil. The opening on the top is large enough that you can easily pour the contents of a store bottle into the pitcher without spilling. The pitcher even has milliliter measurement markings, which can be useful in some instances.

As for its design, this is a practical container and I like that the opening on top is large enough that you don’t need a funnel. The spout is small, and I wonder if a thicker liquid could be poured from here without any problem. I’m likely going to use this pitcher for olive oil, since that is something we use frequently in my household. I have considered pancake syrup, but the thickness might be an issue.

The markings on the side of this container can be useful, but there are no ounce markings, only milliliters, so be ready to convert, if necessary. There is also a small plug that comes with this, to block the opening on the spout and keep things from getting in through the small opening. This is a good idea, but it’s only a matter of time until this small plug gets lost. When that happens, you will need to cover it with a small piece of plastic wrap or something similar. Also, the glass seems thin, so one needs to be careful or else this will break.

I like having small contraptions around the kitchen for storing and serving. This glass oil dispenser is good to have around, although certainly not a necessity, since store- bought containers are just as convenient. It seems fragile, but it’s still got enough going for it to recommend.

text:
Underwhelming desk - concerns for longevity. Overall, this desk looks nice but leaves me concerned with its longevity due to flimsy feeling materials.

Pros: the desk looks nice, and is the advertised size. Height seems good, but I don’t yet have chairs to see how well it fits with a standard height chair. Relatively easy to assemble. Minimal screws and parts made it easier for me to assemble myself. The desk is also surprisingly light, and moves easily across the carpet for positioning. Metal Frame seems sturdy.

Cons: one of the tops came damaged, and shows just how thin the veneer on the top board is. The biggest con for me is how flimsy the whole top feels when any sort of weight is put on it. This seems to be largely due to the top support plank, which runs from one end to the other (also mdf). I believe it’s supposed to prop both of the desk top halves up to support the middle of the desk, but as you can see in the photo, this board was flexed and does not support both sides. Additionally, all screws were hand tightened, but you can see how the screw posts pulled into the soft mdf, immediately damaging. These will loosen up quickly over normal use of the desk and don’t leave me confident this desk will last very long with two people using it. Lastly, the description advertises cable management via the desk holes, but it also mentions built in usb ports, which are not on this desk. Misleading advertising.

text: Recommend with reservations.. I bought this French Press for my camping trip. I thought it would be an easier method for making coffee, which it was. My main complain with French Press coffee brewers is that the coffee gets cold while it sits and brews. I thought that the thermal design would eliminate this problem.  I was wrong. It still cooled off unacceptably while brewing. The problem is that, even though the double walled design should hold in the heat, the opening in the spout allows the heat to escape through the top. I improvised a solution of my own by plugging up the spout with a wadded up paper towel while the coffee brewed. This was somewhat successful and allowed me to have hotter coffee than if I hadn't stopped it up. Plugging up the hole again, while I drank my coffee, kept the left over coffee warm enough to have a second cup, though it was cooler than the first. Without doing that, the coffee would be completely cold by the time I finished my first cup. If Planetary Designs wants to improve this design, I would recommend a completely closed system that allows the coffee to brew without any heat loss. The thermal, insulated design is really useless without that.

text:
Just so-so. Does this egg cooker cook? Yes it does. Does it do it well? No. The directions are really unclear, mostly because the measuring cup that measures the water, and the directions on how to use it are nonsensical. I read it several times when trying to make some hard boiled eggs. In the end, I had to just make my best guess. The same with the "poached" eggs.

I made two different kinds of eggs with this. I made 6 hard-boiled eggs and 2 "poached" eggs (cooked separately). First, the "poached" eggs. Why the quotation marks on "poached"? Because the directions tell you to smear the little poaching cups with butter. That is the way I cooked them, by following the directions. Most people poach eggs to avoid adding fat. I haven't tried to do it without butter. Don't know if it will stick to the cup or not. Either way, the eggs didn't cook evenly. There is a hot spot in the heating pan. One egg was cooked perfectly, and the other one was still had runny whites and was under done. I had to zap that one in the microwave for about 15 sec to finish the cooking. The unit DID shut off this time.

When I cooked the hard-boiled eggs, the water went completely dry, and it didn't shut off automatically like it is supposed to. It actually started to burn the bottom of the egg that sat over the hot spot. The shell turned brown from the heat. All the eggs were over-cooked, making the yolk chalky (instead of creamy) and gray all around the outside. Luckily, I had set a timer so I could check on it. The instructions said that it should take about 12 minutes. As I said, the unit didn't shut off when the water went dry and 12 minutes over-cooked the eggs. 10 minutes would have been better.

PROBLEMS:
1 - Unclear measurement markings.
2 - Hot spots on heating pan lead to uneven cooking.
3 - Automatic shut-off doesn't always shut off when the water goes dry.

Does this gadget cook eggs? Yes it does, but you need to set a timer, experiment with it a bit to get the right water amounts and times, and set a timer to check on it. Useful and recommended...with reservations.

Works Well But Surface Gets a Little Too Hot. This is my first exposure to electric kettles, having used a whistling tea kettle for many years. While it seems to work very well and it does what it is supposed to do I found that some caution is required when using it due to surface and steam heat.

The idea of this type of kettle is very straightforward - it contains an integrated hot plate in the bottom of the kettle that heats up quickly and is used specifically for boiling water. Because of the low wattage it draws less electricity than using a stove top kettle or the microwave and because of the rapid heating it boils water very quickly which saves time.

I have used the kettle to heat a small amount of water and to heat the full kettle's worth and understandably it takes longer to heat more. This should not be a huge surprise. That said, it still works quickly and the water boils in a lot less time than when heated up in a microwave (which I find to be faster than the stove top). It does a great job of getting the water boiling quickly and without risking a spill.

In spite of its usefulness in saving time and energy, I have two reservations when it comes to using this kettle. My first observation is that the surface of the kettle's pitcher gets very hot, to the point of discomfort when you touch it. Well, of course it's going to get warm but the fact that it gets as warm as it does concerns me. It would have been nice if the pitcher was better insulated (or, rather, insulated at all). More unpleasant, though, is that after the water is hot if you open the top for pouring a cloud of steam tends to billow out and it's a little too easy to get a steam burn if caution is not used. Sure, you should not stick your hand in there and it should be obvious that there will be steam but the fact that it comes straight up and out is concerning.

This is not a bad kettle. It's actually a nice product and it works as advertised. Unfortunately, it needs a design revisit.

Light duty shelving only. These shelving units install reasonably well to studs, which is the one option I currently have for them. They are made of semi-heavy plastic and hold up ok to light to medium loads. For getting junk off the work bench and out of the way, these are a nice option. That said, they have limited functionality because of their somewhat small size.

Because these shelves are narrow, they will not adequately hold something like a regular-sized plant mister, or a paint can. A smaller mister or a regular spray can will fit with little effort. To be sure, these shelves provide a very nice solution for getting small containers of liquids off the bench and out of the way without creating a crammed, chaotic catch-all system where there are multiple layers to pick through.

These shelves are heavy plastic so they will hold up under moderate load. That said, I would not trust them to hold a full row of liquid containers reliably, especially if they are installed in a warm environment - plastic tends to warp and break down when in that kind of setting so keep this in mind.

The shelf with the compartments is ideal for in a small workshop - nails, screws, clips, small light bulbs, etc. can be served up easily without needing more jars. The flat shelf is good for cans and jars and bottles, and the slotted shelf is excellent for the likes of screwdrivers, punches and similarly shaped tools.

These shelves are handy for light organization but lack the depth to hold anything larger than a spray can. For a modest shop in need of some organization these will server well, but for more serious tools shops and garages these are not large enough or sturdy enough to be useful.

Very Nice Crockpot, But Not Really Programmable. We use crock pots in our house almost weekly for the convenience and for their ability to tenderize meats. I have used mostly Rival and Hamilton Beach crock pots but I am familiar with several other brands, but Bella is a brand which which I was previously unfamiliar. My impression of this crock pot is positive, but it is not programmable as it has been advertised.

Most crockpots have either two or three temperature settings - warm, low and high. The Bella crockpot has three, and all of these work as one would expect. There's no rocket science here - the element heats the ceramic liner to a specific temperature and maintains that temperature through cooking.

This is an easy to use crockpot that heats nicely and does a good job. It seems to cook at proper temperatures and it does not get too hot to touch on the surface. The lid fits nicely too, which is a plus. Things we have made with this crock pot have turned out right so far.

This particular is touted as being programmable, but it isn't. Instead, it has digital settings control with a built in countdown timer. So, for example you can set it to cook on low for 8 hours through the use of some button settings. When the time is up, the crock put turns off completely. The programmable crock pots I have seen switch to the warm setting after the time is up, which makes better sense. Any advantage to having a digital control is lost if it is unable to change modes automatically.

Another oversight in the controls is that there is no notification that the time is up. A sound alerting the user that it has completed the cycle would be a nice thing if it's not going to change modes, but this is not there either. So, a user must be conscious of when the crock pot is actually going to finish. This really defeats the whole purpose of having a timer on it, and it actually is a negative. If the user isn't aware of when it cuts off, there may be cold food waiting for dinner.

This is a decent crock pot and it looks nice. Some real thought went into the design of the appliance and the digital controls are easy to use. It is unfortunate that the timer and programmability aspects just aren't there for the user. If you want a programmable crock pot, look for other options. If you don't mind keeping track of cooking times and paying attention to how much time is left on the timer, this is not a bad device.

This finish is where the problem lies with his peel. The finish is not even and it looks like the peel was set down somewhere when the finish was still wet as there is an obvious mark indicative of making contact with another surface. The mark is rough and unbaked dough catches on it when sliding a pizza into the oven. It is a shame - this could have been avoided with a little bit of sanding before it left the manufacturer. I can certainly fix it, but I shouldn’t have to.

Otherwise, this is not a bad peel. Others have reported cracked wood and shoddy finish, and while they may be true the only issue I have with mine is the finish being rough. It supports the size of pizza I like to make and it does a good job of allowing me to remove a pizza from the oven without trouble.

I have read a number of the other reviews and many point out flaws with this peel. Mine was flawed, but in a different way than what other reviewers have shared. This means something important - if you choose this peel, inspect it very carefully for problems as there seems to be some issues with quality control.

Decent Set but Lacks Fit and Finish. Westinghouse is not a name I would have ever associated with cookware. Until now, in my mind the Westinghouse brand meant electronics and in particular light bulbs. I was curious to see how well this cast iron cookware would compare to Lodge and Griswold/Wagner, and so far I have found it to be less than great. It is a good dutch oven/skillet set, but it lacks in the fit-and-finish.

This is a 3-quart dutch oven with a 10” skillet for the lid. This is a great combination and makes fine use of an otherwise wasted lid. I have used cast iron skillets and dutch ovens for years, and I especially like the way cast iron retains heat and also how it heats evenly. It is more consistent than aluminum, and it does not leech aluminum into the things you cook (it leeches iron, which is better for you). The trade-off is a lot heavier than most other cookware.

These are marketed as pre-seasoned, and that is not entirely accurate though it is consistent with other manufacturers’ labeling. This set does have an initial coating toward pre-seasoning but this is not sufficient to prevent things from sticking. Plan to season this set again after washing it. This is not unique to this set; I would give the same advice for Lodge pans that have been pre-seasoned.

My main issue with this set is the fact that it is very rough surfaced and feels like sandpaper. If you plan to cook something like eggs in the skillet, plan to spend a good bit of time cleaning it with a stiff brush over and over until there is a very thick layer of seasoning. For vegetables, oily fools like sausage, spaghetti sauces and other things, it’s fine. Entry Level Gaming Chair. I selected this item for my son who is a gamer and spends a good bit of time in front of the computer. It’s a rocker style gaming chair, a style of chair with which I was previously unfamiliar, and I was hopeful that it would be an enjoyable accessory for him. Unfortunately, it is not as good as we had hoped and it doesn’t really meet the need. For what it is, it is acceptable at the price point.

Trades Power for Convenience. My wife has been after me for a vacuum cleaner like this that is small, lightweight and is easy to handle. I selected this one for her and we spent an evening testing it out and putting it through its paces. It has some excellent qualities but we were both disappointed with it in several areas.

Taking this fellow out of the box, it comes disassembled to save space in shipping. Assembly took less than 5 minutes, and most of the time spent was taking the parts out of the box and getting them out of the protective plastic. That was a good sign right off the bat.

This is an extremely lightweight unit, even with the battery installed. It is definitely easy to handle and that’s excellent for her, as she doesn’t like pushing around our heavy Dyson. When it’s broken down and being used as a small convenience vacuum, such as for doing the stairs or working in the car it is even more lightweight. This one gets high marks for the size and weight.

Our first task for this vacuum was the linoleum kitchen floor, and it did a fantastic job with it. We ran it on low power, and it managed to pick up almost everything, the exceptions being things that were stuck down and had to be scraped from the floor. Because of the size and the swivel action of the head, it is super easy to maneuver around corners, along the cabinetry and under chairs and tables. We kicked on the “turbo” mode and it didn’t seem to make any difference in this scenario – not a big deal, just a data point. Even when on full power, we were pleased with how quiet this vacuum cleaner is compared to our corded upright.

We moved over to the carpet and hit a high-traffic area, and as we predicted it did a fair job but not as good a job as our Dyson. I expected that a battery-powered vacuum would trade the convenience for power, and I was right, though it did well enough to pick up most visible debris from the carpet.

Where this vacuum really showed its compromise in power, though, was when we decided to clean cat hair from the couch. We have two cats, and they love our cloth-covered couch, so there’s plenty of hair to vacuum away on any given day. We converted the vacuum to a handheld, attached the upholstery head, put it on high power and proceeded to vacuum the couch cushions. It did a fair job, but it left as much as it collected and we reverted to a different vacuum to finish the job.

When finished, we emptied the collection bin, and this proved to be the easiest vacuum to empty of any we have used. Press a button on the side to pop open the canister door, and simply dump out the contents into a plastic bag. It doesn’t require partial disassembly or anything. It is smaller than most, of course, so it will not collect as much.

We ran the battery completely out of power and plugged it in to charge. It literally took 5 hours to go from completely empty to fully-charged. That’s a lot of time to charge the battery, to get 30-45 minutes of run time! That requires some planning ahead when using this unit. In light of this, I looked into getting a second battery, and was startled to find that batteries are presently selling for $100. That’s 1/3 the cost of the vacuum itself. I was hoping the battery would instead cost $50-$60, which to me is a reasonable cost. On the plus side, the battery does not need to be in the vacuum cleaner itself to be charged.

This vacuum cleaner is an interesting unit. It has some excellent qualities, among them being size and weight and the ability to convert to a hand-held with no cord, but it has some downsides too, such as the battery cost and the lack of power in certain circumstances. I can’t say this is a bad unit, but consider how you’d use it: if you’ll be using it on hardwood or linoleum, it’s really great, but if you want to use it on carpet of furniture it struggles to perform. Also weigh the cost/convenience of buying a second battery – it’s an appreciable chunk of money for a fairly short runtime.

Limited Usefulness, Depending on Size/Shape of the Bread. I have been making artisan loaves of bread for over 20 years to feed my family and to share with friends and coworkers. Sandwich loaves are easy to store – put them in a plastic bag and they’ll stay soft. Baguettes and peasant loaves are another issue: those should stay crusty on the outside and when stored in plastic they soften quickly. Their odd shape also makes is awkward to store them as well. These bread savers are a solution to that. They’re not ideal but they work well enough and they seem to be made well.

The idea is simple. Instead of wrapping the loaves in plastic wrap, these rubber caps go over the end of the loaves to keep the sliced ends from getting stale while leaving the uncut end exposed to air, allowing it to remain crisp. In theory this is ideal. However, there are a couple of issues, neither are deal breakers but should be kept in mind. First, these are basically sleeves and the portion of the crust that is covered will soften. This is unavoidable but is better than having a squishy loaf. Second, these are not one-size-fits all. They are stretchy and will fit over the ends of most peasant loaves, but they will not fit over a traditional baguette (they’re too large to stay on) and they will not work for large boules (wrong shape and often too small). For the average peasant loaf or Italian loaf, though, these work well enough.

I’m on the fence with these. They answer a need for keeping bread from staling on the ends, but the size and shape limits their use.

Not Great on Carpet; Lightweight. I selected this vacuum cleaner with the hopes that it would be a suitable replacement for a very cheap and inexpensive upright vacuum cleaner. I’ve had good experiences with Black+Decker tools as well as kitchen appliances, so part of my reason for selecting it was based on brand recognition. It has been a big let-down and I can’t recommend this vacuum cleaner without reservation except in specific cases and for specific uses.

Almost everything about this vacuum feels like it was made with lower-quality materials, the exception being the metal extending tube which is actually solid and well-made. The plastic tubing to which it attaches is cheap and is held to the metal tube only by friction, not unlike pipe fitting without adhesives. The attachments also feel substandard, and the housing feels lightweight.

The main attachment which is used for carpet and hardwood is probably the biggest issue with this whole system. It does not work smoothly on carpet and it takes real effort to get it to roll. I thought perhaps I had the lever on it set wrong (the lever moves the leading brush which is useful for pet hair), and that wasn’t it – moving the lever so it protruded the brush made it appreciably worse. I did figure out that on carpet, turning down the power does make it roll better, but then the suction is reduced and it doesn’t pick up as well anyway. Slightly larger wheels would solve this issue, I think.

When using with the edge attachment or small brush, this vacuum becomes a serious contender. This has a lot of power and it can definitely suck up dirt and debris from small spaces. I did not understand the reasoning behind the variable speeds – at first. Once I realized that full power is not always ideal, I got better results and found the unit easier to maneuver. The power level also affects loudness too so it can be operated at slower speeds when quieter operation is desired.

When the metal extension is removed from the mix, this vacuum works quite well as a car vacuum. It is powerful enough to get most things out of the flooring and from between the seat and base. The brush works well for dusting the dash as well. It’s also excellent on hardwood floors and linoleum where there is no carpet with which to contend.

The unit is lightweight and relatively easy to carry. It is not as easy to carry as a cordless upright, but it is not a tank either.

I have mixed feelings about this vacuum cleaner. On one hand, it does a sub-optimal job on carpet due to the design of the floor attachment and the overall unit feels of substandard quality. On the other hand, it is good on non-carpet floors and it has plenty of power. Your mileage may vary. For me, this isn’t my first choice when I need to vacuum my living room but is my go to when I want to clean my car.

The grinding process also is significantly quieter than when using my blade grinder which is a big plus and one of the reasons I selected it. The capacity can be varied so you can grind enough beans for 2 cups, 18 cups, or anywhere in between.

The unit disassembles easily enough for cleaning which is good. It even comes with a small brush for getting into the reservoir where the beans are ground (not where the grounds are deposited, though it will help a little there too).

The main issue I have with this grinder is the coarseness setting. It is supposed to allow for grinding beans coarsely for a French press or very fine for espresso, with varying degrees of grit in between. On the most coarse setting it still grinds the beans quite finely, almost to a soft powder and totally unusable for my French press and nearly borderline for my drip coffee maker. I haven’t found a way to adjust this any more than just using the coarseness knob.

I like this grinder but I have reservations about recommending it. It would be so much more useful and effective if the coarseness setting was more accurate and was more in line with where it should be. It’ll work great if you want espresso or cappuccino, and it works acceptably for drip makers, but it’s a non-starter if you use a French press.

Great Bottle But Very Overpriced. I prefer glass bottles to plastic and metal, so the Soma water bottle is a good choice for me. It’s made well and it looks great. The only reservation I have about it – the price.

The bottle is heavy glass borosilicate. This particular type of glass is somewhat more resistant to shattering, though its strength is in being fairly impervious to rapid temperature changes. This bottle is not designed to be used for hot beverages so I suspect it could have been made with a lower grade of glass and still be shatter-resistant. It’s not unwelcome, either way. Because it is glass and not plastic, it doesn’t stain which is great when you fill it with something colorful and fair to wash it afterward – it still comes clean.

The bottle has a rubbery sleeve that serves two purposes. First, it is an insulator and it will keep you from freezing your hands when drinking something very cold. Second, if your hands are wet it is still sufficient to help you maintain a good, solid grip on the bottle.

The cap is the weak point though it is relative. It is plastic on the inside, with a heavy bamboo outer shell to protect it. It will likely survive it you drop it, though it seems like this is the one part that is most likely to fail. So far, I have used the bottle and kept the cap on a nearby shelf, so I don’t have an opportunity to drop it but this is more so I won’t actually misplace it.

My one concern with this bottle is the actual cost. As I write this, the bottle is selling for $25-$30 based on color and that’s just absurd. I can see asking between $15-$20 at most. At $30 though (I have the white one), I will not replace it when and if I somehow manage to break it.

Other than being priced unreasonably high, this is a nice water bottle. It has some heft to it, it can survive short drops and jostles, it has a non-slip sleeve and it looks great. Before buying, though, wait for the price to come down or catch it on sale.

Works Well but Needs a Design Revisit. The best slow cooker I have used has been a Hamilton Beach Stay or Go, so I was excited to try this new one by Hamilton Beach. It has an interesting feature set and it works well, but I dislike some of the design decisions.

The listing states that this is a stainless steel crock pot, and that’s true when referring to the outer body of the cooker. The liner itself is aluminum (a detail that is not highlighted but is mentioned in the listing) and is coated in some kind of non-stick material (not sure if it’s Teflon). That’s ok, but that needs to be more clearly described. The liner is very lightweight and is easy to handle and easy to clean. Being the clumsy person that I am, it means I can’t drop it and break it like I can with a stoneware crock.

This is a 6-quart cooker, so it can handle a full pot roast or roasting bird. Unlike the Stay or Go line, the lid does not lock in place – that’s ok, if you do not need to transport the cooker anywhere. Because the lid does not lock in place for transport, it’s a simpler design and easier to clean.

It happened to arrive on a day when I needed to use the slow cooker for dinner. Instead of using my Stay or Go, I used this one instead. Dinner turned out exactly as expected and this cooker did a good job.

However, there are a couple of things about this cooker that turn me off. First, the controls are not granular enough. You can set the temperature to Low, High and Warm at the press of a button which is great, but you cannot set the time in any less than 2-hour increments, up to 10 hours. If you need to put something in for any other interval, there isn’t any way to do it. Second, the cooker has absolutely no time display so you have no indicator of how much time remains. It does change the time setting as the time counts down, so it shows what two-hour block it’s in during the cook cycle. Whether there are 2 hours or 5 minutes left, it says “2 hours”. Finally, the outer surface is definitely less insulated that any other slow cooker I have used and with no effort at all I got a first-degree burn on my hand. The liner gets hotter than a stoneware crock too and it’s easy to get a wicked burn in no time.

This isn’t a bad cooker, but there are some design decisions with which I disagree than make it a less-than-ideal choice. The controls and display need a revisit. A little better unsulation on the outer part of the cooker would be greatly appreciated. And to be honest, I would rather have seen the liner be made of uncoated stainless steel instead of coated aluminum. It does work well and it’s easy to clean which are pluses, but to me these are not enough to counter the negatives. This is a cooker I will use when I need a backup or more than one at a time – I’ll stick with the Stay or Go as my go-to slow cooker.

Room for Improvement. I have wanted a fat fryer for a while and I was pleased to have the opportunity to try this one. For the most part I am pleased with it but I do see a couple of areas for improvement.

This is a generous-sized fryer, holding about 1 gallon of oil. That’s a generous size for making all kinds of good things like onion rings, fries, or my favorite, oysters. It has dual controls for time and temperature that are very easy to understand and very easy to operate. It has a lid that closes over the baskets so splatter is minimized during the cooking process and there are ridges on the baskets so they can be clamped above the hot oil to drip off excess fat before serving. Overall, the design is nice.

I have made three observations that leave room for improvement, though none of these are deal breakers:

1. This unit takes quite a while to heat up. Do not expect to turn it on and have hot oil 5 minutes later.

2. There are two baskets, but one large oil chamber. So, you can cook two things at once, but if they’re not the same thing you can get mixed flavors. A good case in point is shrimp and fried potatoes. The potatoes will come out tasting like shrimp. It would have been nice to have either a permanent division between them or a removable partition so that you can cook things together if you want or separately.

3. The baskets are very, very cheap. When I took the fryer out of the box I could not use the baskets until I bent them back into shape so they’d fit. I understand that they do not need to be solid, heavy wire frame baskets, but they should not be so flexible that they get misshapen in shipping. This is my biggest disappointment with this fryer so far.

Overall, I am happy with this fryer but there is very definitely room for improvement. It works well, it is easy to understand and use and it produces good results. But, there’s enough improvement that can be made to give me pause.

This is a set of 7 tools though I say that begrudgingly. There are 4 actual utensils – a knife, a spatula, a scraper and a fork. Also included are a knife sheath and two squirt bottles for oil and/or sauces.

It looks like a nice set, but it isn’t anything special. The problem is in the quality, or rather the lack of it. The knife isn’t high end either, being comparable to a store-brand generic.

text: The truth about this percolator. Visually this percolator looks virtually identical to the original Farberwares from the 1950's that were made in the USA.  The new units being sold today are manufactured in China. The base and handle are made of dense heat resistant plastic that emulates the phenolic material used in the original models. The result is a slightly lighter pot. The finish on the metal is less resilient than found on the older models and somewhat more susceptible to discoloration. This won't be an issue if you care for the pot properly and keep it clean. The brew cycle is quite fast which some people will like. The downside to a quick brewing cycle is much less yield from your coffee grinds.  It takes at least 3 standard scoops to yield 4 cups of medium strength coffee. That's about 50% less efficient than what a decent drip machine will deliver. On the upside, the quick brewing cycle doesn't overcook the coffee and yields pretty decent results. The Achilles heel on these machines appears to be the heating element. If you get a good unit you can expect 3 or 4 years out of this pot with regular use, perhaps a bit more if you're lucky. That said there seems to be a fair number of these units that suffer from premature heating element failure. The elements are either made cheaply, not big enough, or not always installed properly.  That said you'll be hard pressed to find a nicer looking retro styled pot that makes decent percolated coffee for $50. No, it's not the same as the virtually indestructible Farberware pots from the 50's and 60's but it's a pretty decent product all things considered. Purchase an inexpensive Square Trade or similar extended warranty on it for a few bucks for peace of mind and you won't have to worry if you end up with a bad one.

We use a lot of these. We have been using this little timer for about three years now.
To be clear, we've used MANY of this STYLE of time over the last few years.

back and forth until you get just the right angle to actually view it. (Even then, I sometimes
cross my fingers that I read it right!)

They are easy to set. Because of the difficulty I have in reading them, I just count the minutes
while pushing the minute button!

If you are doing several batches, like when you bake cookies or muffins, you have to push
the Min and Sec buttons at the same time. Just push the start button to get it going.

The timer makes a beeping sound when it goes off. The beep gets weaker with time, so within a
couple months of regular use, you'll have to really listen for it carefully.
The magnets are useful - they have a magnet on the back, so we stick them to the vent hood
over the oven.

I'd like to find a reliable wind-up time, but haven't found a decent one yet that got good reviews.
So until then, we'll keep buying these 3 or 4 at a time from the local dollar store, and enjoy
them while they last. They come in three colors - black, blue or red.

Keep on shopping - okay for a buffet table, but that's it!. This one has a ways to go before it is useful.
I bought it because our family loves deviled eggs and I make them almost weekly in the warmer weather.
I wanted a way to store more deviled eggs, as the container I had only held 12 halves. Not enough! The fact that each tray held 18 halves was really a great thing, so I thought. I also wanted something that wouldn't take up a lot of refrigerator room, and thought this might slide in on top of other items in the fridge.

The item came with the two trays and lids shrink-wrapped together. There are little clamps on the egg portion of the tray that hook to the lid portion. Not well, but they hook. There is NOTHING remotely sturdy about this set. You cannot pick it up by the handle. If you think you can quickly grab an egg and pop the lid back on, think again - it is not quick and you will probably need both hands.

The tray itself holds the eggs very well. Almost too well - the indentations are deep, and we found ourselves using a fork to get the eggs back out. No big deal, but something you should know about these. They would work very well for a buffet table (that is at your home, and you did not have to transport them in these trays anywhere). Some others have said they put ice in the upside down lid and put the tray on the ice. I could see that being helpful in a picnic situation.

Bottom line is that they do not fasten well enough in any way. I would not trust them for transporting eggs. I would not trust lifting them out of the refrigerator. I would not even trust them to keep the eggs fresh, because the seal is not tight on the top/bottom. It basically sits on top of the gg tray, and you use the little latches to pretend to hook the top to the bottom. Meh at best. I would have returned these, but as mentioned, I can see these working well for a buffet or self-serve party situation. That's ALL they would be good for, in my opinion. Just too flimsy for anything else.
I have already purchased a different set via Amazon that is perfect for our needs and airtight too.
So, if you have a lot of home dinner parties or family dinners, this will work on the food table.
If you don't and might want to drive to somewhere and bring your deviled eggs with you, please get a different container.

You'll note in the photo that the ornament they display is actually very small, and does not have a drop-down hanger of any kind - it is a very short little hanger too. text:
Clean & Convenient (Bags Beat Bins For Sure!). First, I think Oreck deserves a lot of very high praise for being the first to make one of these types of cordless vacuums that have a bag (which they call a Pod, of course). I hate the collection bin-type of vacuums because I do not like the mess and dust inside the collection bins.

At the occasional $399 discounted-by-Oreck price, I give this Oreck Pod Vacuum 5 stars because it is a bagged cordless, which means no mess and dirt and dust inside a collection bin you constantly see and frequently have to clean. When this vacuum is sold at its full retail $569 price, I will deduct 1 star because I feel it's too expensive at that high price.

I also deduct 1 star because this vac cannot be used with the a/c cord plugged in. If the battery power is depleted (or if in the future the battery no longer can hold a charge), the vacuum becomes absolutely useless. It would have been really nice if we had the option of running the vac with the power cord plugged in just as a backup.

One more negative: The soft bristle brush easily sheds its bristles--and the bristles easily become deformed--by just running the brush lightly over bed sheets or a soft blanket, etc. (And you might want to use this cordless vac on those types of things to vacuum up hair, etc. I have received multiple replacement brushes from Oreck just in case the one I received was an anomaly, but they all do the same shedding thing as mentioned, and quite badly.

This cordless vacuum is lightweight, and it has good suction. It is convenient to use on stairs, and on bathroom and kitchen floors. On low or no pile carpets it also works well. On medium to high pile carpets it is not as easy to push and pull, but it works well.

If you dislike dirty vacuum collection bins and if the price is in your budget, this Oreck Pod Cordless Vacuum is certainly worth considering...and assuming you do not get a defective one, you'll probably be happy you purchased it.

Decent Grinder, Hard on the Hands. I like this grinder, it produces a perfect grind for my French press. However if you want a super fine grind for espresso you're not likely to get it. You change the grind by tightening the top knob that also holds the handle on. This means each time you refill the whole bean container you're going to have to guess how tight you had it beforehand. It's a little aggravating because there's no set grind levels. Your grind will be different every time.

I'm disabled and have some serious nerve damage in my hands as well as arthritis trouble just about everywhere. Today, the third time I used this grinder, I wanted to make two large mugs of coffee. I had to open and put whole beans in the grinder three times. Unscrew the small and somewhat hard to remove knob. Remove the cap and handle then fill the cylinder with beans then put it all back together to spend several minutes grinding away. After I was done with my third cycle I was pretty sore but I did get a couple great cups of coffee for my efforts.

In the end it works okay, again for a grind great for a French press, which I think is the best way to make coffee. It can give you the sense of accomplishment to hand grind your own beans and it is a bit more gentle on the beans. But it's a lot of effort in the morning. Me? I'll used up the bag of whole beans I bought to test this with and then I think I'm going back to buying fresh ground coffee.
I received this item in exchange for my review.

text:
Does The Job (edited). Heater warms up quick, heat output is rather impressive and warms my 12-foot x 12-foot bedroom in just a few minutes. There was a brief smell as it initially started up but that was even shorter than I expected. The timer and remote, which is fairly basic, work fine. Setting a temperature allows the heater to turn on and off over time maintaining the room temperature. I like that a unit at this price point has a removable and washable filter. I gave it four stars because we can't award half stars, this is really more a three and a half star item because of the. . .
Cons -
The display is on the top, the unit uses the same beep tone for everything. So you can't see temperature or any changes you make to the system. I wake up in the middle of the night, it's chilly and I want the room warmer so I grab the remote, there's a couple beeps and. . . I have NO idea if I've changed the fan, temperature, turned the swing mode on. You need to get up and look at top of the unit to see what's what.
The temperature only changes in five (5) degree increments. Why? I like specific comfort levels and it's really hard, for me at least, to be comfortable at 75° when I want it to be 72° and 60° is too chilly when I would prefer 63°. It may be nit picky but I see no reason in 2020 for a heater to only operate at five degree intervals.
I have no idea what the swing feature does. The unit doesn't pivot and it only has one exhaust vent so. . . what's it do? The instruction book doesn't say.
(here's the edit) Found another con, this is enough to drop the rating to three stars. I don't like my room hot, warm is more than enough. I'm quite happy to have the temp set to 60° or if it's a bit damp and raw 65°. Turn the unit off, as an example, when you're going out and don't want to leave a heater running when you aren't home and it defaults to 70° when you turn it back on! That just. . . annoying! Who makes these arbitrary decisions and why? This is dumb. Especially since the manual says it starts up with the previously used settings. It does not. (end edit)
The unit operates either vertically or horizontally so there's no tip-over protection.

text:
What's It Doing?. Is it? Isn't it? I ran this continuously for a month in my 11' x 12' bedroom. I've checked the filter a couple times and it appears to be nearly as clean as the day I got the purifier. I made sure to close the door quickly, spent 12+ hours at a time in the room and to be completely honest I haven't detected any difference in the air quality/feel of the room with this running and without.
Construction seems decent, it's sturdy and things snap in and out with satisfying solid sounds. Moving this I found next to impossible, the handle is shallow and slopes at the wrong angle to get a good grip. There's also nothing inside the hole to grab onto, it's just a rectangular hole in the back. I'm disabled and almost dropped it twice just moving it to the back of the house. There's a UV light inside to kill mold and bacteria. I know the technology works, the local hospital has them in every room and our A/C vendor keeps trying to sell us one. When you turn on the UV light a half ring across the face of the unit lights up BRIGHT blue. You can't dim the light and there's no built in cover. You're not going to want to run the UV light when you're trying to sleep. In the past I've slept with lights on in the room (usually hospitals) and I can't stand this on when I'm trying to sleep. Speaking of sleep. You won't want to run this on anything but low if you're using this in a bedroom. Medium and high move a LOT of air (be sure to keep away from drapes) and make a LOT of noise. On the subject of noise. In the course of the month I've been testing this unit the fan, on low, has gotten almost twice as loud as it was when I first plugged it in. I've vacuumed the filter and checked the visible parts of the unit over and it seems fine so the fan's just gotten noisier which I find exceptionally annoying as I have very sensitive hearing.
In the end? I don't know what if anything this is doing beyond running air through the device. I don't feel healthier. The air doesn't feel healthier. My eyes and sinuses bother me exactly as much as they did before this got here. I haven't seen or felt any benefit from this room air purifier.

The glass top is easy to wipe clean and has a hefty feel, but the plastic base is extremely lightweight and feels cheap.The plastic door to access the batteries feels cheaply made. I do like the look of the glass top, and this has a small footprint on the counter. Also, the fact that it takes two AAA batteries (vs. button-cell batteries like my thin-line digital scale) makes it easier to find / replace batteries (my thin digital scale requires unscrewing the battery compartment door to replace the batteries).

Verdict: This is fine for those looking for an entry-level scale, particularly for those weighing portions, or for weighing small letters, etc., but more experienced bakers and those who frequently cook using metric will want a scale that offers more versatility.

Good concept, but needs work (would have been four stars if lid snapped onto colander!). I own numerous OXO gadgets, many of which I wouldn't cook without. When I had the chance to review the 3-Piece Berry Bowl and Colander Set, I was excited. The 1.5-qt bowl has a nonslip bottom and all three parts are dishwasher safe. I used it to wash and presoak mung beans and fresh blackberries. For the mung beans, I stored them in the fridge overnight, and ran into the major design flaw: the lid is designed to snap onto the bowl, but only if the colander isn't inside. I had my mung beans sitting in the colander (in water) and the lid continually fell off when I would move it in the fridge. Likewise, if you have already rinsed fresh berries, you will want to store them in the colander to keep them from sitting in moisture. Also, my lid didn't fit the bowl; to make it snap on required a lot of contortion and hand strength, making it unfriendly for those with arthritis (which OXO products are marketed to). It was also extremely difficult to pry off once the lid was on the bowl. The bowl itself is smooth with no handles, so you'll find it hard to hang onto the slippery bowl and pry off the lid at the same time.

By making the lid so it doesn't fit the colander (the colander has handles that extend beyond the edge of the bowl to keep it from falling in), OXO has really decreased the potential utility of the design. Also, the OXO website states "The 3-Piece Berry Bowl & Colander Set is the perfect size for rinsing berries, quinoa, beans and more;" I agree that it is great for rinsing berries and beans, but rinsing quinoa would be a nightmare, as the holes in the colander are far too large to rinse quinoa without most of it ending up in the water (or down the drain).

If OXO would fix the lid design so that it would snap securly onto the colander, this would be a four-star product. Also, with the colander inserted, the storage is very small (even without the colander, it is too small to be used as an effective mixing bowl unless you're beating an egg or two).

text:
Good, but has some design shortcomings.... My faithful [[ASIN:B0009VELTQ Cuisinart CBK-200 2-Pound Convection Automatic Breadmaker]] finally died after years of faithful service, so I was happy to be offered the Black and Decker B6000C Deluxe Bread Maker. I used my Cuisinart regularly to make yeast bread (white and whole wheat), sweet bread (on the dough setting), and jam. Because I am more familiar with the Cuisinart, I will use it as the basis for comparison here.

As I unboxed the B&D, I was surprised by how light the unit is (the Cuisinart had a metal body and lid). The unit is larger due to the shape of the pan and the fact that it bakes 3-pound loaves, but it does not have handles like the Cuisinart, which makes it difficult to move or put it away for storage. I was also a little dismayed to see that the large, heavy lid relies on a very small plastic hinge, which seems like it will crack / break sooner rather than later (the lid also tends to wobble a little when closed). The metal pan seems a bit thin, but I liked the fact that the two paddles are straight rather than curved like the Cuisinart. The B&D also seemed to do a better job at kneading due to the two paddles, but you'll still want to stop and scrape down the sides of the pan using a nonstick tool.

After getting the bread maker set up (I had to move it because the unit is tall and narrow and I could not open the lid fully because it kept hitting the underside of my cabinets), I used the included recipe to make a 3-pound loaf of herbed garlic French bread on the French cycle (setting 3). As other reviewers have mentioned, the LCD readout is a touch on the faint side, and may be difficult to read (my old Cuisinart did not have that problem and was easy to read from several feet away). I found I had to add extra liquid to the recipe, as the dough was far too dry at first and didn't come together, but the resulting loaf was moist and fluffy. I also liked the way the bread baked in the B&D; my Cuisinart tended to overbake everything, even on the "light" crust setting.

Here is one area where the Cuisinart excelled over the B&D manual: the Cuisinart bread machine includes dozens of recipes for each of the machine's settings, with ingredients scaled for 1, 1.5 and 2-pound loaves. The B&D manual only has ONE sample recipe for each setting, and the ingredients are automatically scaled for the largest 3-pound loaf size. Also, the Cuisinart listed the exact length of each step in the cycle for all of the settings; there are no times listed for the B&D. This can be problematic if you want to remove the paddles before the bread enters the baking cycle; the Cuisinart would beep before the final rise, but the B&D does not. Because there are no times listed in the manual, it takes a bit of guesswork (the LCD does underline which step of the baking process you are on).

Overall, I would still recommend the [[ASIN:B0009VELTQ Cuisinart CBK-200 2-Pound Convection Automatic Breadmaker]] for the many included recipes, variations, nutritional info, and design features, especially for new bakers. The B&D does turn out a decent loaf of bread, but the lack of included recipes (and scaled ingredients for smaller loaves), and more crucially the lack of knead and rise times, can make this less than user-friendly.

text:
Looks great, but lacks some basic features that less expensive models have.. I am fairly new to the world of slow cooking; I purchased my first-ever slow cooker, a [[ASIN:B005GZ2OBW Hamilton Beach Stovetop Slow Cooker - Black/silver (6 Quart)]], about a year ago and have been slow cooking several times a week ever since (I have several slow cooker cookbooks that I rely on constantly, including [[ASIN:054700303X The Italian Slow Cooker]], [[ASIN:0547744455 The Mediterranean Slow Cooker]], and [[ASIN:1936493578 Slow Cooker Revolution Volume 2]]). I use my slow cooker regularly to make all manner of desserts (cakes, cheesecakes, bread puddings), soups, and entrees. This All-Clad slow cooker was the first All-Clad appliance that I have used (I also own several made-in-the-USA All-Clad pans that I use regularly and swear by).

First and foremost, I am not thrilled that it is made in China. It's obvious that the quality control isn't up to the same standards as their US-made cookware; the heavy ceramic insert has numerous tiny bubbles / holes, is rough on the bottom where the insert is not glazed, and the lid does not fit the insert snugly (nor is there a latch / locking mechanism or hole for a thermometer/temperature probe). The unit LOOKS impressive on the counter, although it is absolutely massive (it weighs close to 20 pounds with the insert in).

On to setting the cooking mode and time: you are limited to 2-8(?) hours on high or 4-20 hours on low, at which point the slow cooker will automatically switch to warm mode. This is first unit I've had with a programmable timer, but I did like the solid feel of the buttons. The cooking time limits seemed kind of arbitrary; it seemed strange that I could only program the unit on high for a maximum of eight hours, but up to 20 hours on low.

I used the All-Clad slow cooker to make several dishes, including a Greek shrimp and tomato dish. I went according to the time in the recipe so as not to keep removing the lid (it recommended cooking the shrimp 10 minutes on high; they were VERY overcooked, whereas in my Hamilton Beach, I had to cook them for a few extra minutes).

Naturally, I was apprehensive after reading the hundreds of one-star reviews about the ceramic insert cracking and breaking, or the electronics would suddenly stop working. I have not experienced either of these yet, but I was very careful to hand-wash the insert (even though the manual claims that both the insert and lid are dishwasher-safe, I'm not chancing it). During cooking on high, I did notice several very loud popping sounds coming from the insert that were audible from two rooms away; I was sure that the insert would be cracked, but could find no hairline cracks after washing and drying the insert (I waited until the insert was completely cool before washing). I have a feeling based on so many others' experiences that the insert will be the first thing to fail; luckily there is a one-year warranty, which I registered for immediately, and I plan to continue using this as my primary slow cooker.

Bottom line: it does what a slow cooker is supposed to do, but for this price, I expect a solid, flawless appliance that will stand up to several years of frequent use/abuse, an insert that does not crack, and responsive customer service.

The good:
+ I liked that there is a rubber seal / gasket that the ceramic insert rests on; as it is so heavy, it makes moving the slow cooker (and removing the insert) much more manageable.
+ It does come with a (small) collection of starter recipes, including Asian Beef Stew, Mahogany Glazed Pork Loin, Peach Melba Bread Pudding, Chicken with Mushrooms in White Wine Sauce, and Tunisian Spiced Turkey Breas with Root Vegetables.

The bad:
- Even on low, the temperature seems to run hot
- Finishing on the ceramic insert; small imperfections in the ceramic insert that can lead to cracking
- If/when the insert cracks (and it seems to happen quite frequently based on reviews), expect to spend a good $75 on a replacement if your unit is no longer under warranty

Worth it if you're especially squeamish. For $18 at the time of this writing, this product comes with two non-reusable sheets. That's quite expensive for what this thing does.

The design of this toilet unclogger is one that relies on an airtight seal with the toilet seat and the air pressure that can be created from that seal. A couple of issues arise: If your toilet seat covers too much of the rim of the toilet, this sheet will not be able to create the seal it needs without removing the seat. Even with a good seal, the pressure that can be generated may not be enough to move the clog.

What is good about this product is that when it works, it allows one to unclog the toilet without all the mess that might come along with it. If you're especially squeamish, then this product might actually be justifiable. Otherwise, the traditional plunger is still the better choice.

Good build, but not sure of the aim of this design. The KORVOS Cutting Board is made of good bamboo material and soft silicone footing for drying. It has stainless steel on one side and bamboo on the other. It also has a notch for hanging. It has a good build quality and has a nice weight.

The bamboo side has a liquid channel, but it doesn't go around the entire board. I suppose with this board being only 15x11, that may be enough.

As far as the stainless side, I'm uncertain when or why I would choose to use it. Metal on metal contact always gives me the willies and no matter how well it's built, there will always be a gap that liquid can get trapped in. So if cutting meat on the stainless side, blood can get trapped in the gap and allow bacteria to propagate. That would be the worst-case-scenario. In a milder case, water being trapped between the metal and bamboo would still encourage mold growth.

One should always use separate cutting boards for meat and vegetables. I ended up using this board for veggies and only on the bamboo side.

I suppose it does make a good presentation platter. You can choose to present your food on the bamboo or have a nice stainless surface to show it off.

text:
Some people will not be able to use this in their car if a grounded power outlet is more than 17 feet away. I am no stranger to carpet cleaners (shampooers). I own a [[ASIN:B0045I8E4M Hoover MaxExtract77 Multi-Surface Pro Carpet & Hard Floor Cleaner FH50240]] and an older version of the [[ASIN:B00450U7QS BISSELL Spotbot Pet Handsfree Spot and Stain Cleaner with Deep Reach Technology, 33N8]]. I also purchased for my boyfriend and have used myself the [[ASIN:B000ASDCWK BISSELL ProHeat 2X Select Upright Deep Carpet Cleaner, 9400M]]. In general, I found Bissell cleaners to be more than satisfactory with the exception of the [[ASIN:B001EYILAW BISSELL PROdry Fast-Drying Carpet Cleaner, 7350]] which I threw out because it was that bad.

For this auto cleaner, I listed the PROS and CONS below and found the unit to be only satisfactory for my purposes.

PROS:

- This can be used for the home or auto.

- Assembly is easy; just attach the hardware (one clip and one arm) for the hose and the brush and you are set.

- It comes with a small bottle of 2x Little Green for Compacts solution.

- The solution has a nice, yet subtle fresh scent.

- The solution tank is easy to fill and the dirty water tank is easy to rinse out. Be careful when inserting the solution tank back into the unit because when I turned the tank over, I held the tank a little too tight which caused the solution to start squirting out. Once I changed my hold to be more subtle and on the upper part of the tank, this squirting ceased.

- The built in heater took only 25 seconds to heat up as opposed to the 30 seconds mentioned in the manual. I also found that the water does come out "warmer" than the other cleaners I have.

- A two-in-one crevice tool is supplied which can be converted with the flip of a switch from a small tiny brush to just a crevice tool that I assume can be used to soak up a puddle of water (although the manual does not say).

- The cord is relatively long for a compact unit which I measured to be around 20 feet; that's about 19-1/2 feet of useable extension. (See the CONS with regard to the cord, which is why I could not use this in my auto.)

- The unit has a quick-release cord wrap which enabled me to unravel the cord easily.

- The solution is easy to dispense and is dispensed out in a fan pattern over the stain. The further away from the surface of the carpet you hold your brush while dispensing the solution the larger the area it covers.

- Although the unit does not pick up as much water as my Spotbot does, I still felt that it picked up enough.

- I thought it spot cleaned my house carpet as well as any of my other cleaners. For my type stains, which are usually cat vomit, that means it lightened the stain. As a result, I suspect it would be great on upholstery and auto interiors such as floor mats, seats, etc. (although I wouldn't use it on the headliner--that's the material on the underside of the roof).

- I was able to clean my removable car floor mat by bringing it into my house for cleaning. It was black in spots and it came out almost spotless although I did use a lot of elbow grease when working the brush over the mat. In fact the dirty water was pitch black when I was done.

- The crevice tool (with the tiny brush) and the small brush that comes with the unit means that this is mostly for spot cleaning; however, with enough back and forth over the affected area, you could clean as much as you wanted.
- Customer service is available Mon to Fri 8 am -10 pm and Saturday 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern Time.

- I called them twice around 9 p.m. Eastern Time to clarify the WARNINGs in the manual and both reps gave me the same answer which you'll read about in the CONS.

- The unit comes with a 1-year limited warranty.

CONS:

- Only those who have a garage or access to a grounded power outlet within about 17 feet of their car would be able to use this. I said 17 feet because you do need some slack to get into the car even though the hose will extend some. I was unable to clean my car with this because the power cord was not long enough to reach and using an extension cord might cause a severe electrical shock or (as the reps on the phone told me) blow out the circuit breakers in my house. I made sure to call Bissell twice and ask if I could use a cord rated higher than the unit and they said no. I did not ask if this could be used with a jumpstart or other battery pack with an AC connection, although that might be an option, but I would caution you to check first. I live on the 2nd floor and my boyfriend does too, so neither one of us could use this in the car because the WARNING in the manual reads:

WARNING: Do not use an extension cord with the product. The use of an extension cord may result in a severe electrical shock, particularly if the extension cord does not have an electrical rating higher than that of the product, OR if the extension cord does not have a three-prong grounding plug and if the extension cord is not plugged into a circuit box with a ground fault circuit interrupter. Safety precautions such as keeping all connections off the ground and dry will not eliminate the danger.

- I do not like that I can only use the Bissell 2x Little Green for Compacts formula in this unit. This means I cannot use any other Bissell cleaning products in this unit and I called customer service to verify this. The WARNING in the manual reads:

WARNING: Use only BISSELL Little Green formula in your cleaner. Use of cleaning formulas which contain lemon or pine oil may damage this appliance and void the warranty. Chemical spot cleaners or solvent-based soil removers also should not be used. These products may react with the plastic materials used in your cleaner, causing cracking or pitting.

- The user instructions are not so good. For instance, nowhere does it mention that both the built in heater and the unit has to be in the on position to heat up the water; although that is intuitive. Also, the manual should say you should vacuum first before using. I already know this but not everyone would.

- A bit of water stays behind in the channel below the dirty water tank and in the tough stain tool which is expected; however, be careful if moving this around or transporting to another location because if the unit tilts the dirty water that remains in the channel might spill out.

In summary, I selected this product so that I could clean the attached carpet in my auto and the cloth seats in my boyfriend's auto, but was unable to do that due to the extension cord restriction. However, I still feel this is a satisfactory carpet cleaner / shampooer that can be used to spot clean carpet or upholstery in my home or the removable dirty floor mats that I can bring in from the car. As long as one has access to an outlet close to their car, based on the results in my home and on my removable vehicle floor mats I have no doubt this would work on cloth car seats and the non-removable auto carpet. I do wish I could use another Bissell cleaning solution (such as the pet solution) besides the one that came with the unit; but that did not take away from the cleaning power; it just takes away from the options. In essence this unit has only one cleaning option, the Bissell 2x Little Green for Compacts formula.

I feel this unit was 2.5 stars because of the limited options and rounded up to give it 3 stars. If the first two CONS were addressed, then I probably would have rated this four stars as it does clean as well as the three other units (including the Hoover) that I listed in my introduction. Nevertheless, as a potential buyer, only you can try to determine based on the the various posted reviews if this unit is right for you.
