text:
floor lamp. It comes disassembled. It took me about 20 minutes to twist all the segments together. The lamp I received is a matte black. The tubing is metal. The lamp is LED. There is a spot on the main tube of the lamp that is supposed to allow you to turn on the lamp and dim - it does not work. If you use the remote, you can use the toggle on the main tube to dim either the large or the mini lamp - but it will NOT turn the lamp on or off. The remote uses a really small barrel shaped battery (came with it) but looks like it will be hard to find. Eh. But the remote turns on and off both lights, dims them and changes the light from a blue or "warm" color light. The mini light has a goose neck that you can manipulate. The large light has two options, straight up and flat (pointing directly at the ceiling) or at a tilt (which I prefer for dust). I like the light, but disappointed that the main tube of the lamp doesn't work - not that I am terribly surprised it doesn't. It says to light tape the toggle - big nothing. You can tap, gently hold or bang it - NOTHING happens. Thus the 3 stars. TIP NOTE: because the tube is metal, and you have to twist the segments together, be SUPER careful to get them twisting correctly so you don't strip them or get them stuck at the wrong angle.
PROS: LED, doesn't flicker.
You can change the light from a white/blue to a warmer yellower light.
Dimmer option.
The mini light is nice if you read in bed or at the sofa.
CONS: You cannot turn the lamp on or off without the remote - even though you are supposed to be able to. Bad battery size - will be a pain to find replacement.
If I loose the remote, I will not be able to use the lamp. Eh.

text:
Starfish pillow slipcovers. These slipcovers are simply elegant, beautiful! I LOVE mother of pearl and the starfish is beautifully sewn and finely finished. The linen color is definitely what I would call 'ecru' in color. They are just lovely. The look is 10 stars in my opinion.... however... in use, zero stars. I have full, standard 16x16 pillows - sadly, the way the slip covers are sewn, the zipper opening is less than 12 inches (please see photos). So, to get my pillows in the slipcover would have destroyed the covers. They don't begin to fit - even a little. I did think about returning them and reordering the 20x20 size, however, once the pillows would be in the cover (I am assuming a wider zipper opening), they would have been loose and ill fitting - NOT a finished look at all. I contacted the sellers to inform them of the design flaw - their response was less than cordial and in fact demanded proof of the size of my pillows and misrepresented the size of the zipper opening as larger than it is. It doesn't offer the zipper opening info in the ad and probably should. I do really love the slipcovers, but so very disappointed in how much I paid for them only to find I could not use them as I had hoped. I have included photos of the actual zipper opening, less than 12", The standard thickness of my 16x16 pillows, my pillow and lastly a photo of the slip cover laying loosely over the top of my pillow - wishing I could magically make them fit because they are so beautiful. This also shows my pillows are indeed 16x16. Unless you have very thin, fold able pillows (in order to accommodate their tiny opening), I would not recommend these. I am hoping they will update their design or at the very least include more accurate measurement info. I think this comes down to my pillows are not the right kind to be slip covered (their outer cover is not removable) and their design is not useful unless you have a very thin pillow form. For the price, I would have liked to have used them on the pillows I have. I never hesitate to update my reviews should new info seem useful and i hope my review today was helpful to you!
UPDATE: 10/17/2019.. I purchased some thin 16x16 pillow forms and some fluffy 12x12 forms. The thin ones were too thin to look full and healthy in the shams, so I put the fluffier 12x12 forms in the back... they look ok. Had to spend $40 additional dollars to make these shams work somehow. I have to say that as lovely as these shams are, I cannot recommend them. Even after purchasing brand new forms they still are a bit off - so I can't fully blame my original pillows and a bit of a design flaw.

text:
Ok but not really what I expected. I really wanted to like this thermometer. It had what looked like a lot of good features and I had wanted to try a Bluetooth thermometer for a while. Initially, it looked good. It comes with the thermometer, a charging base, and a charging cord. It doesn't come with a charger, but we have those all over the place.

The first odd thing I noticed is that according to the instructions it must charge for 20 minutes every time you use it. Initially, I thought this was a showstopper because I've been using an electronic thermometer for several years and it is always ready to work. When I used it for the first time, I realized that in most cases there is at least 20 minutes of prep time, and you don't need to put the thing in the meat right away. So, that's annoying but not a showstopper. What is really goofy is that you can't even set it up until you charge it for 20 minutes. The charging base shows red when it is charging and green when it is done, but it also goes back and forth. When I was charging it for the first real use, I looked over and it was green. Then I went to get it a few minutes later and it was red.
The biggest issue is the app that comes with it. It's very primitive and doesn't look like it has a lot of options. You can choose one of the "BBQ" menu items and in most cases, it will then give you the option of various degrees of doneness. It works ok but is really limited in terms of connection. It says you can connect up to 165 feet, and that is only if you have the lid open on the grill or oven. I don't know a lot of people who use a grill with the top open, and I know of no one who uses an oven with the door open. It does say in the description that if you close the lid of the grill you will get about 20 feet before it disconnects. I'd say that is pretty accurate but means that you have to stay pretty close to the grill, and that's not why anyone would get a wireless remote thermometer. I suspect the battery is very weak which is why you have to charge it all the time and the weak signal is the reason it doesn't work over 20 feet. This may be fine if you are in a small kitchen and using it with the oven, but normally I move around a bit.
The worst thing about it is that it won't turn off. I used it and two days later it's still running even though I thought I ended it. Evidently, you have to go in and actually force it to stop. This is definitely a security issue and a battery usage issue and just a horrible customer service issue.
Overall, I can't give this device more than 3 stars. The app can be updated, and hopefully this will happen, but the weak signal is not something that will be fixed and the need to charge it every time you use it is another limitation. I expect a wireless thermometer to be pretty simple to operate and have an app that is easy to use. This has neither of those basic features and having no way to close the app is a definite security issue.

It was delivered in very good condition.. First, it was a beautiful table. 2nd, there's no way this item weighs only 60-something lbs. Not even the table-top by itself. The delivery guys refused to deliver the box up a single flight of stairs to my 'man-cave'. Or even help me haul it up the stairs. They cited safety concerns. So I did it myself. I'm a big strong guy too. Unfortunately I fell with it, taking a big gash out of my front door and the table, probably destroying most of the table's re-sale value.

text:
Buy the EVOS German alternative instead.. I just bought (and have been using) both the competing EVOS German-made reusable cloths and also these Trendy Tripper brand Swedish reusable cloths, so I can offer what I hope is a useful comparison.

First of all, congrats to the Europeans: compared to either product reviewed here, our US-made Handiwipes are a joke.

Based on my heavy use over the past couple of days, I have concluded that the EVOS German cloths are FAR superior overall to these Trendy Tripper Swedish cloths:

The EVOS cloths cost only about $8 for 5 cloths.

The Trendy Tripper cloths cost about $17 for 6 cloths.

EVOS are about 14" x 14" in size (and are easily folded if you want something smaller in your hand).

Trendy Tripper are only about 5" x 6".

EVOS absorb far more than TrendyTripper.

EVOS dry out faster than Trendy Tripper.

I think a lot of things will bug you if you buy this. I had the previous model of this bissell and was excited to use this new model. I am a little bummed out at how the unit works though. Assembly was easy. Instructions were simple to follow. But:
• I noticed right off the bat, the removable, washable filters are in a separate canister found under the holding container (where the dirt goes)and can only be accessed if you pop off the holding container. Then, you must once again, pop off an additional top to get to the round spongy filter so you can wash it. Total extra step.
•Then, there is no more retractable cord. You must manually wrap the cord round the machine. Only, look at attached pic in my review. There is not enough room for the cord. I had to shove the cord in "just so" to make it fit. It does hang off to the left. In my opinion, this is preferred, because I hold the cord with left hand while I vacuum.
•Next, the unit is HEAVY and clunky. I am a fit middle aged woman and had a hard time getting vacuum to lift over the edge of my area rugs. I had to manhandle the unit over. It did not glide smoothly. Because of it's weight, this may be a problem for you to handle comfortable.
•My biggest irritation of this thing is that the base swivels. You know how it feels when the handle of a mop or vacuum hasn't been secured correctly to the base? You over compensate your movement up top for the wiggling at the base. This has that exact same sensation. And it's inessential to the workings of ANY vacuum.
Totally not needed imo.
•also not needed, the "reduced suction" option found on the hose (see picture). Initially it was set to that and I didn't know. I went over my rug 10 or 15 times and nothing came up. I looked thru instructions and found nothing pointing it out. It took my scouring over vacuum for a good while trying to assess what was wrong. I finally found the option and turned it to "full suck"
The suction is o.k. Not the strongest. Nor the weakest of vacuums I've used. The vacuum self-propelled but, because of it's weight, your arm still fatigues.
•there are no side bristles sticking off the vacuum base to help with floorboard and edge dust.
•the detachable hose has a massive handle on it that is clumsy and sticks out when you try and store it.
Over-all, I feel like they tried to add too much to this. Collectively all these extra things just don't work. Do the 1 thing great.
Make a vacuum that "sucks" , whose filter can be quickly accessed and washed. Make the cord stow away correctly, make the extension hose easy to get off and on and the extension tools easy to store. Too much to ask? On this unit, yes!

text: Just okay. This is a beautiful skillet. I love the helper handle at the top and the long cool-to-touch handle at the base. Also nice are the 2 pour spouts on each side. First off, the black part is textured. It’s very strange. My food stuck to it and when I tried to clean it with my cast iron cleaner, I scratched it. Second, it was the slowest skillet ever to heat up. I cooked shrimp on this and I swear the pan took 15 minutes to heat and cook. I was shocked. I had it on medium high heat. text:
A whole lotta extra work just to boil eggs.. This little gadget made pretty good eggs and was simple to set up and use. Not my first air fryer, its OK. Maybe I'm just spoiled because I'm comparing this to an air fryer that I already love, but I found this one to be sub-optimal.
Air fryers, if you are unaware, are basically small high powered convection ovens that can simulate the effect of "frying" on certain types of food (like french fries). To do this, you need precise temperature controls and timing, since it happens rather quickly (a difference of a minute or two in the machine is significant). So one of the first things that turned me off to this one is the fact that the timer is a manual dial that WON'T LET YOU ADJUST THE TIME once you've set it. In other words, if you overcrank the time (say, to 10 min instead of 7), you can't turn it back down. You have to just wait out that amount of time until it finishes. That's a silly oversight if you ask me. My other air fryer, for contrast, has a digital display for the timer which can be adjusted at any time during the process. This one? You have to unplug it if you don't want it to continue running for the time you accidentally set.
Also the slotted tray insert comes out of the drawer rather easily, but the plastic tabs need to be lined up again for it to go back in (you have to push it with your thumb to slide it back into the open position). Just a silly nuisance that could have been avoided since I know other air fryers at similar price points don't have this issue.
As far as the food, it DOES work, as long as you preheat it first. And the first time you use it, of course, you should let it burn out for 30 min to avoid new appliance smell on your food. It's an alright air fryer, especially if you get it for a bargain sale price, but otherwise I feel like there are better models on the market with less quirks.

Not quite the "poor man's mini split" I was hoping for- heat requires water removal!. Portable AC units are great for times a traditional window unit isn't an option. However, I was particularly interested in this one because of the supplemental HEAT function as well.
You see, I have a room that was added on to my home without attaching to the house's central HVAC. It is always noticeably hotter in the summer and colder in the winter in that room. I looked into installing an efficient mini-split unit which would solve this problem, however I could not justify the cost (thousands of dollars!).
This unit seemed like a possible work around: I can either pipe it to a window or drill a hole in my wall to pipe it out of (still much cheaper than a mini split!!), and have supplemental cooling AND heating!
Well, it turns out, using any mode other than cooling requires you to empty a water bucket. Dehumidify I understand, but I was surprised to learn that the heat pump mode (essentially running the AC in reverse) also fills with water and requires draining. There was not a lot of information about the heat mode before ordering it, and now I see why. It really does seem to be an afterthought, the cooling mode is the important feature. We have accepted that perhaps it is better to clean parts at a time rather than the entire house at once, but I'd have hoped this would last longer or at least come with a spare battery to swap and keep going.

My son was using it to vacuum our stairs the same day and accidentally knocked the cup loose releasing all the debris all over the stair case, including some shards of glass that were still inside. If they made that part more secure and the battery life longer, I would gladly give this 5 stars. For now, I'd give it a three.

text: Don't expect much. We have four mostly-indoor pets, and now that it's almost spring, the shedding has gotten out of control. Our entire downstairs is wood flooring, and I did not want to pull out our large vacuum every day to pick up the fur. I bought this hoping it would help with light day-to-day vacuuming. It's compact and convenient enough, and I do love that it's cordless. The suction on it is TERRIBLE, though - really, really disappointing. When I leave it on the "bare floor" setting, the suction is only strong enough to suck the fur to the machine, but not into the canister (leaving me with a big clump of fur and debris on the outside of the vacuum's mouth, which is just gross). It's much more effective when I turn on the carpet setting and at least the rotating brush helps propel the fur into the canister, BUT, using the carpet setting wears the battery down significantly. I can only use this vacuum for about 15 minutes straight with the roller spinning before the battery gets drained and the vacuum basically begins to moan and sputter. Also, this is good enough to vacuum up fur and hair/dust, but does a poor job at sucking up anything with more mass - I can hardly get it to pick up stray cat food kibbles or even pine needles that the dogs have tracked in. I'm disappointed this isn't a slightly more robust vacuum, but I suppose the cheap price indicates what you can really expect from this.

All I really know is that I like freshly, consistently ground arabica beans that are brown. This is my first electric burr grinder. For as much coffee as I drink I really haven't bothered to learn much about making coffee. All I really know is that I like freshly, consistently ground arabica beans that are brown, not black. I seriously need to advance my knowledge beyond that. I will say that this grinder produces a fair amount of fine dust along with any coarseness of grounds, which I'm told is the sign of a cheap coffee grinder. OTOH it does a night-and-day better job than my previous, blade-chopping "grinder". I had to choose a new grinder in a hurry because my old one broke down.

Also the static cling on the plastic hopper is pretty bad. I do what I read in another review: I just shake the grounds (and dust) out of the hopper through its intake hole. That keeps mess to a minimum. I bought a refurbished one since I figure such a grinder will have received much more QC attention than a standard assembly-line example. I also got the extended protection plan, which buys me a few years' worth of maintenance, which at least forestalls this thing's date with a landfill (SIGH)... I hate buying disposable appliances/amusements, but I was overwhelmed with research on grinders ranging from $30 to $3,000. My plan is to use this grinder to simply defer the decision. I will use this for [I think 3 years?] after which I expect it to expire and nobody will be willing to fix it. At that point I will have accumulated enough knowledge to purchase a grinder that I can use my whole life, and somebody else can enjoy it when I'm gone. My next/final one will be a highly regarded, serviceable, conical burr grinder with a glass receptacle - that's all I know so far.

Now that I'm thinking about it, the purchase price seems good until I consider that I'm really just buying time to figure out which grinder I really want. I'm not proud of buying something that was clearly designed to be disposable.

EDIT 2016.05.20: I spent a week in Portland, and it pretty much ruined my life. Sampling the lifestyles there there has warped my mind like few things ever have. I now ride a bicycle pretty much everywhere I go - got rid of one car (share one with wife). I have lost all interest in chain restaurant food. After a week of swimming in really great coffee - culinary *experience* coffee - it's too hard to go back to my old, lower standards.

I finally started to read up on home roasting and brewing. I bought a Lido 3 hand grinder and I hacked my second popcorn roaster to add temp and fan controls (fire hazard - don't do it)! I found Kansas City's only top-tier coffee joint, Oddly Correct, and I bug them with questions. I've been to About the Coffee once and plan to take some classes there. I took the factory tour at Roasterie.

I think the Cuisinart was a good stepping stone for me. At the time I was hooked on "good" coffee but I wasn't interested enough to dump lots of hours into learning the whole process of making iteratively better coffee at home. This grinder is good in that it is reliable and consistent (from grind to grind). I put numbers on the coarseness dial with a fine Sharpie - returning to the click marked "6" will mean the same thing today that it did a year ago. A year ago my main problem with this grinder seemed like a quibble: it produces a lot of fine dust. Now that I'm beefing up my skills in taking coffee from green beans to finished drink, this shortcoming is becoming a limiter.

The static cling is annoying but I can totally live with that. I'm a hardcore coffee junkie now - to get my daily fix I would be stealing ratty old bicycles and smashing the front windows of pawn shops if it came to that. I see the extreme lengths to which some people go to get a better cup of coffee and I can totally imagining my own mental state degrading to the same level of obsession. Static cling is the least of my problems.

I'm satisfied that I took my coffee making as far as it can go with this grinder. At the time of purchase I thought it was a real step up - going from a blade type coffee chopper to a grinder with "burr" in the name - WOW haha! It's like all my hobbies - all I needed when starting out was to *think* I had good gear and the excitement carried me through. And to be fair this grinder was a huge step up from a blade type chopper. I'm happy for the experience I had with this Cuisinart grinder, but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone wanting to make good coffee.

I'm satisfied that I got my money's worth out of it - I bought a refurbished one with a 3-year warranty, which was the epitome of cheap reliability. I will continue to use it when a portable hand grinder is unsuitable (volume, time, broken arm, Japanese apartment with insufficient room to extend both elbows).

If you are currently satisfied with the coffee you drink at home and you just want a fast way to grind beans, then count yourself lucky and be happy with the Cuisinart grinder. This is luck on the order of maturing to adulthood without ever learning about war, famine, or the question of whether god exists.

Here is my advice to people who want the whole coffee experience - zen rituals of preparation, culinary exploration, etc. Plan to invest in an immersive hobby. Invest in the following order:

TIME: research, finding the best coffee joint in town, taking classes, plan a vacation around coffee tasting and learning. start by finding people who demonstrate their expertise by handing you a cup of the best coffee you've ever had. everyone can talk, but not everyone can roast and brew. those who can, can recommend books

BOOKS: get some real info. the internet is full of people who get all their info from the internet. At my current, novice level it is too hard for me to discern real experts from randos.

GEAR: roaster, grinder, brew gear.

Stay on guard for gear fetishism - it seems to affect a lot of coffee enthusiasts. Remember that you love *coffee* - not coffee *gear*. For me a reliable guide to gear and utility is to stand in a room, meditate for a minute, open my eyes, and ask, "What in here is ugly?" - and then get rid of the ugly things. Ugliness extends to every criterion: utility, aesthetics, undefined sensibilities. When used as my exclusive method - i.e. no "What's the best I can get?" or "What are the available choices?" - I end up with very good gear that works great and looks appropriate for my house. I end up with the *right* gear. A consort of good coffee gear is like an ad-hoc sculpture - perfection is achieved by removing that which doesn't belong. Adding more *stuff* is generally a step in the wrong direction.

Aggressively avoid advertising for coffee gear, which includes the pap that passes for journalism. It's like *Raiders of the Lost Ark*: one look and you will be destroyed.

Focus on one thing at a time. Probably stay in the area of brewing first, then move on to roasting. Progressively wean off the best, fresh-roasted beans in town to your own, home-roasted beans. Forget about incremental gear upgrades - spend your resources figuring out what you like (hands-on) and then do what it takes to acquire the necessary skills and gear. For me I don't really need flexibility or programmability or automation - I just want to consistently get the best results possible with a reasonable amount of time and effort. The Cuisinart grinder did that for me for a couple years, but because of my rising skill level, it is no longer suitable. It has become ugly, and as such must be relegated to storage.

Good luck on your quest into the magical, hidden world of coffee!

Neat-o, fun, beautiful. However, the coffee isn't as good as other methods.. I love the ritual, but I'm underwhelmed by the coffee it produces. For a 1-cup ritual I prefer french press and pourover. Even real espresso in a cheap home machine is better IMHO - more crema and flavor.

I originally found a Bialetti at a thrift store and didn't know what it was. I could see that it was for coffee so I brought it home and tried it. I liked the device itself quite a bit and did some research. I thought I had a one-cup version but it must be a three-cup version. I ordered this one thinking it would be six times the size of the one I found, but it's only 2x. It makes enough "espresso" (more like Americano IMHO) to fill one American coffee mug 3/4 full.

I'm just starting home roasting, and one of my goals is to roast something that really shines in the Bialetti. As it stands it is really most valuable as a conversation piece.

If you are looking for a fun method for brewing one cup of delicious coffee, I would first try pour over and french press. Those are hard to screw up. The Bialetti is neat-o and great for entertaining, but it's not really in the hunt for best cup of coffee IMHO.

text:
PowerFresh Steam Mop - not so great. Over the past several years, I have purchased several steam mops: Shark Pocket, Haan, Euroflex Monster and now this Bissell Power Fresh Steam Mop (purchased locally). I wanted a mop to put out nice hot steam that is hot enough to cut through stuff, swivel and ALSO fit under my kitchen cabinets.

This Power Fresh Steam Mop by Bissell DOES have a low head to fit under cabinets and it does swivel. Compared to the Euroflex Monster (steam temp is 212F per product specs), this Steam Fresh doesn't come close. Even on the hottest setting, the steam is less hot and abundant. (The Monster has steam from both the bottom and the front). Also, using the medium and highest settings left my floor SOGGY.

I was quite interested in the fresh scent disks for leaving that clean scent (yes, I know -- don't have to smell a fragrance to be clean). The scent to me was very minimal.

Pads: They are about the thinnish quality of the Shark and get soggy quickly. My floors aren't that dirty, but I have to use two or three (only 2 included) to do a medium-sized kitchen floor.
Handle: Sturdy, but they unit tips over easily.
Tank: Very small, but easy to refill.
Steam: Not very hot (compared to the Euroflex at 212F)- hold the mop over an area for 20 seconds to sanitize. Yikes .. takes ages to "santize" an entire floor.
Head Maneverability: Nice and low height.
Fresh Scent Disks: Barely noticeable (but might be my nose).

Bottom line: The steam only comes from one area on the bottom (as opposed to several jets). The clugging/chugging noise (normal, per instructions) is a bit annoying. I DO like the swivel head, and the fresh scent (such as it is). The low height makes it nice for cleaning under cabinets. The steam isn't that hot and one has to leave the mop over an area for 20 seconds to sanitize leaves much to be desired.

For Sanitizing and cleaning a large area, I'LL STICK TO MY EUROFLEX MONSTER. This will work for smaller areas.

text:
More of a robotic sweeper than a vaccum. TL/DR (Conclusion): this unit really only does the job of eliminating routine light sweeping of floors. You will still need to get into corners with a broom. The dust bin needs emptying (very) frequently and the roller becomes clogged with lint quickly due to it's small diameter and width. The low height is great as it fits under most furniture. Daily automated program does not work properly. 2.5 stars. REALLY wish it had a smartphone app.

The price I paid, $109, was a great deal. The unit does a decent job of basic sweeping of floors on demand. It is capable of remembering obstacles, even though it is not really supposed to be able to map your home. If a new obstacle appears in its path, it will tap it, reverse, work it's way around it, and remember it is there for the duration of the cycle. It does seem to remember hard boundaries (walls, furniture), even though mapping is not supposed to be one of its features. I also purchased the magnetic boundary strip to keep it out of a specific area, and this works perfectly.

It does a decent job sweeping up dust and light particles, although it cannot quite reach all the way into corners with the brushes. The suction is not very strong unless you use the Max setting, but this depletes the battery rapidly. You will need to use the Max setting for some larger particles. The sweeping roller is not very long or wide and becomes clogged up with lint very easily, requiring a good cleaning about every third run or so. The dust bin is tiny, and requires emptying after every use in my small space, and likely several times if used in a larger area. The unit itself is gloss black on top and gets very dusty every time it is used, requiring frequent thorough dusting/cleaning. I did not bother purchasing the mop accessory, because online video reviews point out it is not really mopping, just the equivalent of dragging a wet cloth around on the floor, and is quite useless in this respect.

The primary reason I selected this model were the positive video reviews elsewhere conducted by an independent third party which brutally tests all robotic vacuums and records all tests on video. This model is the same mechanically as another top-selling robot which is simply private-labeled. This is apparently the OEM, and is significantly cheaper as a result.

By far the best feature is the low height/profile. This is the slimmest robotic vacuum I have ever seen. It is only 7.2cm tall! It can easily go under sofas, my media center, chairs, and most furniture with a wide enough opening for it to enter. It is also quite good at getting itself out of tight "traps" (i.e. behind furniture or under a couch with stuff there), but will stop if it becomes tangled or stuck, issuing a loud beep in the process. This is one reason I wish it had a smart phone app so it could alert you when it gets stuck.

What doesn't work:
1) The automation aspect does not function properly. I tried setting it up to go every day at the same time, and it did it for two days, then stopped without explanation. I tried again, and could not get it to hold the program. Then about 8 months later, following a brief power outage at home, it started automatically cleaning every day at the same time again, as though it had remembered the program or the feature had been re-enabled, but the time was not as previously set. When I tried to change the time, it seemed to save it, but it has failed to clean automatically on any day since. If I want it to run, I just grab the remote and hit "auto". Not such a big deal, really, but I wish it worked.

2) It cannot navigate any threshold with a height greater than about 3/8". This means in my house it cannot move from the hardwood in the living areas to carpet in bedrooms, etc. This is very frustrating. I have to give it a push if I want it to try to vacuum the carpet on the other side of the threshold. Which leads to number 3...

3) This unit is about 75% useless for vacuuming carpet. It will pick up surface debris, but that's it. If you want a proper vacuuming, you need to use a MUCH stronger vacuum. Even on Max suction mode, this does not do a deep cleaning (not even close), and the rotating brush becomes clogged with fibers very quickly due it's small diameter.

Conclusion: this unit really only does the job of eliminating routine light daily sweeping of floors. You will still need to get into corners with a broom. The dust bin needs emptying (very) frequently and the roller becomes clogged with lint quickly due to it's small diameter and width. The low height is great as it fits under most furniture. Daily automated program does not work properly.

Recommended? Yes, if it is on sale for about $100 (it frequently is). If I had paid $200, I would have been disappointed and may have returned it. Just keep your expectations realistic: this will sweep your hard floors and suck up the particles. That's it. If you have a lot of carpet, I would not recommend this unit.

text:
Not as cool as it sounds. I absolutely hate washing greasy pans, so being a bacon-aholic, I had to find an easier way to get crispy bacon on the table ASAP or sooner. I've been using a microwave safe plate, and zapping the bacon for about 5 ½ minutes on 70% power, but couldn't resist trying out this product, just because.

Comparative results:

Bacon a la plate:
1. Put a paper towel on the plate
2. Put the Bacon on the paper towel
3. Put another paper towel on top
4. Zap at 70% power for 5 1/2 minutes
5. Remove top paper towel
6. Put bacon in another plate - ready to eat
7. Discard greasy bottom paper towel
8. Allow plate to cool, add dishwashing liquid and water for a few minutes
9. Wash as usual

Bacon a la gadget
1. Put bacon on grooved side of gadget
2. Put a paper towel on top (I hate cleaning splatters off microwaves too)
3. Zap at 70% power for 7 minutes
4. Zap again depending how it comes out
5. Remove top paper towel
6. Put bacon in another plate - ready to eat
7. Reserve gunky stuff at bottom of gadget if you're going to use it later
8. Apply generous quantities of dishwashing liquid and hot water, leave gadget to soak
9. Wash off whatever comes off, then leave to soak longer
10. Rinse, and soak again
11. Realize that sticky stuff isn't coming off the sides of the ridges or the inside rim of the gadget
12. Apply more detergent and use brute force with a brush to the problem areas
13. Remember to brush both sides of each ridge
14. Wash again

Summary:

For bacon without all the mess
Just use the microwave
There's no real need to use a pan
Unless it's fat you crave

All you need's a dinner plate
And two thick Bounty sheets
The rendered fat helps it to cook
Providing crispy treats

This gadget works, make no mistake
But it's too hard to clean
Use the flip side as a plate
And zap some quick cuisine

Amanda Richards, December 20, 2007

Inexpensive, makes great coffee, great purchase!. UPDATE--4/14/17
I took two stars away since apparently I am experiencing what many other reviewers had mentioned when machine stopped working. You can hear the brewer heating the water, and then the pump kicks on. However, nothing comes out. I've used distilled water since Day 1. Honestly I was uber happy with this machine however disappointed that this seems to be a reoccurring issue with this model. But it did last 5 years so I shouldn't complain. Trying to decide if I should just by a Keurig this time or take a chance another model of this Mr.Coffee machine.

I got this as a pre Black Friday Sale for only $49.99 off of Amazon (regularly $89 or $99). I absolutely love it! Ton of my friends and family have a Keurig so I was hesitant in buying this versus a Keurig itself. I am so glad I didn't. This machine does the same trick as the regular Keruig machine. It comes with a reservoir like the traditional Keurig machine which is on the back top side versus on the side. The reservoir isn't a large as some of the Keurig's come with but it easily will make three large cups before needing to be refilled. This isn't a huge deal since I am the only one who drinks coffee in my house. I've had no problems with leaking. I use distilled water which I've been told helps keep the machine clean and running better. The other good thing and one of my main requirements was that the tray pulls out so i can fit a travel cup since I often take my coffee to go. Some of my travel mugs don't fit but the standard and the majority of mine do.

By the way, Keurig makes the Mr. Coffee Keurig machine so it's essentially the same machine just without all the bells and whistles. I am very pleased with my Mr.Coffee Keurig machine especially at the unbeatable price I got it at.

text:
Thoughts from a Gaggia Classic user. I’ve used a handful of espresso machines over the past few years ranging from cheap to expensive. This machine falls in the middle of both taste and price.
This machine is easy to use once you find the settings and pods you like, which took me about a month of trial and error. It heats up quickly and is pretty portable. You can get pretty consistent results, which is also nice. But the taste of the espresso and the milk foam simply don’t compare to my manual Gaggia Classic. I can get much better results from an extra 5 minutes with my Gaggia and quality espresso beans. Most pods I tried tasted bitter or weak until I found the single origin Rosabaya de Colombia, which has a decent flavor. I also struggled with the size of the Nespresso shots and the volume of milk. Whereas it’s simple to make a 16oz latte with a few tablespoons of espresso beans and my Gaggia, I found that using two Nespresso pods is a must to make a drink that size with the Creatista. I do one Ristretto shot and one Espresso shot to get enough espresso volume for a 16oz drink, but that makes the cost per drink upwards of $2. I was actually fairly impressed with the quality of the milk from the Creatista, but my main issue was the temperature. Even on its hottest setting the milk only got to 155 degrees. I typically manually froth my milk with my Gaggia to 160-170 degrees, which is about as hot as possible before giving it a burnt taste.
Overall I did find this machine superior to a Saeco super automatic machine I’ve tried that was three times as expensive. The display is simpler and the milk was better with this Creatista. If you can get over the cost of the pods and absolutely need to save another 5 minutes for each drink, this is the way to go. For me, I’d rather put in the extra time for a superior taste and lower cost.

text:
It's ok. Filter lasts about a month.. Physically, what I don't like about this pitcher is that the little "handle" they put in the lid so you can lift it off is pointless. The lid snaps in, and the little groove you're supposed to grip to lift it off isn't nearly sufficient. So you end up sticking your finger in the end where the water comes out, which I don't really care about but someone might if they're very concerned about germs.
Secondly, the pitcher really doesn't filter much at a time. Even if you fill it once and then refill it again, the second time the water takes so long to filter that it's just easier to do it one at a time.

I like the way the water tastes when it's filtered. It's not for everyone. It's like how it tastes when you buy bottled water that's been "mineralized for taste", which really confuses me since this supposed to filter out most things. But whatever--I still like the taste of it.

However, I actually bought this not to drink with but to water my plants and fill my humidifier. I have a few sensitive plants that demand distilled water, rain water, or super filtered water like this (living in the desert prevents me from collecting rain water). Since I don't have to water my plants a lot I'll probably keep using it for that.

I was using it to fill my humidifier each night to prevent the "white dust" that can settle around humidifiers and also prevent hard water build up inside it. It was certainly effective, but I had to use so much water just to fill up my humidifier each night that I used up the filter fairly quickly. I filled the pitcher probably 3 times per day for my humidifier, plus add in a few extra fills for watering my plants, and the filter lasted about a month.

After about five weeks of using my humidifier with this pitcher, my humidifier started smelling fishy, which I thought was strange considering I had just cleaned it the week before. I ended up cleaning my humidifier multiple times and refilling it thinking it was my humidifier at fault, but I was wrong. I finally thought to smell the water that was filtered from the pitcher and it was the water that was smelling fishy. So obviously the filter had run its course. I tested with the TDS meter just to see what the filtered water was at, and it read 088.

Considering these filters cost over $12 a piece, I am not going to continue to use the pitcher to fill my humidifier. I'll just deal with the hard water consequences. I will continue to use it for my plants and I'll probably start drinking it since I liked the taste. I'll be interested to see how long a filter last doing that.

text:
Fair To Middling For Me But Your Mileage May Vary. These bowls are solidly made and do work well in the microwave. As a 73 year old guy with some health problems though, I do have some issues with them. These issues may or may not apply to you.

The primary issue for me is that the stacked bowls are really stuck together hard. It takes quite a bit of effort for me to peel one bowl off the stack. If the bowls were any less durable, they would rip apart in the process. That's how hard I have to work at it. Prying an edge of a bowl up with a fingernail so I can grab it even hurts a bit.

A couple of other concerns turned out not to be issues at all, though a different hassle did pop up. I used a bowl to heat up a can of Campbell's Chunky Beef Stew. The bowl looked so shallow I wasn't sure it would hold the whole can's worth of stew but it did. If you've ever heated up any of Campbell's Chunky soups in a microwave, you know their soup has a tendency to bubble up and pop, splattering soup around your microwave. I wasn't sure the lid would stay on the bowl the first time I used it. Indeed, I had my fingers crossed that I wouldn't end up with a messy microwave. Well, the snap on lid stay firmly in place and my concern was groundless. That lid did raise another issue though. Taking the hot top off the bowl was another Ouch! to my fingertips.

text:
Pretty huge disappointment. I was pretty excited when I putting this vacuum together and reading the manual but... I’ve vacuumed my house once and was just more and more disappointed. I do want to say that I am the type of person that vacuums at least six days a week (sometimes twice a day, because toddlers) and I also detail with the vacuum at least every other day. I need a vacuum that does the job and does it efficiently. Maybe if you’re one of those people I’ve read about that vacuums once a week this would be ok for you. If you actually want a detailed clean, keep searching.

So let’s start with the good points:
I do like the idea of being able to take apart all of parts and wash them. And the idea of having a washable filter is great. It does work well on the floors, we have mostly wood and a few shorter pile rugs. The cord rewind is also a great feature (in theory) but I find that having to yank 25’ of cord out to be a little annoying already. The dusting accessory is nice and works well for house plants and shelves. And that’s it for the good parts... like I said, pretty huge disappointment.

Now the not so great parts (and there’s a lot of them, so buckle up and grab a snack):
The washable filter was originally what sold me on this particular vacuum but now that I’ve used it once (see pictures) I know I’m going to have to wash the filters at least once a week because hair and a ton of dirt gets directly to the filter. Which means ordering extra filters because they have to air dry and as I said before, I pretty much vacuum daily. I know understand WHY the whole vacuum needs to come apart for cleaning, hair gets stuck and wrapped around all over the ‘cyclone’ parts of the dirt cup. This vacuum doesn’t have a light! That’s my own fault for assuming it did, but I honestly didn’t know that modern vacuums didn’t just all have them. I find it incredibly annoying that I now have to switch on all the lights in every room to make sure I don’t miss anything. Even my super cheap stick vacuum has a light *facepalm*. Now let’s talk about these accessories... man o man what a HUGE letdown. Let’s start with this huge joke of an “extension” hose. It’s a foot long. That’s not much of an ‘extension’ in my book. I don’t know what kind of giant they have in the pictures but I’m 5’3” and I am now going to have to haul around a step stool to reach pretty much everything above my head. Using the crevice tool gives you another foot but you can’t use the other accessories on the end of it. And speaking of the crevice tool, if you’re using the extension hose there’s no where to put it so you have to carry it around while you use the other tools. The corner tool is the most awkward thing I have ever used and you have to stoop down into an awkward angle to use it. It’s just a weird design and not very user friendly at all. The ‘turbo pet eraser’ is another total letdown. Even the pressure from its own suction is enough to stop it completely. You have to have a very light touch while using it which means it’s actually pretty useless for getting the dog hair off the couch. It doesn’t work at all for pillows and couch covers because the fabric lifts up slightly and that’s enough to stop the brush head. Being that their whole advertisement scheme is based around being a pet friendly vacuum I’m left feeling pretty confused about that. The swivel feature is ok but kind of awkward to get used to and the roller can only fit about two inches under the furniture.

Overall, huge disappointment. I don’t know who they use for product testers that told them this thing was ready to go to market but they need to hire some people who have actually used a vacuum before; this thing is a disaster. I’m not sure if I’m going to go through the hassle of cleaning this thing to return it yet, but I’ll update if I do.

text:
The pillow of my dreams! - Upon Purchase; Time to replace - 13 months later. I have had every high priced pillow on the planet (yep, I'm a gullible gimmick geek) - memory foam, cooling gel, latex foam (those were the high priced ones back in the day), down, down alternative - and I've bought every el cheapo within driving distance. Nothing ever satisfied me. Low expectations in place, I ordered this pillow. Yes, the individually Thank You note inside is really, really nice; of course the THANK YOU! on the outside of the box makes you feel good about your purchase. But the true test is lying down, doing the flip-twist-flip of getting into the perfect position (I don't have just one sleeping position, I vary from night to night). I was amaZzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzed :) at how truly incredibly comfy this pillow sleeps. I will never, ever, ever buy another pillow of any brand or hype again. This is THE PILLOW.

************UPDATE: It is now September 2015 and for about a month I've wanted to replace this pillow. It doesn't look flat, but I lie down and no matter how much I punch it and flip it and fluff it, the second my head hits the very poofy looking pillow, it goes straight down to the bed like the pillow was full of nothing but air. The "5 stars" feelings of one year ago lasted a couple of months before the euphoria (and some of the pillows perfection) wore off. I would guess that every time I washed the pillow, per manufacturer instruction mind you, it lost a star. Five stars in August 2014 down to 1 star September 2015 averages to 3 stars overall, I'd say (the current rating I've given in this review). Do pillows this price really only have a one year life span?

text:
I expected Melt in my mouth roast, not so.. This is my first time with a Chard Vacuum Tumble Marinator, or any type of Marinator etc.
For the first time using this, I bought a chuck roast that is a less expensive cut of meat, needs marinating, tenderizing etc. to find out if this really works.
Thought I would get a melt in your mouth roasts after using this. Not so sure about that!

it comes with EASY Simple directions, Pictures, And a Phone number .
But the Red Function light never came on for me!!
Although I did not think that make a difference in the way this worked.

This is a large, 1 1/2 Gal. Tumbler, which holds allot. The chuck roast I put in was only 2 1/2 lbs and it looked small in this.
Comes with only 3 recipes ! (I expected more.)
1. Grilled shrimp and scallops kabobs.
2. Teriyaki chicken wing’s.
3. Lemon pepper pork chop marinade.

The tube is connect in a little compartment under where the tumbler sits to suck the Air out.
Connect the tube to the tumbler, Turn the knob to Vacuum. It automatically will show the time, and will shut off when the time counts down.
Before sucking the air out and tumbling, I put allot of seasoning on my Chuck roast, even used the tenderize thingie I have by hand to put holes in the meat..
Then Putting it into the Tumbler to suck the air to infuse the spices.
Also the meat expands to let the seasoning all in.
After I put it on the Tumbler mode, as I believe this tenderizes the meat.
I was making a chuck roast for the crockpot..
When the tumbling stopped, I then put the roast into a hot Pan to Sear it, with Olive oil, Red Wine, & sliced thick mushrooms.
Added more garlic.

Before putting the roast into the newer slow cooker, I put in a large trader joe container of beef broth, potatoes, carrots, celery, & onions, along with the
drippings, more seasonings, and everything that was inside the Sear pan. Along with my chuck roast into the slow cooker for 8 hours.

After 8 hours, we ate it for dinner. We where expecting this roast to melt in our mouth!! Both my Husband and I didn't think this lived up to its potential,
Of a melt in your mouth roast, with tons of seasoning, and it was even kind of dry tasting, not as tender as expected, although covered with liquid etc while cooking.!!

Just want to mention, I have made this type of roast before, but Not often, although putting it inside the oven instead of the crock pot, and not using this
tumbler, it has been before , a melt in your mouth awesome roast.

When people say they used this for chicken, and it was so tender. I have Never make a Chicken or any chicken parts that where Not Tender.
I usually only make chicken breasts, which is white meat and is dryer then other parts that are dark meat. Never have I made dry chick breasts.

This is my 3rd day of this left over cooked roast sitting in my Frig. And today it finally tastes tender, & juicy.
I never had to let a chuck roast marinate after cooking for 3 days for it to taste like it now does.
This is my reason for giving this 3 stars..(maybe should have been 2 stars !)

I’ll give the Chard Vacuum Tumble Marinator, another chance using a Brisket (another type of meat that needs tenderizing).
That said, before when I make a Brisket, slow cooking, I let it sit in my frig for 3 days before eating it.
But not a pot roast.

If it comes out more tasty, more tender, right after its cooked, I will be back with a update.

Polyester/cotton blend. Average softness compared to other poly blends. Loose threads after washing. First off do not mistake the description for actual 800 thread count "cotton". These are a blend - 55% cotton and 45% polyester to be exact. I am not a fan of this trend in bedding products of listing thread count in big, highlighted print on the label and then the tidbit about it being a blend in small print way below in the description. (Real 800 thread count cotton pillow cases usually cost three figures by the way)

For a polyester blend fabric, these pillow cases are of average quality. They are soft and feel ok against your face - they aren't scratchy or rough by any measure. Mine are standard size and our extra thick, shredded latex pillows fit without oozing out. After washing and drying them in a normal cycle with warm water and a set of sheets in a similar thread count blend, these pillow cases didn't shrink. However.... I do see a couple of little loose threads in the top, decorative hemstitch. So my bottom line is a one star deduction for silliness with phrasing and description and a one star deduction for overall quality versus value.

Works, but wastes 1/4 of the juice. Quiet and easily cleaned. Lots of parts. Let me just say up front, we aren't typically inclined to juice. I mean, we drink juice and we eat fruit, but we buy it ready made for many reasons. Not the least of which is convenience. This machine was my way of trying to do some stuff at home to save a bit of money and perhaps time when compared to the old hand juicers or buying it.

I was a little taken aback by the size of this machine - it's really big and next to our full size Kureig coffee machine it requires the same amount of counter space. That's a big footprint. Dragging it in and out of the pantry means handling several loose parts each time, but leaving it in place full time makes the kitchen look cluttered.

I have made several different juices with this and it handled everything easily. We have done orange and pineapple, mango and pineapple, papaya and grapefruit (gross), and just plain limes to mix with tequila later tonight. (Don't judge, who has time to squeeze a lime when there's drinking to be done?) You have to peel everything, remove the cores and the seeds and then you can put the fruit in the machine. Honestly, it's considerably less work to use an old hand juicer and less messy. Nonetheless, the juice tastes good - it does froth like crazy though. I'll give them credit, the motor is very quiet.

My issue here is the amount of wasted juice in the pulp catcher. Easily a quarter of the juice goes in the waste catcher rather your glass or pitcher. That irks me after all the work/time to clean, peel, cut and juice the fruit. Especially an entire pineapple! For our regular, daily consumption, this isn't worth the effort. I would rather just buy cut fruit and eat it on the go because it's faster, easier and I get all of it.

text:
Doesn't cool as well as window units with lower BTUs. If you are looking at the 12,000 or even 14,000 BTU ac units to cool larger spaces, be aware that these portable machines aren't quite as capable as traditional window units of the same BTU measurements. I don't really understand why that's the case, but it is. We have a 640sqft weekend cabin with two window units in it - one is 8,000 BTU and the other is 10,000. They keep the cabin a very comfortable 72 degrees all summer - even when it's 96 degrees outside with a heat index of 104. So that's my base point for comparing this portable, 12,000 BTU machine to our existing set up.

This machine loses out to window units in a small space because it takes up floor space and still needs to occupy window space for the vent hose. Yes, it can be relocated to a different room if needed, but you still have to have a free window there and a three prong outlet - this is on wheels, but it weighs the same as a window unit.

As to the actual cooling ability....well that depends on your room size and insulation and the weather. I'm in East Texas with both high heat and high humidity so our heat index (misery factor) has been 102 to 105 for the past week. I first used this machine in the cabin living area - about 350sqft and the upper limit of this unit's ability. I normally have the 10,000 BTU window in that area. This machine does cool, but nowhere as effectively as the window unit - it never felt quite as comfortable as normal and we ended up going back to the window unit on the second day.

We moved this to the bedroom next - roughly 275sqft and cooled very effectively by an 8,000 BTU window air conditioner. The Midea portable did cool just as well and the room stayed at 72 degrees for three days of use. However, it required removing a small chair to accommodate this air conditioner and that's a big negative for me. Every inch counts in a small space.

For us, the window units are definitely more comfortable/cooler in the cabin and they certainly take less space and trouble. Yeah, window ACs are ugly and a portable can't be seen outside, but that is less important than being cool to us. I don't care what it looks like if it's 98 degrees outside and 72 in the cabin. In the end, this machine will be relegated to an emergency back up only.

Historically, I dislike coffee - it always tastes bitter and burned to my palate unless it's mixed into one of those pricey store bought milkshake things. My husband though has always been a coffee guy so I chose this espresso machine primarily for his benefit. As it turns out, I'm completely hooked on it and use it multiple times a day.

This machine is really attractive and looks nice in our kitchen and it fits perfectly in the spot the old Kuerig used to live (that thing and the K- cups are outta here!) The initial setup took me about 40 minutes plus another 20 minutes reading the book cover to cover and breaking the machine down so I could fully understand how it works. Only then did I try making a beverage and I haven't stopped since in a week. Heck, I'm drinking a chocolate cappuccino as I type this.

The bean hopper holds a lot of coffee beans and feeds them directly into the grinder and brews a cup of magic. The used grounds fall into a container in tight little circles to be disposed of later. Making a coffee that even I will love has proven astonishingly simple and consistent and that amazes me. The milk steamer/frother thingy is the reason. It's best with ice cold milk straight out of the fridge - also, chocolate milk works in it and makes a chocolate latte to die for! I'm sure coffee afficianados already know that trick, but as a first timer it was the best little surprise. (We drink only real, natural whole cow milk - no fake vegetable oil "milk like" stuff, so I can't speak to how the steamer works there.)

You can select the brew strength and type of drink you want from a super strong little espresso or cafe crema, to a mid strength full size cappuccino with a very light, fluffy foam that you can swirl a design in. My husband and my mother are very happy with the traditional versions and both prefer a very strong coffee from a dark roast bean. I'm incredibly happy with the light roast and a low medium strength with hot milk and a dash of sugar. It makes great tasting coffee with simple, generic beans too - so far we've been using an Amazon Basics dark roast bean and a light roast Columbian bean under the Wally world label, both costing less for two pounds of beans than a latte at a coffee shop.

You definitely want to keep an empty mug under the spouts when your made coffee is finished - the machine does a quick rinse off the milk nozzle and before it goes into sleep mode, it rinses the coffee nozzle. Because it's actually fresh grinding the beans, it's loud as it starts your drink - you aren't going to sneak around making cappuccino at 5am, you better plan on sharing with whomever you wake up. Bottom line is that the Picobaristo is reasonably easy to get the hang of for a first time user and it is simple to operate even half asleep at 5:30am.

Burned one loaf, two others were fine. Moves a lot while kneading. Not as good as my older maker. I have a very inexpensive ( under forty dollars) Sunbeam bread maker that's happily produced good bread a couple of times a week for almost four years. It's larger than this Hamilton Beach machine and significantly heavier. This machine is prettier with it's stainless and black color - it matches my big appliances.

As for the actual bread making, I think this one has it's good points, but in the end, my old machine is better overall. This one does have a handy little tool for removing the paddle from the fresh loaf and the included flour cup and tea/table spoon.

I made a simple, buttermilk sandwich loaf first and bacon cheddar bread the second time. Both are our standard, go-to breads here and I typically make one of each every week. The buttermilk bread on the light crust setting came out dense, moist and a little chewy as it should. The basic cycle here is actually about 14 minutes longer than with my old Sunbeam maker. The bacon cheddar bread on a medium crust setting didn't fare so well. Halfway through the bake cycle, smoke billowed out of the lid and I had to unplug the entire thing - the uncooked, slightly blackened bread went in the trash. There was nothing in the bottom of the machine to cause the burn, so I don't know what the problem was. I have since made another buttermilk bread without a repeat of the smoke.

My real issue with this bread maker is that it bounces, wobbles and walks all over the counters as it mixes and kneads the dough. This could present a serious safety problem if you have limited counter space or set it too close to the edge. It moves about 8 inches every time I use it. My old machine literally has never bounced or shifted one iota. So, because of the bounce and the smoke issue, I will only use this again as an emergency back up to my older bread maker.

Terrible milk frothed design/process. I have to say that if I hadn't been using my Saeco automatic espresso machine for two years, I would probably love this machine. However, in a side by side comparison for two weeks, I much prefer the Saeco for several reasons. If I had to replace my Saeco, it wouldn't be with this DeLonghi.

This machine is bigger, far more complicated and delicate than my other espresso machine and it is significantly slower. This unit does hold more water, but fewer beans. This one does have a specific setting for iced brew, but it tastes exactly the same as when I just make a lungo over ice in the Saeco - so nothing special there.

In side by side use, the DeLonghi is significantly quieter than the Saeco and that's a plus early in the morning. However, it literally took seven minutes to brew a simple lungo from start to finish - my other machine had already finished and I was drinking that coffee before this one finished. I will say the DeLonghi does offer a finer grind and a slightly smoother finish using the same beans, but both coffees tasted good.

My primary complaint is the ridiculous way this machine does milk for a cappuccino or latte. It's manual and you have to provide your own container. The wand goes directly in the milk and you have to lift and twist your container to get all the milk steamed/frothed. Then you have to pour it into your pre-made coffee and stir... Ummmm no. That's not automatic in any way shape or form. My Saeco has its own pitcher and the machine forces the milk through the steamer and directly into the cup and then the coffee is added - you get a hot cup of coffee with hot milk and real foam all at the same time. That one thing is reason enough to put this machine in the closet as an emergency back up in the event our good Saeco dies.

[[VIDEOID:92802fd7aaa86092f4cb77c6f2a66f96]] We got this AFMAT steamer trough Vine, but we didn't like it at all, and ended up paying for the PurSteam. The main issue is the convoluted trigger button system. With your thumb, you have to slide up a child lock tab, then press down on the button. You see if you get close to an oven knob, you don't want to press too hard, the steam will bounce off the knob, you need to lighten your press. They don't give you enough magnets.... THE GOOD:
--------------
* Universally sized so it should work with most home washer and dryers.
* Keeps clothing from falling off the back.

THE BAD:
------------
* Not enough magnets. Sure they're earth magnets, but they're small and spaced too far apart. There needs to be more of them. I think the bottom should be one long strip of earth magnet. Actually, I bet you that it doesn't have to be earth magnets. It can be standard tape magnet, but if it's continuous and covers the entire bottom rails, I bet you that would be stronger than small earth magnets that are spaced far a apart.
* Moves easily. You can flick it with your fingers and the entire wall wobbles. Again, this is due to not having enough magnets.
* For best strength, DO NOT connect the middle. It just so happens that in my situation, I need to split the middle anyway because there is a shelf bracket in the way. But even if I didn't have this shelf bracket, I would still split the middle. The reason is because if you connect the entire thing, then the entire width will be much shorter than the entire width of both your washer and dryer. The top of washer and dryers machines will also vary in design, some have raised edges, which makes it tricky to make sure all the brackets are connected on the same raised level. So I just split it up. This way, it's easier to manipulate how and where I want the brackets to stick. This may sound confusing, but you'll see once you buy it.

Overall, this is a so-so product. Every day we're fixing the brackets cause it gets moved a lot. So it's doing it's job in terms of not letting your socks fall off the edges, but it is not sturdy. I will install extra earth magnets when I have the time. I'll go 3-Stars.

It's not height adjustable, so I don't get the point of this.... JAN. 15, 2022 UPDATE:
---------------------------
* Since my review, they've removed the stock photo I mentioned that I thought was misleading, that made me think the box was height adjustable. This is a nice box. Probably more suited for your children's room than for the garage. I just think paying a higher price for the collapsing feature doesn't make sense. I thought the price was tied to the "adjustable" feature. There is no such feature, and the stock photo has been removed.

ORGINAL REVIEW:
----------------------

THE GOOD:
--------------
* Spacious 42L at about 17.5 x 13 x 13.
* Stackable.. that's it, that's all that's good.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Their 6th stock photo mislead me. I thought this box was height adjustable. I got it because I thought if I had any issues with clearance, I can just lower the height of the box. That's not the case at all. That stock photo is just showing you how thin it is when it's shipped to you.
* Lots of parts... you got the main frame, you got the bottom plate, you got a bumper guard that goes over the frame to give it stability, then lastly, you got the lid. When I was putting it together, I was asking myself, "What's the point of all this if it's not adjustable? Why not just get a sturdy one piece box?"
* All these moving parts, all this foldability design does not benefit you at all. It only benefits the manufacture because it allows them to save space when they ship them out. Think about that... the only time you'll fold this up, is if you don't use it. But why are you buying a box if you're not going to use it? I thought this thing was adjustable. I was thinking, wow, what a cool invention! LOL! It turns out, it's not. The fact that it folds benefits nobody but the company that sells it. Or, those rare occasions where you need to take a bunch of these boxes to some location. Realistically, how many are you going to buy at $42 a pop? If you're buying 5 to 10, and you need to transport them somewhere, yeah I get the benefit, you need to pack flat. Oh wait, I just described the company's scenario, right? LOL! They are selling hundreds or thousands of units, they need to pack flat to save on shipping!
* Price, these are not cheap. They are charging us more for a nifty design that benefits them, not us. Think about that. LOL!

In my garage, there is no point to all these moving parts, which are all points of potential failure. There are more economical solutions that are one piece (two with lid), and more sturdy than this box. BTW, I've seen the baskets that collapses at Costco, but I don't think twice about them because they don't cost $42 a pop. I don't understand the point of this design, if you have to charge consumers more for it because really, it doesn't benefit them. So I think 3 stars is generous.

text:
High quality, but usefulness? maybe not so much .... I've owned a couple of other "handheld" spiral cutters and currently own the larger hand-crank Paderno spiral cutter. So I've had some experience with these devices and eat spiral "noodles" a couple of times a week.

First, if you've never owned a spiral cutter and you're thinking of trying one, this might be a good choice. Much better design than most handheld units, easier to set up and operate, etc. It's a bit pricier than the cheaper ones, but the better design makes it worth it. It handles softer veggies (zucchini, cucumbers) fairly well, but you do have to be careful of the diameter. Still, it might be a good intro to the sport/art of cutting veggie noodles

If, however, you have experienced the pleasures of a well designed "crank" style spiral cutter, you will be very disappointed in this. The size makes it difficult to do larger veggies (sweet potatoes, rutabagas, etc.) without serious paring down to fit the small opening. Also the effort needed to twist the holder with the veggie is not trivial. As someone with shoulder and hand arthritis, I had difficulty with this.

Even if you've never used a spiral cutter, it might be worth it to add a few bucks to the cost of this and go for the other Paderno hand crank cutter. It's so much easier to use and you'll have more options (with less waste) of veggies to cut. I've been using the larger Paderno cutter a couple of times a week now for about 6 months, and it's going strong with no sign of any failure. Paderno makes quality stuff, and this little cutter appears to fit my quality expectations for the brand. Pity it's not more useful/easier to use.

I'm giving this an "It's OK" rating -- 3 stars. Just not that useful for me; might be a good intro to veggie noodles for a novice.

text:
Inexpensive Duvet with Minor Quality Issues. This duvet came pretty quickly after ordering. It's dyed a nice consistent color and is very soft (although microfiber, so if you sweat a lot, use a cotton top sheet under this). It came in simple, disposable, shrink-wrap packaging (unlike bedding which comes in a thick, plastic, zippered pouch so you can wash and store linens without them getting dusty, though, and typically purchase bedding that comes in this manner for this reason). The duvet cover is very thin, and appeared wrinkle-free, with clear buttons at one end and ties at each corner (on the inside), so you can tie the duvet to it.

As soon I'd opened it up, I'd decided to put it on the new, white down comforter that I had also purchased here on Amazon. After turning the duvet cover inside out and all four corners were tied to the comforter, I turned it all inside out (if you haven't learned to roll up a duvet and cover to put it on easier, check out a video on YouTube) and buttoned it up.

It looks pretty, but I had to sew part of the duvet cover, as the factory managed to miss a six inch portion at the top of the duvet cover that wasn't sewn. I was annoyed that right out of the gate there was an issue with quality, but I knew it wouldn't be an heirloom piece with the low thread count and the price I'd paid. The comforter was not that expensive, and I didn't have a lot of money to spend on a cover, but I just wanted to save the duvet from getting soiled with regular use. I think it will do the job but I suggest anyone buying this brand to do a quick quality check when your item comes in, so you can return it within the window. I'd not contacted the manufacturer because I don't have the time or energy to send it back, so I docked stars for a lack of quality control, instead.

Not bad, not great, merely MEH. I wanted to give this teapot five stars. But there’s some real issues with it. Some may think these are minor issues, but to me they were great.

First, the good things. It is pretty; it maintains the heat of the tea, if you preheat it; the handle is large enough so even someone with large hands can pick it up.

The problems are all associated with the lid. If you keep the infuser in the pot the whole time you’re drinking the tea, the lid is tight. However, if you keep the infuser in the pot for the entire time that you’re drinking the tea, the tea becomes bitter. And in my case very better. So, I do not use the infuser. text:
Not what it’s cracked up to be.. I’ve owned a Bunn coffeemaker for years that was on its last leg. I decided to venture out and try something different and after watching YouTube reviews for 4 hours and reading reviews, I decided to take the plunge and buy this maker as it had the highest rated in the price range I was looking at I love my coffee and am by far not a coffee “connoisseur”. I just love a good strong cup of coffee to get my day going. I’m a Foldgers kind of gal occasionally who occasionally steps into the wild side and buys Starbucks coffee (already ground) and maybe some flavored coffee here and there.
So let’s get to the “beans” of this. The maker itself is flimsy. As most pots do, it “sticks” to the counter as you pull it out to fill the water. The first time I pulled it out, I pulled the whole top section off the machine. Yes, heart attack ensued thinking I broke it. After wrestling with it and getting it back together, I push a washcloth under it for easier gliding. One would think for that amount of $$ it wouldn’t come apart quite so easy and wouldn’t be plastic. You’re unable to put the top of the carafe on while the filter is still in place. It’s not a huge thing, but beware of steam burns when you’re dumping the hot grounds.
Next, when you dump the water from the thermos carafe into the maker, be prepared to have water all over your counter. As there isn’t a pour spout in the carafe it makes a huge mess. A pot of coffee is done in about 6 minutes which is nice. No waiting for 10-12 minutes. The coffee itself is, well a cup of coffee. I didn’t notice a huge difference from my Bunn, and I even ventured out and bought some fine ground Genevalia. The coffee is good and hot, which is where you can tell a significant difference from a Bunn. My Bunn temped at 165 and this one temps at 200 after a cycle completed. The thermos carafe does keep it warm, but not for an extended amount of time. Maybe an hour tops, but make sure you get the lid to the carafe on immediately when it’s done or a lot of heat is lost quickly. Now for my very least favorite thing about this maker. It states it’s a 8 cup coffee maker, which is true. BUT, one very grave point I breezed by in my research is the 8 cups is actually 8 5oz cups. Very few people I know, including myself, drink out of a 5oz coffee cup. Most coffee mugs are 10oz mugs, which means you get 4 regular sized cups of coffee from one carafe. This isn’t ideal when you’re jetting around getting ready for work and have to stop to make another pot.
To sum this up, I’m disappointed with this purchase and had I not have thrown the box away when I got it, I’d send it back and buy another Bunn.

text:
Disappointing! Not as expected. I like OXO products, but, for the first time, I am disappointed in an OXO product. (1) If you look at the bottom of the chopper, you will see that the transparent cup fits into a black rubber seal that also serves as the base of the chopper. I have noticed that some commenters have written that this seal or gasket can be removed, but, if so, my hands are not strong enough to remove it. I can't get it off at all and previously assumed (before reading the comments) that it was permanently affixed to the transparent cup. The seal comes-up about 1/8" to form the base. I discovered that chopped bits of food were wedged down between the seal and sides of the transparent cup. These will not rinse out. If your hands are not strong enough to remove the seal (if it can be removed), you will have to figure-out a way to remove the trapped food either with a slender kitchen utensil or with your fingernail. (Sorry, I know it's gross!) I don't know whether or not I received a particularly badly made chopper or whether this is a design flaw. NOTE: See UPDATE below. (2) It takes a good amount of effort and time to chop the food. Even though the transparent cup shows that it will hold 1 cup, in reality you can only chop about 1/4 cup and then will need to empty the transparent cup. If you don't, the chopping blade does not have enough vertical space to operate well. It will take a fair amount of force to chop manually, so this gift is not ideal for a senior or anyone with limited mobility.

Like all OXO products, it is well made and seems sturdy. The blade did a good job of chopping the vegetables. As one commenter noted, however, you will have to chop the vegetables into small chunks to fit them inside the small transparent cup.

I plan to use the chopper (if I don't toss it) for celery, shallots, and similar kinds of items.

I have never owned a chopper before and so can't comment about this chopper in comparison to similar products. I do like the OXO brand, however, and was surprised to discover that this item has been disappointing.

UPDATE: Since writing the comment above, I discovered that the base with black rubber seal is easy to remove if I run it under very hot water and then punch the base lightly to push it out of the transparent cup. « Show Less
