text: OKAY BLENDER FOR THE PRICE; A COUPLE NICE FEATURES, ATTRACTIVE. The first thing I noticed about this blender is that the blending cup seemed very short and it seemed like it wouldn't hold as much as my other blender which hold 5 cups and is taller.  This holds 6 cups and the reason it can hold more without as much height is that the blending cup is bigger around.  The cup is nice thick glass and is one of the better features of the blender.  The blender is attractive, with a silver colored base, but the base doesn't appear to be metal, but more like a pastic coated with silver material.  Seems powerful enough to do most jobs, but probably more of a light duty blender.  The wattage is 550, which seemed like a lot, but in checking other blenders some are in the 700 to 750 watt range and I'm sure they go higher as well.  The gasket is not a separate piece which is a real plus.  I suppose 12 speeds is nice, but how many speeds do you really need?  I don't even use the 8 speeds on my old blender.  Instructions say that to blend hot liquids you need to leave the cover loose and cover it with a towel.  Seems like a hassle when other blenders will handle hot liquids without doing anything special.  When using it with hot food and liquids, you'll now have a dirty towel to wash.  I usually don't read what other reviewers say, as I don't want to be influenced one way or another, but I noticed several who had a problem with the plastic blender cup base breaking easily.  With a two year warranty and the low price of this blender, you probably can't go wrong, but it's not fun to wait for replacement parts.  You also have to search for your receipt and whatever else might be required for warranty service or return.  If I wanted a quality power tool, I wouldn't think twice about selecting Black & Decker as they make good power tools.  Are their small appliances as good?  Probably not.  I recommend buying a blender from a manufacturer who has a long history of making quality blenders.  Apparently Black & Decker acquired General Electric's small appliance division in 1984, so it would seem they have over 20 years of experience, but contrast this with the Waring Blender company that has been making blenders since the 1930's.  There are so many blenders available in the market and there probably isn't a lot of difference amongst them until you start getting up into higher prices.  Seems like there is a lot of competition in the market for blenders and this is a low end competitor is good enough for people who don't use a blender every day.  If you are constantly using your blender (like for a daily smoothie), select something more rugged that costs more.  This is by no means a food processor; I think it is wise to spend more and get a combo food processor and blender, which should serve your needs longer.  This is probably good for a cheap, attractive gift, especially for someone just starting out who really needs a blender.

text: Nice Set of Heavy Duty Glass Containers with covers; better than plastic for food storage. Nothing beats glass for food storage.  Plastic containers always seem to warp or take on odors or colors of the food.  Also heating in plastic is less than ideal.  This is a nice variety of different sized glass containers.  The plastic covers seem to fit tightly.  Note that there are 4 pieces that I guess you would call dessert cups with a decorative border along the top and these do NOT come with covers.  I thought maybe the similar size dish covers would work, but they don't fit.  You only really want to use those 4 for something that you would finish eating at one time.  If you have food left in them, you would have to transfer it to a container with a cover or cover with plastic wrap.  The set is heavy thick glass and seem less likely to break if you drop them than thinner, cheaper glass containers.  I didn't drop one to find out if it would break.  Pyrex is a trusted name in glassware and I have some older Pyrex that has been in use for years.  One reviewer says that new Pyrex does not use the same glass formula and that these are more prone to breakage especially when subjecting them to temperature variations.  Some common sense here probably would easily prevent any problem.  Even if the glass can withstand it, generally it is not a good idea to take a container of food that has been heated and stick it in the refrigerator right away.  Let it cool to room temperature first and then refrigerate.  Also if you take something out of the refrigerator, don't heat it up right away; again give it some time to reach room temperature.  Those precautions are smart to use with any containers, but especially glass and should prevent any potential shattering problems.  The full set is quite heavy and difficult to lift, which is the main downside if you want to transfer the whole set from one place to another.  Of course once you take it from the box, you probably wouldn't be moving the whole set at once.  Just be aware that if you want to use this as a gift, it is heavy and difficult to move.  If you are a strong, young person you probably can manage it okay, but you wouldn't want to carry it very far.  One other thing I didn't like was the color of the covers.  In addition to red, it would have been nice to have a couple other colors such as green, blue or yellow, just for some variety and potentially color coding your food items.  Not a big deal, but the red seemed a little garish.  The marked down price that Amazon is currently offering seems very reasonable for a set like this.  A few single pieces of quality glassware could cost you as much as this whole set.  Remember those that in addition to the 4 dessert cups, you really only get 12 other pieces of glassware, as the 12 covers count as part of the total 28 pieces.

GOOD QUALITY CHAIR FOR GENERAL OFFICE USE. This is a good basic office chair. First the good:
- seems to be good quality
- easy to assemble
- back of the chair is comfortable and tilts back for extra comfort
- arms are adjustable slightly from side to side, so you can make the clearance a little wider if needed
- seat adjusts up and down to several heights with lever, just like most adjustable chairs
- attractive

Now the not so good:
- arms are not adjustable up and down, but seem to be a good height (arms could be removed if you didn't want them)
- arms are not padded, but reasonably comfortable; could get uncomfortable after a while
- seat angle seemed to push me forward somewhat, so I had to keep re-adjusting myself to stay at the back of the chair

I am using this chair at the dining room table for eating and playing cards for a couple of hours. The only problem is that the arms are at a height that they keep hitting the edge of the table. If I lower the chair so that the arms fit under the table, the seat is too low. I had one problem with this chair, but not especially the fault of the chair. I was sitting in it and assembling something in front of me that required some bending. I bent over a little far and the chair skidded out from under me and I fell and hurt myself. It should be noted that care needs to be taken when using a chair with casters, like this one, on tile. It moves very easy and can be a hazard if you aren't careful. Not the fault of this chair, as this will be true of any chair with wheels. Not a chair for klutzes, especially if using on a hard floor. As a final word, I would say this chair is comfortable for a couple of hours, but might not be so much for more time than that. Price of the chair seems reasonable for the quality, but you might find an equal quality chair on sale for less.

text: Easy to Assemble; replaces box spring and base. I needed a new bed (mattress and box springs).  When I saw this was available, I ordered it right away, as it eliminates the need for the box springs.  It's a base and mattress foundation all in one, so you can put your mattress right on top of this.  It appears to be well made and strong enough to hold a mattress and the weight of two sleepers.  Another Zinus bed frame I had did not look very strong and was poor quality.  This one, however, seems to be much better quality.  Assembly was very easy.  You can almost do it alone, but it helps to have someone hold some of the pieces while you put in the screws.  Two of us put it together in under 1/2 hour.  The illustrated assembly instructions are easy to understand.  You do not need any tools, as it comes with an Allen wrench, which is the only tool you need to assemble it.  The screws went in easily and seemed to fit well and were tight.  Nice clearance underneath, so you can clean under it.  My current bed has to be moved to clean under it, which is a major job.  There are mounting holes in the two end pieces so you can add a headboard and foot-board if you wish (not included).  That would keep the mattress from sliding around, as I have some concern that it might, as there is nothing to keep it in place other than gravity.  Of course on any bed, the mattress just sits on the box spring anyway, with nothing to secure it, so this is no different.  I have yet to sleep on it, but I am sure it will be fine. text: Nice full featured coffee maker; much larger and taller than expected. I got this Coffee Maker to replace an older one that lacked two important features that this has:  programming when you want the brewing to start and automatic shutoff.  This also has a nice feature that lets you pour a cup of coffee before it has completed brewing; you have 25 seconds to put the carafe back in before the filter basket overflows.  The machine also shuts off any drips any time you remove the carafe.  My old coffee maker would just drip coffee on to the heating element.  This coffee maker keeps the coffee warm for 2 hours before automatic shutoff.  It would seem to me that for a roughly $100 coffee maker, it should include a feature to set how long you want the coffee kept warm, rather than just a per-determined 2 hour shutoff.  You can always manually turn it off of course or unplug it.  You also can start it manually with a brew button.  If you don't want to use the timer or if you want to override the timer, you can do that with the manual button.  Of course with a built in timer, you have a clock displayed on the control panel, but that's one more thing to set the time on when there is a power failure.  A battery backup for the clock would also have been a nice feature that's not included.  One nice feature that is included is an optional carbon filter inside the tank that makes the coffee taste better.  Also note that this comes with a permanent filter brew basket, negating the need to buy paper coffee filters.  Another feature is a "small batch" button when you are only brewing 2 to 4 cups, but I couldn't see the point of it since it will still brew 12 cups of you fill the coffee maker with 12 cups of water.  Overall it's a nice coffee maker with some good features.  So what's wrong with it?  It's a bit pricey.  It is also very large; a big hulking machine.  My old coffee maker that makes the same 12 cups is only 11 inches high.  This is a whopping 15 1/2 inches tall.  It is also 9 inches wide; my old one is only 6 1/2 inches wide.  Both my old one and this one are 10 inches deep.  Of course a little extra size is needed for the digital control panel.  If you are using this on a counter with cupboards above make sure you have at least a 16 inch clearance as this is the "incredible hulk" of coffee makers.  I knocked one star off my otherwise 5-star rating for the huge size.

text: Excellent for moving & storage & floods!. I purchased these for multiple reasons. The main reason was that I was moving. I was moving bc my apt kept flooding.  Luckily having been through other floods I generally store all my stuff in plastic containers anyways. Sadly a couple of my vintage Singer’s in wooden boxes had been left out during the last move & the last flood got them moldy & ruined them.  I am a bibliophile & these bags held not only huge stacks of my hardcover books, but my 40 pound Singer sewing machines. I also carried hundreds of pounds of yarn (50 per bag) and thousands of pounds of quilting fabric during my move.  It held up to paints, plants, garden pits, & pretty much anything I threw at it. I even put my pots & pans in these bags.  While I still thought they were a bit pricey I did buy some on sale & I think I bought 18 total that I was able to pack & take to my new place & unload & go pack again. Tho I now intend to leave some of my yarn in them as it’s waterproof.  Tho I intend to place it on a top shelf just to be on the safe side. Lol. Not one bag ripped, tore, or had an issue so far that I am aware of tho I have not checked them over very well. And I had no issues with the zippers tho I am positive that I packed several bags well over the weight limit on accident bc I was trying to keep certain quilting fabrics together for a quilt project.  I’ve bought some real duds on Amazon, but this was not one of them. This has by far been one of my better purchases & I’ve told my kids that are planning to move to buy the bags too bc it is just so much easier imo.  I literally used a taxi to move half my stuff (disabled & don’t drive) & was able to fold the bags back down to how they arrived after unpacking to take them back to be packed again.  I also made little tags and used color coded handkerchiefs I hung on the handles so I knew which room the bags went in or knew what was in them without having to open them in the wrong room once I moved.  It saved time.  I live in an apt & these bags take up a lot less space than the massive sterling & Rubbermaid hard sided plastic totes I normally use for moving & craft storage.  I still have them & use them, but storing them is a challenge.  Also, the bags fit under my zinus/spa sensations type elevated platform bed. It’s a frame amazon sells & you buy your own mattress. Normally I can fit 8 hard sided tubs under my bed (queen bed), but I’m limited by the height of the tubs. The bags fit or I’m able to squish to fit if I overfill them which is nice.  Depending on how full you pack them you can get 4-8. They are different sizes than my plastic tubs tho.  I only wish I had stumbled across these bags years ago given how many times I’ve moved. Lol.

Tough on garlic, easy on arthritic hands. As someone who frequently cooks Mediterranean menus heavy on fresh garlic, the Oxo garlic press is a chef's best friend. Rubber-coated handles make gripping and squeezing more user friendly than all-metal garlic presses, and cleanup is a snap. Like most garlic presses, you can choose to pre-peel the garlic before pressing it, but you'll still need to clean the press in-between uses. It comes with a built-in cleaner, and usually a quick run under the tap will remove most debris. The garlic comes out as more of a paste than it would if you were to chop it, and is a much faster way to add flavor to soups, salads, and more with minimal effort.

I've owned my Oxo press for years and haven't had any of the problems that other reviewers mentioned (handles falling off, hinge breaking). I do usually hand-wash, and I don't prepeel my garlic, and the press is still going strong 2+ years later. Perhaps my press was subject to different quality control standards: I bought it several years ago and had it stored until recently.

A big step up from bargain toasters.... I spent years in graduate school making do with a five-dollar toaster. After moving into my first home, I decided it was definitely worth the splurge to upgrade to a toaster worthy of my homemade breads. I was given a KitchenAid 2-Slice Toaster as a housewarming gift, and the love affair hasn't stopped since.

The KitchenAid performs all the usual functions of a toaster, with many choices from light to dark, but also features a bagel setting designed to toast the cut side of bagels more thoroughly than the crust, and a "warm" setting to keep your toast warm without turning it into charcoal.

The toaster has a nice solid construction, with heavy-duty metal parts and a well-built crumb tray that slides out, eliminating the mess from trapdoor-style crumb trays found on cheaper toasters.

Since I bake my own bread, I tend to slice it thickly, and it turns out perfectly in the KitchenAid. But beware: if you use store-bought (or other thinly sliced) breads, the extra-wide slots mean that your toast may turn out very light and need an extra toasting since the bread is held further away from the heating elements. But it performs beautifully on bagels, English muffins, and thick slices of bread. Whoever said that man cannot live by bread alone failed to toast it in a KitchenAid toaster!

Pros
Toasts evenly, bagels come out perfectly done

Cons
Sometimes frozen breads require extra toasting, warming feature ineffective

text: My Krups Power XL6 is my new best friend and favourite toy.. I received it as a surprise gift this past holiday season, and I am completely impressed. My Krups XL6 Combi blender came with a food processor attachment, making it even more versatile. Authentic Italian espresso at an affordable price. After many happy (and dare I say, naive) years with our DeLonghi Caffe Espresso, it was time to replace our old workhorse. Having just spent the summer in Spain, where no bar is complete without the standard superautomatic Gaggia espresso maker, I decided that truly great espresso was a daily necessity. I was tired of incompetent teenagers / college students who work at local coffee shops mangling something as simple as a cappuccino (one part espresso, one part milk, one part foam) into a milk-drowned latte with no foam.

I wanted something in the range of $200, with a dependable track record and plenty of power to spare. I waded through a myriad of reviews for the Gaggia Carezza, hailed as a champion of its class, but read a number of negative reviews concerning design shortcomings.

Enter the Gaggia Evolution. Although the Gaggia Carezza and Evolution share the same innards, the Evolution boasts several improvements in design. With its 17.5 bar pump and high wattage, dual element boiler, the Gaggia Evolution is ready to brew in around 5-10 minutes (I always prime the boiler first).

Design improvements over the Carezza include: a larger drip tray, a cup warmer (although, as usual, it's more effective to preheat your cups by filling them with hot water, which can be done during priming), anti-vibration mounts (once primed, the Gaggia Evolution is nearly whisper-quiet), and a brass commercial portafilter (the spouts on the Carezza were changed to plastic). My Evolution came with the Perfect Crema device (which is supposed to go under the single filter basket in order to create additional pressure/allow a coarser grind), but having read numerous negative reviews of the ineffective device, I simply left it in the box with the packing material.

Five stars for the instruction manuals and CD-ROM: the Gaggia Evolution comes with not one, but two instruction manuals: one from the manufacturer (Gaggia), and one from the North American importer (Importika). The Importika manual is intuitive, easy to read and injected with coffee humor, although the Evolution is not among the Gaggia models listed in the Appendix. The included CD-ROM walks you through setup in the form of short movies and narration, along with more advanced tips and techniques for coffee connoisseurs. We put our laptop on the kitchen table and followed along after unpacking our new Gaggia (thankfully, nothing was broken in the mail, as happened to several Gaggia Carezza owners). Although the manual hinted that your first coffee might not be potable, we'd followed various tips online (prime your new machine several times to remove any residue and plastic-y taste), and our first espresso was laden with crema. The Turbo Frother attachment made the creamiest, densest microfoam I have ever seen-it looked more like meringue (hint: use skim milk for best results). My only complaint would be the cheapness of the included coffee scoop, and you definitely want to invest in a better tamp for maximum extraction (the Gaggia takes a 58 mm tamp at a recommended 30 pounds of pressure).

If you're not in the market to buy a $200-300 grinder (Rancilio Rocky or Gaggia 8002 MDF Burr Grinder) to go with your new Gaggia, Illy makes a delicious, dependable espresso grind, available in tins (decaf, too) or Pods. The Evolution is Pod-ready, simply use the single shot basket with the portafilter. Tip: "classic" double shots should take around 20-25 seconds to extract.

The Evolution is a steal for the current price, since it contains the same innards as other Gaggias in the $400-500 range. Although it runs around $50-100 more than the Carezza, I appreciated the design improvements, stylish lines (I have a Tuscan kitchen with hand-painted ceramics and terra cotta tiles and was afraid that the "modern" styling would stand out, but the Evolution is much more traditional-looking and unobtrusive than the Carezza), and performance. (Note: the Evolution is also available in an all-silver model, but it will set you back another $50. The black model features a black base and sides and a silver front and silver drip tray.)

Excellent for the espresso novice or connoisseur, easy to use and clean, and it makes better espresso than some $500-1,000 machines I've tried!

Stops spills, but the design could use some improving. I first saw the Kuhn Rikon Kochblume at Sur La Table, and was intrigued. One of the messiest things to clean up is a pot that's boiled over, so I was interested to see if it would work.

I read other reviews and followed the following tips, and it worked as advertised:

* First, this is made for pots with a diameter of 5.5 - 9". Any larger, and the spill stopper will slide into the pot / not catch overflow that extends beyond the diameter of the pot!!

* Two words: steam burns. Other reviewers advise not checking the pasta for doneness, as there is a LOT of steam built up under the spill stopper, which forms a seal to keep water from boiling out. Also, if you lift the spill stopper to test for doneness, there's the potential to dump starch and boiling water all over the stovetop. I also don't recommend lifting up only one side to check; again, steam burns, ouch! Common sense applies: don't lean directly over the pot when removing the spill stopper to check / drain pasta.

I tried boiling a LOT of dried pasta in a small pot to see if I could get it to boil over: nope. The foam bubbled up through the petals and crept for several inches beyond the pot's edges (still several inches away from the edge of the silicone) but the sturdy silicone prevented the foam from running over or water to escape between the edge of the pot and the spill stopper.

The little "flower" in the center is held in place by a plastic clip; it can be removed for cleaning or to create a splatter shield according to the package directions. My only complaint here is that the "petals" are very thin, flimsy silicone that would be easy to accidentally rip (and these are what keep the starchy foam from overflowing). Some reviewers have had the petals rip off and bond with glass, so I would wash the spill stopper separately. The starchy buildup can also be a pain to remove; thank goodness it's dishwasher safe!

Verdict: Yes, it works. Definitely invest in the large, which fits 5.5-9" diameter pots (including my Italian pasta pot).

Great for tile / wood floors, attachment tools could be better.... I needed something to vacuum up my tiled kitchen floor and linoleum bathroom floor, and the Electrolux Ergorapido fits the bill nicely. Setup was a breeze; the unit should be charged up to 24 hours before use. This 2-in-1 stick vac consists of a canister vac that snaps into the stick vac (the canister vac contains the filter). The storage base also holds a crevice tool and "dusting brush" (more on that in a moment). The Brushrollclean Technology allows the brush to self-clean, which is a great feature.

There are numerous features about the Electrolux that I really liked; the swivel head is great at reaching under the fridge and oven or along baseboards. I also liked that there are lights along the leading edge, so you can see if you've gotten everything. One off-putting thing was that upon the first several uses, both the canister vac and stic vac smelled strongly of Band-aids (must be from the plastic or components). I was also not crazy about the cheap feel of the charging cable cord, which seems brittle and lightweight. The charging stand and footprint are fairly small (you can also wall-mount the stand).

After using the stick vac in the kitchen and bathroom, next I tried using the canister vac in the car, and here is where I ran into problems with the attachment. I had an old Black and Decker canister vac that I used to use, and it had a brush that snapped directly onto the vacuum nozzle. The Electrolux requires that you first snap on the crevice tool (which is a good 8"-9") and then the brush; there is no way to attach the brush directly. Also, the dusting brush's bristles are MUCH softer than my old vac, so the bristles bent easily (I was using it to clean the leather seats). However, it did a good job at cleaning floormats and leather seats, so I'm happy. The reservoir holds a LOT, and the Electrolux definitely did a much better job at picking up dirt / debris than my old vacuum.

Overall there are many pluses for the Electorlux EL2021A; I loved the swivel head, the lights, the fact it is easy to store and maneuver (I can't comment on battery life as I've only used the vacuum for short runs so far). The two-year warranty was also a plus. My only critique is that I wished different tools were included, but otherwise it does a great job on tile / wood floors and as a hand vac.

Blendtec Classic 575. For several years, I made do with a fairly inexpensive, retro-styled Oster blender...it did a decent (not great) job at blending (I frequently enlisted it to help with my award-winning San Antonio cajeta flan cake, which took second place at our first-ever squadron baking contest), however it was not so great at crushing ice for drinks.

Three years ago, I finally splurged and bought myself a Vitamix Pro Heritage 750. I was amazed at its ability to churn out smoothies, milkshakes, nut butters, flours, as well as piping hot soups. I loved the presets and the easy cleanup (add a drop or two of dishsoap and warm water just covering the blade assembly.).

My best friend is a manager at Bed Bath and Beyond and swore by her Blendtec. So when I had the opportunity to compare the Vitamix and Blendtec side by side, I was interested in putting the Blendtec through its paces.

The exterior on the unit I received is a white plastic that will fit in well with pretty much any decor. Also, Blendtecs have a digital control panel vs. the sliders / dials on older Vitamix Models, which took a little getting used to.

The 575 has four presets and the included instruction manual (which also has Spanish instructions) includes a few starter recipes.

Noise-wise, I found this a bit louder than the Vitamix due to the more powerful motor (1,575 watts). I liked that the blender blades are blunted compared to the "ninja star" design on most blenders that result in lacerations when cleaning / drying. Also, the Blendtec does not require a tamper due to the design of the WildSide blender jar (I appreciated the paper insert that illustrates the correct stacking order for ingredients!). It does a great job with smoothies (I haven't tried the other presets yet), no chunks of unblended ingredients and I love that it has an 8-year warranty and is made in the United States. (If you want to see it in action, there's a hilarious series of Blendtec promo videos called "Will it Blend?" where they put items like iPhones (don't try this at home!!) into a Blendtec and pulverize them...)

If you are looking to add a high-performance blender to your kitchen (and it is an investment that really does pay for itself!), you would do well to consider the Blendtec Classic 575 Blender.

Handy Little Appliance to Have In The Kitchen. The Tiger 5 1/2 cup rice cooker has performed flawlessly on everything we've tried. Not only did it produce excellent results on various kinds of rice (white rice, brown rice, multigrain rice, wild rice) but it's also been good for cooking porridge (steel cut oats in our case) and even hard-boiled eggs). Nothing we've used it for has turned out less than perfect.

This cooker even has a synchro-cooking mode which allows you to cook concurrently using the included cook plate. I have not used this mode yet but have already picked out several fairly simple recipes which I plan to attempt in the near future.

Since cooking with a rice cooker is a new experience for me, I appreciated the Tiger operating instructions included with the unit. It is very thorough and contains helpful sections including basic how-to information and troubleshooting. Also included with this rice cooker is a cookbook which includes 25 recipes, many of which are for synchro-cooking. To help you explore the world of rice cooker cooking, I strongly recommend purchasing a basic rice cooker cookbook to accompany the included material. This will assist in unlocking the full potential of your rice cooker, a consistent and dependable option in preparing one-pot meals, side dishes, etc. You will find that the Tiger rice cooker is a surprisingly versatile addition to the kitchen, especially considering how little counter space it requires. It is easy to use and clean-up is easy, too.

If you have the time and patience, you could prepare many of the same things on your stove top that this rice cooker does, thereby saving the cost of purchasing one. The question to consider is whether the Tiger 5 1/2 cup rice cooker is worth its price in order to have the convenience of being able to set it to cook perfect rice while you do other things. That convenience is worth a lot to me, and I'm guessing to many other people as well.

I keep my Asobu at my desk at work; you simply add any standard-grind drip coffee to the metal mesh filter, pour water over in a circular motion, and let steep. The mesh is fine enough prevent coffee granules from slipping through and falling into the coffee, which is nice. It's important to add the coffee grounds in stages; you add the first third, wet thoroughly, then continue to add grounds and water, finally pouring cold filtered water over the top.

When the coffee is finished brewing in 12-24 hours depending on how strong you like it (you can pop it into the fridge overnight), you simply press the button to drain into the insulated carafe (which comes with a spillproof lid), add ice, and you're good to go!

The bad: It's rather large (technically it IS portable, but this is not something you could transport easily while in a car, etc.; as others have mentioned, it does tend to leak and there are issues with the fine mesh filter). As with any homemade cold brew, it's not fast...but you get several servings from one carafe, and over the long run the Asobu has saved me a lot of money as an iced coldbrew from a major coffee chain can easily run $4 a cup.

It's a great solution if you you have the time and counter / fridge space to make ahead, but does require some advance planning.

Durable AND beautiful. I'm a dedicated (amateur) home baker who bakes several times a week, and there are two final frontiers still unknown to me: yeast breads and fancy layer cakes. Unlike simple Bundt cakes or single-layer cakes, layer cakes are composed of two (usually three) or more layers of carefully arranged cakes glued together with some sort of icing (fudge, chocolate, buttercream, etc.). If you're trying to assemble and frost a layer cake on a stationary cake stand, it's much harder to achieve a smooth finish when frosting the outside as you have to keep manually turning the stand, which can cause the cake to wobble and become crooked as you're trying to ice it.

I decided to take the plunge and invest in an Ateco revolving cake stand. It has a very solid cast iron base with a lovely vintage white finish and a 1/8" aluminum top. It also comes with a nonstick pad that can either be used under the stand to keep it anchored to the countertop, or on top of the stand to stabilize your layer cake.

There are several different companies (Magic Line, Wilton, Ateco) that manufacture similar cast iron revolving cake stands, but I chose Ateco based on prior brand purchases (cake decorating equipment) and the fact that the stand is constructed in the USA (other than Nordicware, Libbey and Anchor, it's increasingly difficult to find items made in-country!). It came highly recommended by America's Test Kitchen as well. The packaging was very secure and I received my stand without any scratches or dents.

This is a hefty stand, both in weight and cost, that will stand up to a lifetime of use and is well worth the investment if you're a professional baker, pastry chef, or a home cook who makes a lot of layer cakes. If you're just a casual layer cake baker, consider Ateco's US-made plastic revolving stand for 2/3 less. But this is the rare piece of kitchen equipment that is not only useful, but aesthetically pleasing as well; I leave mine displayed on my baker's rack when not in use.

If you're looking for starter ideas for layer cakes, some of my favorites are [[ASIN:1580085628 The Pastry Queen: Royally Good Recipes from the Texas Hill Country's Rather Sweet Bakery & Cafe]] by Rebecca Rather (Texas-inspired layer cakes and baked goods), [[ASIN:1584797215 Baked: New Frontiers in Baking]][[ASIN:0609604538 Kaffeehaus: Exquisite Desserts from the Classic Cafés of Vienna, Budapest, and Prague]] (Matt Lewis and Renato Poliafito), and Kaffeehaus (Rick Rodgers).

Total gamechanger, even if you own other Zojirushi rice cookers. Even though I could have purchased the same model locally in Japan for much less, I made the choice to purchase a Zojirushi made for the US market (120 v). This was important to me for a number of reasons: not only for the convenience of having English menus and documentation, but also the fact that rice cookers in Japan run on 100v, and unless used with a step-down transformer, can burn out much more quickly on US voltage. Since I make rice almost daily, I wanted a rice cooker that would work in both Japan as well as the US and one that offered a number of functions.

So when I had the chance to test out Zojirushi’s updated Umami model (NL-GAC10) I jumped at the chance. Not only does it have settings like jasmine, quick jasmine, sushi, mixed rice and brown rice, but it also has a setting just for quinoa and Zojirushi’s exclusive umami mode, which soaks the rice longer to produce a moist, fluffy rice. The Umami model also comes with a steamer basket, making it easy to quickly steam veggies, fish, or eggs and create a complete meal.

I love the fact that it has settings not found on other rice cookers, particularly the GABA brown rice setting. GABA brown rice is sprouted brown rice that is much higher in gamma-aminobutyric acid and fiber and is said to be more easily digestible. It requires a long soaking and heating process (using the GABA Brown Rice setting activates the GABA in the brown rice by soaking it for two hours at 104°F before cooking), but the resulting rice is fluffy, moist, and flavorful. And those looking for traditional breakfast options like congee or okayu will find special modes for those as well. Another unique feature is the “slow cook” setting, which lets you make soups and stews right in the rice cooker, and the rewarming feature to bring cooked rice to the perfect serving temperature.

The timer function makes it easy to have perfect rice ready and waiting in the morning to make bento boxes, or have dinner ready when you get home (takikomi gohan is a favorite in my household).

I put the Umami Micom through its paces making several batches of umami, sushi rice, GABA brown rice, mixed rice, and basmati rice cooked on the jasmine setting, as well as following Zojirushi’s recipe for slow cooker minestrone and caprese rice salad. You’ll also find a wealth of other great recipes on their website at https://www.zojirushi.com/app/recipe/rice-cookers and Just One Cookbook’s website.

The Zojirushi Umami micom rice cooker is incredibly versatile; whether you’re shopping for your first Japanese rice cooker or an appliance that can handle a variety of tasks from steaming to slow cooking to making perfect white, brown, jasmine, and sushi rice, the Zojirushi Umami Micom (available in 5.5 and 10-cup size) is the perfect all-in-one appliance, especially if your family eats rice or grains daily.

Avoid cheap imitations...Bodum Chambord is the *original* French press. As the Bodum box says, "Give up bad coffee for good!". The French press has been around for decades in Europe, an easy alternative to pricier espresso machines and Italian stovetop Moka pots. Bodum is the foremost name in quality French press pots (styles include the Chambord, Brazil, Kenya, and Eileen), and the Chambord is the flagship line, available in 3, 4, 8, and 12 cups.

*NOTE*: the "cups" listed on the box refers to the *European* 4-oz. espresso cup, not a 6- or 8-oz. U.S. cup, so the U.S. measurements are: 3 cup = 1.5 U.S. (12 oz.), 4 cup = 2 U.S. (16 oz.), 8 cup = 4 U.S. (32 oz.) and 12 cup = 6 U.S. (48 oz.).

The Chambord press is simple, efficient, and stylish, and most importantly, solidly constructed. Made of a borosilicate beaker and chromed brass with a molded handle, with proper care, it will last for years. Parts are dishwasher safe, but I prefer to hand wash. There are a number of cheap, made-in-China imposters to be found in discount kitchen stores, but these do not compare to the Portuguese-made originals.

Because the French press takes a coarser grind and doesn't use a paper filter, this allows the coffee's oils and essences to be extracted 100% for a full-bodied, intense brew reminiscent of espresso. Unflavoured dark roasts yield the best results.

To make the perfect cup of French press coffee, use one Bodum scoop (2 Tbsp, included) per 4-oz. cup of coffee (coarse grind ONLY). Add hot, not boiling water, stir with a chopstick or plastic spoon, and put the lid on (with the filter pulled to the top in the closed position). Do not press down. Allow grounds to steep for four minutes. Leaving the spout in the closed position, grasp the handle firmly with the spout pointed away from you. Using the flat of your hand, push the handle down *slowly and evenly* (if you shove the handle down, there is a chance that scalding coffee may shoot out!) until the filter is at the bottom of the carafe. Pour and enjoy. Be sure to thoroughly clean the filter after each use. Replacement carafes and filter parts are available from Bodum's website, [...] Say goodbye to stale, bland coffee; take the plunge (bad French press pun intended!) with Bodum's Chambord and see what you've been missing!

Bakery-quality bread at home. A family member purchased the Cuisinart CBK 200 Convection Bread Maker and loved its ease of use and excellent results. After a recent move to San Antonio, I was given my own Cuisinart Bread Maker as a gift, and make a minimum of two loaves every week.

The Cuisinart CBK 200 is easy to use: simply remove the pan, attach the kneading paddle, and add ingredients in the order listed. You can choose between a 1, 1 ½, and 2 pound loaf, and from 16 dough settings, including dough, quick bread/cake, gluten-free, low-carb, whole wheat, artisan, sweet bread, and even jam (jam recipes are included). Three crust settings (light, medium, and dark) are available depending on your taste. Cleanup is a breeze: after the loaf has been removed from the pan, simple wash the pan and paddle in hot soapy water.

The included recipe booklet is more than adequate as a starting point for novice bread bakers, and includes detailed instructions on how to measure ingredients, the correct temperature of liquids, and troubleshooting tips. Recipes cover a wide range: sweet breads such as Panettone (Italian Christmas loaf), sour cream chocolate tea loaf, and carrot cake, savory breads (Gruyere and walnut wheat, blue cheese and olive), and artisan loaves finished in the oven. I have tried close to a dozen of the included recipes, and all turned out marvelously. The book also includes a nice selection of low-carb and gluten-free breads.

The only downside is the inability to reset options once "start" has been pushed. The unit has a 15-minute power failure memory, but if you wait 15 minutes to reset your yeast will likely not rise properly since the liquids will have cooled. Another tip is that breads which contain a lot of sugar (such as sweet bread) are more likely to have a dark crust, so you may want to choose the lightest crust setting instead of medium as suggested in the included recipe booklet.

The Cuisinart Bread Maker comes with a generous 3-year warranty, so be sure to register online. This is a wonderful gift for the home baker, with easy, reliable results that rival loaves from your local bakery.

Very good basic bread maker. My very first bread maker was the similar-looking Cuisinart CBK-100, which was a faithful workhorse until the dough bucket fell apart out of warranty (and a replacement would have cost as much as a new bread maker).

I loved the various modes (sweet bread, gluten-free, jam, artisan, dough mode only) and used it several times a week.

So when I had the opportunity to review the Hamilton Beach Premium Dough & Bread Maker Machine with Auto Fruit and Nut Dispenser, 2 lb. Loaf Capacity, I was eager to get back into breadmaking. The Hamilton Beach offers three different loaf sizes (1, 1.5 and 2 pounds) and crust settings, 14 presets for bread, dough, jam and cake, automatic fruit and nut dispenser, and a dishwasher-safe pan. One feature I really liked not present on my other bread makers is the "rise" setting that is meant for use with frozen bread dough. I would have liked to see more sample recipes in the included booklet (I still have my older Cuisinart manual as it has about 40 recipes that all work like a charm sized for 1, 1.5 and 2-pound loaves!).

In looks and setup, it is very similar to the Cuisinart (including the viewing window on top). Do be very careful to always use oven mitts when handling the pan because it gets HOT (as does the outside of the machine; be sure not to push it up against a wall as the convection fan needs air to circulate).

Similar to my Cuisinart, though, I'm not thrilled about the baking performance (I prefer to use the machine on dough mode and finish baking in the oven) as I find bread machines tend to bake unevenly (and never get as crispy as I like for artisan doughs, which I always finish in the oven).

But for everyday use and for kneading and mixing doughs, the Hamilton Beach is more than up to the task and I look forward to experimenting with bread machine recipes from some of my other cookbooks.

text: Fry Daddy. Listen, frying food is NOT a healthy choice, but as a treat? I think it's ok - I wanted something simple and easy to use - this Fry Daddy is truly that. A couple of notes - I have a good silicone splatter guard - I recommend getting one - just really controls the splatter that naturally happens, especially if you're frying frozen foods (with water/ice crystals).  Also note that you cannot put the plastic lid back on the fryer until it has completely cooled.  Be careful where you place the fryer to use as it does get hot on the bottom and be mindful of what may become grease splattered as you are using it to avoid tragedy.  I like it.  Happy to use it. text: Impressive for the price. I've had this popper for a couple of weeks, wanted to wait until I'd used it to review.  It arrived in quickly (I have Prime) and in good condition with a very well reinforced double cardboard box.  There is a minor assembly to do, the glass front doors need to be attached, the bottom screen tray and the kettle.  It came with a non-slotted aluminum scoop (I traded for one with holes for the kernals to fall through that I already had) a pinch of fairly large popcorn bags (NOT flat bottomed, so you can't fill them and stand them up - I bought some small, flat bottomed bags) some unmarked scoops and measuring spoons. NO sample packets of popcorn were included.  I purchased some 8 oz Great Northern Popcorn premixed bags to try. The directions for use that came with the machine and the on premixed popcorn bags was different and ultimately I used the directions that came with the machine.  After using it, I think either way would have worked fine.  Basically, heat the oil and kettle up first, then add the popcorn and salt works best.  It made plenty for 4 of us to eat full (small) bags of popcorn with a couple of refills. There were a lot of unpopped kernals, but I think I may not have heated the oil long enough. The 8 oz kit was done within about 3 minutes. The popcorn was very tasty... but maybe a little tough. I am going to experiment with my own popcorn and oil to see if this is different.  I estimate for our family gatherings I will need to pop 3 or 4  8 oz popcorn kits. I also plan to try using coconut oil that doesn't have all the yellow dye in it. Further, I purchased a set of 12 different popcorn seasonings for fun. Just sprinkle in the bags after loading them, not in the machine. I was dreading the cleanup, but honestly, it really wasn't bad at all.  I do recommend wiping out after each use to avoid harder to clean build up.  All in all, I am very happy with this suprisingly well made machine. It's glass and metal with some plastic and is fairly heavy.  There is a manufacture date on the base of the machine that says April 2014.  I will quickly update my review if we have any issues.

text: Bed bug oven. So far, so good.  We haven't had bed bugs, but know people who have.  Plus we travel with fair frequency and they are everywhere.  The bug oven is an insurance policy. My husband is handy - he can build things and do electrical stuff... he built a simple stand for the oven to sit on - not too high so you can lift suitcases and such into it but keeps it off the epoxied floor of our garage.  An "x" shape plywood stand with a top that is big enough for the ovens to sit on opposite sides. Your oven comes with 4 yoga blocks (foam bricks) to make sure the heated air is circulating and you get a sensor to put inside your bags - and then a sensor reader that sits outside the oven - allowing you to see what the temp inside is without opening the oven.  We have been able to heat things thoroughly through within  about 2 or 3 hours.  The heat kills all stages.  Haven't seen a single one... but I feel much better about taking things into the house AFTER the oven.  You do need to plug in heaters into plugs on separate circuits - or you will pop breakers every time... they also include a heavy duty 25' ft extension cord to make the transition.  We leave ours up in order to be more apt to use it - but like I said, we travel quite a lot.  So far so good , however,  I never hesitate to update my reviews should new info seem useful.

text: medium size egg coddler. So these are "medium size" and will hold 2 eggs - traditionally you coddle one egg in a smaller cup, but this will work.  Remember "coddled" eggs are NOT poached.  They are delicious alternative to poaching or other water cooking.  Rub the inside of the coddler with generous amount of softened butter or olive oil.  Seal the lid top and place in boiling water pan (water below the lip of the coddler).  Cook per your desired temperature.  Around 10 minutes if you prefer a hard cooked egg - or around 5 if you like a more loose yolk - even less if you like a very runny yolk..  Scoop out with a small spoon or dip with toast sticks.  It's a real treat.  These coddlers are very nice because they are clear glass and  go right into the dishwasher. The metal clasps securely hold the lid on which is very important (you don't want water in the coddle) - and are easy to remove with a towel (they will be hot when they come out of the boiling water).  The only negative I will report is that the add clearly states it is a set of two.  I only got one.  Had a "replacement" order placed and again only got one. text: Stainless steel double wall tumblers. These work great.  I purchased two... I keep water in one all day - rinse it out-while it's drying thoroughly I use the other... to help prevent rusting that does occur sometimes at the seams of these types of thermal tumblers. NONE so far with these - but as I said, I careful clean and use them. NO DISHWASHER - even it says they can.  I will say I have filled one with ice added a little water and then used out of a hot car ALL day.  There was still ice in the glass after more than 9 hours.  That is impressive to me.  They did come with little cloth sleeves.. I was initially confused by this as these tumbles are not supposed to "sweat"... and they do not sweat!  So... I am thinking the sleeves are an "easy" grip thing and also helps it to be stable in cup holder.  The plastic tops have rubber like gaskets and a slide opening.  The slide doesn't really stop water from pouring out - but it does slow the process. text:
Brentwood Home 13" Gel HD Memory Foam Mattress. I bought one of these for the guest room and then went back and ordered another for my own bed, replacing a really mediocre mattress at a second home. I own a ridiculously expensive Tempurpedic mattress with an adjustable base, so I had pretty tall expectations. I can say with great confidence that this mattress stands up to that comparison. They arrived carefully shrink wrapped, for shipping. They pop up very quickly after unwrapping. NOTE: They are fairly heavy so I recommend two people to lift. Even the shipping box says "TEAM LIFT" on it. It says 13" but mine is a bit more that that.... Typical of quality memory foam. It would be nice if they sewed on some handles (like Tempur) for easier handling... but even that won't lower my rating... The cover is soft and beautiful. There is a very slight odor... but I am very sensitive and it didn't bother me. After one week, I don't notice any odor. If you are not familiar with a memory foam mattress... it can be very firm or even very soft... I consider this mattress to be medium to medium firm.. of course this is MY personal opinion. It properly softens and recovers for memory foam. My husband and I agree that we toss and turn way less on a memory foam mattress than a regular mattress. My husband sleeps a bit warmer than I do, but doesn't think that this mattress makes him too warm. Another plus, this mattress is made in the USA. The price point and quality to me is every bit as good as the stupidly high cost Tempur mattresses. I always update my reviews if new information would be helpful. Honestly, if you're considering a memory foam mattress, this one, at this price point is certainly worth consideration. NOTE: I am NOT compensated for my reviews in ANY way.
UPDATE: 3/28/2016.... After a few weeks of use, I am still convinced these mattresses were one the best investments I've made. Also remember that 25 YEAR warranty! Might be the last mattress I even have to buy. Literally... and... just an FYI.... Memory foam mattress are NOT friendly to a whole host of critters, dust mites, bedbugs, etc...... in case that is one of your fears. Again, the mattress is definitely not a "soft" mattress... most quality memory foam mattresses are medium firm at best. Tempur does carry a softer, cushier mattress in their "cloud" line... but honestly for the CRAZY stupid price of the Tempur, I'll stick with this Brentwood mattress. You can purchase a more plush mattress cover if you're interested in a fluffier feel.... Even if you purchase an adjustable base from another vendor, you're still just a fraction of the price of Tempur queen size at about $5000.00 or more... depending on your line choice and base.....Thank goodness we have choices in the US of A !!!

They both pump a very economical measure of soap - sometimes I pump twice to get a more hearty amount - but I think it will help in not wasting the hand soap and the dish soap.  They also come with cute wooden tags and a silicone coaster (white) to prevent slipping - which will happen once there is water around the bottle.  I chose not to use the wooden tags. I know which soap is which and I think the tags would quickly become kinda yucky.  But that's just my opinion.  They are not overly tall ( about 6 or 7" tall)or wide at the bottom (I'm thinking about 3 1/2 to 4" in circumference) - meaning they don't take up much space and look so much tidier.  Being glass, they are easily rinsed off.  I think if you really wanted to clean them in the dishwasher top rack you could - but they are easily enough washed by hand.  Overall, I am very pleased so far.  Having said that, I never hesitate to update my reviews should new info seem useful.

text:
Marathon analog desk alarm clock. If you need or like a real clock as opposed to your cell phone, as I do, this is THE perfect one. Runs on two AA batteries... it's a sweep hand so it's COMPLETELY silent which is a big deal to me. Plus there is a setting that back lights the face of the clock in the dark... just a little bit... enough to see if you wake up and want to know the time, but NOT enough to keep you awake because it's a beacon. It's a nice size... a lot of color options.. I chose the black case with the white face. It's about 4"x4" just eyeballing it. For me the perfect size to set on my night stand and I can see it when I don't have my contacts in. Honestly, I've gone through a couple recently TRYING to find the perfect clock and this one is it for me. Arrived quickly (I have prime) and in good condition. As always, if there are any issues, I will not hesitate to update my review. Further I do NOT receive any compensation for my reviews.
UPDATE: 2-15-2016 Just a quick update... Still LOVING this clock... I wanted to mention that the soft light that lights the face when it's dark is an amberish (soft yellow)... so it doesn't keep you awake like a bright white or blue hue. Honestly, it's the best clock I've had in years.
UPDATE: 3-31-2016... I purchased 2 more of these for other bedrooms.... they are just the best. In size and function... in design. They run silently. The are just bright enough at night, but not so bright they keep you up. It's soft, amber glow - a color that doesn't disrupt sleep like bright white or blue hues... I remain a devoted fan.
UPDATE: 4-19-2016... Ok... I purchased yet another for travel... BUT... I accidently ordered the "black" face with white print... I do NOT think it is as easy to read as the white face with black print.... It's still the perfect, silent running clock - plenty noisy when you want it to be for an alarm... BUT I do not recommend the black face and white print. Just a personal opinion...

Honestly it wasn't a tragedy because I was just putting in a ramen (after I soaked in some spicy lo sodium soy) - but if you were going to fry it it wouldn't be nice and crisp looking edges with the cracked pieces.  So - mind the pressure - go slow - if you're really into perfectly pressed tofu.  It takes time to REALLY press - like 60 minutes or so and you'll want to twist just a little every 10 mins or so.  Easily went into the dishwasher for cleaning.  I will say that twisting it to clean it, or put the tofu in, or adjust for storage also takes a few minutes.  I decided to store slightly open. I've only used a couple of times- and not had any cracking or other disappointments with the press itself so far. Great little vacuum for small jobs, price is a bit high.. Update: The more I use it the more I love it. I still don't like the way it empties but it is a powerful little vacuum so I will up it to 4 stars.

This is a nice little vacuum for quick clean up. It has a spinning brush or you can press the button to have it not spin. It vacuums well and is easy to empty but more hands on than other vacuums. You have to remove the handheld vac, open it, remove the filter and the inside cone to completely empty. It's not a push button like a Dyson or Rowenta cordless vacuum. With the Dyson and Rowenta, you just remove dirt cups from the vacuum, push a button and the dirt empties from the bottom.

I'm not sure how long the filter will last. It appears to be a paper filter.

I love that it is rechargeable. I haven't timed how long it stays charged yet. Will do that soon. It's not hard to connect to recharge but the Dyson is much easier. You just slip it into the wall mounted bracket and it recharges. With the B&D, you have to plug it in before you hang it onto the wall mount. Not a huge deal but worth mentioning.

The reason for only 3 stars is the price. My opinion is, this is just a handheld vacuum on a stick with a brush. Not worth over $100. I would go with the Rowenta or the Dyson for power and convenience. If the price would be lower, I would only give 4 stars due to the emptying process.

I checked out reviews of quite a few stick vacuums before this purchase. I couldn't believe how expensive some of them are. I decided to take a chance and ordered one for myself. It came in a day, in good shape. It was easy enough to put together. It's lightweight, pretty quiet and easy to empty. The head swivels and gets into corners. I don't think it would last long with an aggressive house cleaner. The swivel head might not be strong enough to be slammed into walls or corners. I haven't yet used the other tools it came with, yet. The suction is very good and I used it mostly on the low setting, but I don't have pets or children and my floors are laminate or have low pile carpeting so I can't say how it would be on thick carpets, etc. The high power just shortens the battery life. I was happy that the suction was strong enough to pick up crumbs, etc. and didn't just fling bits out the other side. The battery lasted about 30-40 minutes, enough to do my whole apartment with good suction. It takes about 4 hrs to charge the battery, so I wanted to purchase an extra battery to have charged and on hand. It's $33...a third of the vacuum cost...Wow!

I haven't used it enough to comment on the quality (how long it lasts, parts break, or suction weakens) but so far, I'm very happy with the vacuum. It serves its purpose well. If need be, down the line, I'll add to or change this review.

This chair is a BEAST!. Upon opening the box, we were impressed with the fortitude of each part - it is very weighted and similar to chrome (at least in finish and heaviness). This is much akin to a Chevy Bel Air vs modern cars as far as comparing it to previous desk chairs which I have owned, it is clearly built to last and sustain a lot of weight and use.

I left the assembly to my partner, who said that other than the heaviness of the parts when wrangling them, was incredibly easy. The instructions do suggest that you make use of the box it arrived in to help prop parts as you screw them together because you will need the support, and he did this and said it made it much more manageable.

I walked into the room once it was finished and gaped at how large this chair is. In fact, I felt like a child climbing into the seat, my legs left to dangle and I kept scooting back further and further (You can lower it with the pneumatic lift so that your feet touch the ground, it also has nice rounding of the seat front to prevent your back of knee circulation from being cut off!). The seat is HUGE both front to back and side to side and can comfortably accommodate larger bodies. I never had so much room in desk chair seat before! But the solidity of this chair is what has me in awe - I feel safe and comfortable in it. No teetering, no awkward tilting, nothing bad! The only plastic parts to the structure of the chair is the pneumatic lift handle and the wheels (which seem more like high impact plastic and dense), so no fear of parts breaking under weight strain and movement.

I would say that the only downside to this chair is now my partner is jealous of it and we're going to have to get him one of his own so he that doesn't pilfer mine. Excellent desk chair, an easy 5 stars

We have slept so peacefully in ways I cannot express (we both usually wake up throughout the night, but haven't with this thing on us). The weight does not smother, it's soothing. Comforting. We did not experience overheating, even with an additional blanket and our sheet sandwiching us in.

I highly recommend the blanket for anyone, for anywhere in your home.
